When I became the first executive director of the country’s oldest statewide tobacco control coalition in 1999, conversations were already underway about how Colorado should spend its share of funds distributed to states from the landmark tobacco settlement.
Unsurprisingly, interest groups from across our state came forward to argue why their priorities deserved a portion of Colorado’s share of settlement dollars. While policymakers considered how to spend the state’s portion of the settlement, my job was to go to communities across Colorado and explain why a significant portion of the funds should go to tobacco prevention and education programs, rather than unrelated, even if deserving, programs.
I’ve been thinking about that experience in the wake of the $18 billion legal settlement between almost all states and social media giant Meta. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser and others have noted parallels between the two. As states make plans, it’s worth reflecting on lessons learned from the tobacco settlement nearly three decades ago.
The 1998 tobacco settlement numbers were monumental: States would receive $200 billion to resolve lawsuits against Big Tobacco for its history of harm. States had to determine where their share of the money should go.
Before 1999, I had only a basic understanding of what led up to the tobacco settlement — beyond the now-historic clips of tobacco industry executives testifying under oath before the U.S. Congress and saying, one after another, that they believed nicotine was not addictive.
I did know, however, that the tobacco settlement would be a game-changer, and in many ways, it was. It directed hundreds of millions of dollars to states to fund programs. It restricted tobacco marketing that targeted youth, like the cartoon character Joe Camel, and funded the Truth Initiative, a tobacco prevention organization that still exists.
It also led to the release of millions of industry documents, which provided explicit detail about the companies’ exploitative efforts to addict various populations and fight public health protections. The easily searchable online database offered a treasure trove of material for researchers and journalists, confirming some of our worst suspicions about the industry.
But in other areas, the tobacco settlement fell short of its goals. These missteps offer insights for the Meta settlement spending.
For one, the tobacco settlement didn’t specify how states could spend the funds, so it was open season for anyone searching for funding for unrelated projects. While some states spent money to fill budget holes or (in the Carolinas) even subsidize tobacco producers, Colorado appropriated most of its money to health-related programs, though almost all have no direct nexus to tobacco.
As a result, according to the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, tobacco prevention is chronically shortchanged to this day: In fiscal year 2026, “total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue the states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.”
Meanwhile, the shape-shifting tobacco industry continued to innovate new methods to hook new and young users, with teen-friendly sweet and fruity flavors leading to a surge in teen vaping and, more recently, highly potent oral nicotine products like Zyn. From the legislature to city halls, tobacco industry lobbyists and dollars remain omnipresent today, fighting efforts to restrict flavored products, for example.
On the positive side, the tobacco settlement spurred prevention programs to work together to address tobacco and other public health issues. The early 2000s brought a strong focus on educating communities about the harms of secondhand smoke and successful policies to restrict smoking in public places.
There were also successful campaigns in Colorado and other states to increase the price of tobacco, a policy move proven to reduce smoking in adults and youth and fund prevention and cessation efforts. These and other efforts built on the experience and trust forged through decades of policy battles, including the tobacco settlement, even if the dollars weren’t involved.
If I could speak directly to the people now in charge of distributing funds from the Meta settlement, I’d like to offer them three pieces of advice.
First, don’t rely on the industry to protect youth when its business model depends on hooking new customers and keeping them using their product. As the saying goes, fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Whether it’s nicotine or algorithms, the result is the same: reinforcing a behavior that is harmful to users. Policymakers and advocates need to promote laws and regulations to protect youth, following the evidence of what’s proven to halt cycles of addiction.
Second, use settlement dollars to emphasize youth prevention and support initiatives with generation-spanning benefits. While addressing immediate harm is key, research related to substance use, for example, shows long-term prevention provides the highest return on investment.
Finally, consider that the movement to protect kids from these harms is just beginning and will require constant evolution and vigilance to adapt to emerging threats. Since the tobacco industry promised to change its ways, it has continually innovated new ways to deliver nicotine to users, with increased potency and efficiency. The breakneck pace of the evolution — or devolution — of technology will only accelerate, and we have learned we cannot trust tech companies to police themselves.
When companies won’t do the right thing themselves, litigation has proven effective at checking their excesses. However, legal solutions aren’t enough without forward-looking policy and sustained accountability.
Susan Morrisey headed the Colorado Tobacco Education and Prevention Alliance in the late 1990s and is now a principal with SE2, a behavior-change marketing agency that has worked on tobacco prevention for three decades.

Srinagar, Sep 15: Minister for Agriculture Production, Rural Development and Panchayati Raj, Cooperative and Election Department, Javid Ahmad Dar, today chaired a detailed review meeting to assess the progress of ongoing Forest and PMGSY road projects in Rafiabad constituency.
The meeting was attended by Chief Conservator of Forests, Kashmir; Chief Engineer, PMGSY, Kashmir; Conservator of Forests, North Kashmir; Superintending Engineer, PMGSY; DFOs Langate and Baramulla, besides other concerned officers.
During the meeting, the Minister took a detailed review of the status of ongoing road connectivity projects being executed under PMGSY and other Capex-funded schemes in Rafiabad and adjoining areas. He sought project-wise updates from the concerned officers, with focus on the pace of execution, completion timelines and issues hampering the progress of works.
Emphasizing the importance of road connectivity in accelerating development, Javid Dar said that effective implementation of public welfare and development projects is closely linked with reliable connectivity, particularly in rural and far-flung areas. He directed the concerned officers to ensure the timely completion of all ongoing road projects under PMGSY and other Capex funds within the stipulated timelines while maintaining quality standards and ensuring judicious utilization of public funds.
The Minister called for greater coordination among the concerned departments to address bottlenecks, streamline the execution process and ensure that the benefits of developmental schemes reach the people without delays.
Highlighting the considerable tourism potential of Rafiabad and its adjoining areas, Javid Dar stressed the need to create and upgrade infrastructure to facilitate tourism-related activities and promote local economic opportunities.
He underscored that infrastructure development in the region must be pursued in a balanced and sustainable manner, ensuring that the ecological balance, natural beauty and forest identity of the area are preserved.
“Development and environmental conservation must go hand in hand. Our endeavour should be to create modern infrastructure while protecting the rich natural resources and forest wealth of the region,” the Minister maintained.
He called for coordinated planning and execution of road and other infrastructure projects so that developmental needs are met without compromising environmental sustainability.
The Minister directed the concerned officers to examine the pending issues on priority and ensure that all necessary clearances are processed expeditiously to avoid delays in the execution of important public infrastructure projects. He called for close coordination between the Forest and PMGSY departments to resolve inter-departmental issues, accelerate ongoing works and improve road connectivity in Rafiabad and adjoining areas.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says
- Published
Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external.
Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.
Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.
Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.
Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.
Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.
Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed.
Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining.
Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.
While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory.
Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024.
As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found.
Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders.
The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

Is Donald 'drill, baby, drill' Trump helping the world transition away from oil?
Multiple signs point to rise in renewable energy worldwide since U.S. president retook office
While running for the U.S. presidency in 2024, Donald Trump promised to do almost anything to benefit the oil industry. His slogan: "Drill, baby, drill."
But his bold actions since retaking office have in many ways had the opposite effect. While oil companies rake in windfall revenues, Trump's punitive tariffs on China and the price shocks from the war he started with Iran in February have driven many countries to consider the upsides of renewable energy.
"This is Economics 101. If you increase the price of a good and make it riskier, then you will drive people to search for alternatives," said Kingsmill Bond, director of global energy think-tank Ember. "That's exactly what's been happening."
One of the most obvious examples is electric vehicles. A report released last month by the International Energy Agency (IEA) found the global EV market rebounded in the second quarter of this year, even as overall car sales declined.
Statistics collected by Ember show that EV exports from China, the world's biggest EV producer, between March-May 2025 and March-May 2026 spiked — up 117 per cent in Brazil, 127 per cent in South Korea, 175 per cent in Australia and 220 per cent in Italy.
Countries are also adapting their energy grids to the new reality. Earlier this year, the U.K.'s largest energy supplier reported a 50 per cent increase in solar panel sales, year over year, while rising energy costs in Asia have boosted rooftop solar. Even as Canada looks to expand investment in pipelines, the government has announced a nuclear strategy aimed at doubling the electrical grid's capacity by 2050.
"EVs and batteries and solar panels are flying out the door, because people want an alternative," Bond said.
Countries seeking energy security
As Bond points out, the broader energy transition has been underway for a while. In its review of 2025, for example, Ember noted that renewables produced more than one-third of global electricity generation, "overtaking coal power for the first time in 100 years."
But the Iran war gave people the world over new incentive to consider clean energy.
Iran's response to the U.S.-Israeli attacks that began in February was to block the transit of one-fifth of the world's oil through the Strait of Hormuz. As the price of oil rose to nearly $120 US a barrel, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it "the second fossil fuel crisis in just a few years," after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"There is one thing that all these events are making clear," she said. "We are paying a very high price for our overdependency on fossil fuels."
This seems to be a lesson many countries have learned — particularly in Asia.
For example, Thailand has turned to solar in lieu of rising natural gas prices. Soon after the Iran war began, the Philippines declared an energy emergency and its government signed executive orders to speed up grid connections and a number of projects aimed at creating 1.4 gigawatts of renewable energy (roughly enough to power one million homes).
From an environmental perspective, the responses to the Iran war's energy shocks haven't all been positive; coal usage is projected to hit a record high this year, according to the IEA. Some countries that relied on natural gas have had to switch to coal as the main alternative for powering their electrical grids, due to the shipping constraints on liquid natural gas (LNG) through the Strait of Hormuz.
But in some cases, reactively reverting to cheaper and dirtier coal is happening in tandem with a proactive clean transition. Both Pakistan and the Philippines have increased their use of coal to offset some of the dependence on gas, but Pakistan's solar transition has been in the works for several years, with solar's slice of the electricity mix nearly tripling between 2023 and 2025, according to Ember.
Even as most of its LNG supply comes from Qatar, Pakistan's Power Minister Awais Leghari was quick to point out how the country's uptake in renewables would cushion it from the disruptions in the Middle East, telling Reuters, "Pakistan is not expected to invest in any source of power that could put it at risk in terms of energy security."
Erica Downs, a senior research scholar at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University in New York, said electrification inevitably enhances energy security.
"What country doesn't want to be increasingly self-sufficient in energy production and supply?"
Montreal-based Northern Light Capital Partners led a study that showed that by March 30, a month after the start of the Iran war, more than 150 countries had announced they were investing in clean energy for energy security reasons.
"The U.S. administration's tariffs injected erratic volatility into clean energy supply chains," Joanna Klimczak, founder and CEO of Northern Light Capital Partners, told CBC News. "The war in Iran, meanwhile, has been a definitive accelerant for clean energy investment globally."
'A marathon, not a sprint'
The story of the renewable energy transition can't be told without highlighting China's role. It has been producing solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles at a dizzying pace.
Early in his second term, Trump slapped massive tariffs on a variety of Chinese products, including solar panels. One result is that a lot of them were redirected to Africa, where they are helping countries such as Rwanda, Senegal, Ivory Coast and even oil-rich Nigeria end their reliance on fossil fuels like diesel.
"The cost of equipment went down when the trade war started. The Chinese were desperate to offload," Fawen Nyakudya, managing director of Zimbabwe-based PFN Solar Systems, told German media outlet DW.
Klimczak says that as a result of decades of investment in clean tech manufacturing, China has been able to accommodate global demand for renewable energy at a decisive moment.
Downs points out that unlike during the oil shocks in 1973 (due to the OPEC embargo), 1979 (the Iranian revolution) and 1990 (the first Iraq war), "there are technologies that exist today that give people alternatives to fossil fuels that they wouldn't have had in decades past."
They're not only available but, in most cases, are cheaper to deploy than traditional fossil fuels.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, since 2010, the installed costs of solar have declined by 87 per cent, onshore wind by 55 per cent and battery storage has fallen by 93 per cent.
Downs says it's "still a little early to tell" if Trump's trade and military exploits have had a lasting impact on the global energy transition. One key question is whether the price of oil went high enough "to force a more permanent shift to clean tech."
On Monday, the price of a barrel of Brent crude hit $109 US — the highest since May. But oil has yet to reach the lofty levels some analysts predicted earlier in the year.
"Oil didn't hit $200 [a barrel] — didn't hit $150," Downs said. "I've heard some people question, is it actually not a good thing, in the long term, that prices did not reach those sky-high levels?"
The energy transition is inevitable, Bond says, and moments like this accelerate the pace.
"This is a marathon, not a sprint. There is an ongoing shift from fossil fuels to alternatives that's been going on for a long time," he said. "And every time there's a shock like this, it just encourages people [to change] a little bit faster."

Americans are increasingly concerned about the environmental impact of AI, new poll finds
A new AP-NORC poll shows Americans are growing more concerned about the environmental impacts of AI
On the way home from a recent trip, Eriech Tapia drove past a sea of dark industrial buildings lining an already jam-packed northern Virginia road: data centers.
“It was interesting to see how many were going up,” said Tapia, a 30-year-old Republican from Arlington, Virginia, who works in higher education advocacy and policy. He said the data centers lend valuable computing power that can help keep the U.S. competitive with other nations, but he also worries about how much electricity they use.
Like Tapia, Americans have grown more concerned about the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence over the last year, according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago.
The survey data say about half, 53%, of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence's environmental impacts. That is up from 41% last year. Democrats are driving much of the increase in environmental concern, but the poll also reveals broader worries about the local impact of data centers, which power AI and cloud computing.
“We're undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don't think there'll be any putting the milk back in the bottle. Change is scary, and I think some of that is being reflected here,” said Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute that collaborated on the survey.
Rising concern among Democrats about AI's environmental impact
There are thousands of data centers in the U.S. with construction planned for more. Those include smaller, conventional centers that have been around for decades, as well as larger hyperscale ones that are being built to serve artificial intelligence’s added processing needs. Virginia and Texas have the most facilities currently in operation, and other top contenders include California, Ohio and New York.
While 87% of existing data centers are in urban areas, most new data centers are planned for rural areas, according to a Pew Research Center analysis from earlier this year.
“I think that decisions are being made for the company, not for the community that they're being built in,” said Nancy Antunes, a 60-year-old retired Democrat from Waltham, Massachusetts.
A recent United Nations University report predicted that data centers' environmental footprint, which already rivals some of the world's largest countries, will grow rapidly as AI is more widely adopted.
Democrats are increasingly worried about AI's environmental consequences. About two-thirds of Democrats say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about how AI will affect the environment, the poll found, up from about half in 2025. By contrast, about half of independents and about 4 in 10 Republicans are highly concerned about the environmental impact of AI.
Overall, Americans are more worried about the environmental impact of AI than other industries with a substantial environmental footprint. Only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults are highly concerned about the impact of meat production or air travel.
Most Americans support limits on new data centers
While concerns about environmental impacts are higher among Democrats, there is a broad sense of wariness about a rapid data center boom.
About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans.
“There’s a lot of water usage by AI data centers that’s taking away from other things like agriculture and farmers and places that really need it, and people who really need it,” said 21-year-old computer science student Gedeon Kebede, a Democrat from Cincinnati, Ohio.
A majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.
Data centers' use of water to cool AI chips and computers is “nationally modest but potentially locally decisive,” energy systems engineer Fengqi You with Cornell University said in an email. While data centers aren't the U.S.' largest water gobblers, a single large campus can still place stress on a smaller municipal area.
The centers are also powered by tremendous amounts of electricity, particularly larger ones, raising concerns about where that energy will come from. Data centers could account for 11.8% of the U.S.' electricity consumption by 2030, according to a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Report.
“We’re talking about building electric infrastructure on a scale of entire cities, or in some cases, entire states just to serve one data center,” said Erik Nordman, director of Michigan State University's Institute of Public Utilities.
About two-thirds of U.S. adults support requiring data centers to use clean energy sources, such as wind or solar, to supply their electricity needs. About 8 in 10 Democrats support this, along with 56% of Republicans.
Still, some Americans say data center worries feel distant. Mary Fisher, 68, hasn't seen any come up in her Jacksonville, Florida, neighborhood.
“You know, it hasn’t come across my desk as something I should be concerned about,” said Fisher, who is retired and identifies as a Republican.
Republicans see more benefits to data centers than Democrats
About a quarter of U.S. adults say data centers are “extremely” or “very” beneficial when it comes to technological advancement, and about 2 in 10 say the same about job creation. Many U.S. adults say data centers are “somewhat” beneficial or aren't sure, while about one-quarter say they're “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for technological advancement, and about a third don't see a benefit for job creation.
“I see a huge increase in the number of temporary construction workers that are coming to areas, which is vitally important to the U.S. economy,” Tapia from Virginia said.
Republicans are more likely than Democrats to see data centers' benefits. But about 3 in 10 Republicans still think the centers are “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for improved infrastructure and job creation.
Kebede, the computer science student, said he feels pressured to use artificial intelligence. Despite his concerns surrounding the technology, he still wants to be a competitive applicant for the jobs of the future.
“I think a lot of people just feel that it's very much a bubble,” he said. “Ultimately, when it pops, it's going to be very detrimental to everyone, whether you bought into the AI hype or not.”

EU's Ursula von der Leyen says she wants Canada to become an associate member
STRASBOURG, France — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union's first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs drive Ottawa closer to Europe.
Trump's tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Canada to seek closer economic and security ties with Europe. Roughly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States, and Carney has called for a "unique alliance" with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce that dependence.
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during her annual State of the European Union address at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. Carney nodded, rose from his seat, embraced von der Leyen and kissed her on both cheeks as lawmakers gave a standing ovation. He is due to address the Parliament on Thursday.
A Canadian official familiar with the discussions told The Associated Press last week that Ottawa was exploring ties with the EU that could stop just short of membership. The official said Canada would seek an arrangement allowing its citizens to live and work in Europe without visas as part of a broader strategic partnership.
Carney's office welcomed von der Leyen's proposal, saying Canada was deepening ties with the EU "to strengthen our sovereignty" and supported a move beyond their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, to what she called an "Alliance for the Future."
Von der Leyen said the broader alliance would aim to create "a common prosperity and economic security space."
She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.
"Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen said to Carney, who sat in the front row to her left.
"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."
Canada has already joined the EU's defense procurement program
Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she said. "In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible."
However, she gave no details of how the associate membership would work or how it would fit with the other countries negotiating full membership of the bloc.
Canada this year became the first non-European country to join the EU's 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defense program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement.
Iratxe García Pérez, president of the Socialists & Democrats group in the European Parliament, praised Carney for showing "great courage confronting Donald Trump" and said allies were needed to defend "sovereignty, solidarity and international law."
Carney said Tuesday that economic integration, once viewed largely as an asset, is increasingly "being used as a weapon by certain countries." On Tuesday he said discussions would ramp up at the Canada-EU summit in Montreal in late October.
Carney has urged middle powers to work together
Canada has retaliated against U.S. tariffs and rejected trade terms Carney says would weaken its sovereignty.
The EU has taken a different course with Washington, reaching a trade agreement that set a 15% U.S. tariff ceiling on the vast majority of EU exports while Europe eliminated tariffs on U.S. industrial goods.
That contrast has loomed over Carney's push for closer European ties. In a closely watched speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he urged middle powers to work together to increase their leverage in an era of great-power rivalry.
"When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered," Carney said.
"This is not sovereignty," he said. "It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination."
Carney's Davos speech on middle powers in January drew a personal rebuke from Trump, and von der Leyen's overture to America's neighbor could raise the temperature again.
Barry Andrews, chair of the European Parliament's Development Committee, called Canada "a perfect ally for Europe" and said closer ties could bring particular benefits for Ireland, noting that more than 10% of Canadians claim Irish ancestry.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.

Hong Kong unveils first 5-year plan to broaden the city's identity beyond finance
Hong Kong's leader has unveiled a five-year plan to broaden the city's identity beyond finance
HONG KONG -- Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee on Wednesday unveiled the city's first five-year plan in a politically symbolic step that echoes Beijing's approach to development, pushing to broaden Hong Kong's identity beyond international finance to also encompass technology and higher education.
In a speech to the legislature, Lee said the plan aims to make breakthroughs in economic development, enhance competitiveness, improve social well-being and achieve progress in integrating into and serving national development.
The special administrative region has long prided itself on minimal government intervention in the economy, even as officials have increasingly referenced Beijing’s vision for the city. Mainland China in March approved its 15th five-year plan for 2026 to 2030.
Ahead of launching Hong Kong's plan, the city government said it would serve as a framework outlining the financial hub’s strategic priorities and not a planned economy, insisting the capitalist system would be upheld.
Another main goal of Hong Kong's plan is to speed up development of the Northern Metropolis, which will provide land for the innovation and technology industry and build university towns near the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. The proposal, first floated in 2021 by Lee's predecessor Carrie Lam, aims to provide 650,000 jobs and house 2.5 million people.
Under the five-year plan, the government hopes to boost the ratio of domestic expenditure on innovation activities to gross domestic product from 1.63% in 2024 to 3% after 2030.
The plan also includes integrating the city's industry development with academic sectors where Hong Kong holds a competitive edge in the Northern Metropolis.
Each of the three planned university towns would have its own unique position, including one focused on areas such as artificial intelligence and robotics.
The government seeks to speed up Hong Kong’s development as an innovation and technology hub, but also plans to enhance its position as a center for international finance, maritime, trade and aviation.
The city government also proposes to strengthen its role as the world's largest offshore hub for renminbi, mainland China's currency, as well as exploring the use of renminbi to settle government expenditures where appropriate.
Observers are watching whether Lee will use the five-year plan and his latest policy proposals to build momentum for a second term next year.
The former security chief fulfilled Beijing’s long-standing imperative to enact a homegrown national security law in 2024. Officials said the law and a China-imposed security law were necessary for the city’s stability following massive anti-government protests in 2019.
Lee has been under pressure to distinguish Hong Kong from regional rivals and mainland Chinese metropolises, especially after Beijing’s tightening grip tainted Hong Kong’s image as a freewheeling financial center.

Bangladesh national caught smuggling gold from Saudi inside undergarments at Delhi airport

A Bangladeshi national was caught at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport on Monday. The passenger, as per customs officials, was caught smuggling gold from Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
In an official statement, officials said the passenger landed at Delhi Airport's Terminal 3 after his flight landed from Jeddah. The passenger was then scheduled to board a flight for Dhaka, but was intercepted.

(including packing material) was recovered from the passenger, who had concealed it inside his undergarment," the official statement added.
Customs officials added that the passenger admitted to smuggling the gold from Jeddah to Delhi. The Bangladeshi national added that he had been asked to drop off the gold with someone in the transit area at Delhi airport.
"The said recovered gold weighing 1346 grams has been seized under section 110 of the Customs Act, 1962. The said passenger has been placed under arrest in terms of section 104 of the Customs Act, 1962," the officials said.

A Diagnosis for Social Conflict That Gets Lost Along the Way
A new book suggests that arguing isn’t about winning but seems preoccupied with it anyway.
Weddings, famously, create conflict. Before I got married, my parents and I fought over the guest list. A friend of mine struggled with adding some of her husband’s Protestant traditions to their otherwise Jewish ceremony. Another friend had to decode, and then manage, complicated tensions among her future aunts- and uncles-in-law.
All of these issues got resolved, and according to the conflict-resolution facilitator Priya Parker, the process of figuring them out made our weddings more successful expressions of our values. Parker explored the group creation of meaning in her 2018 best seller, The Art of Gathering. In her new book, The Art of Fighting, she writes that arguments are crucial to a group’s ability to do just that. What’s more, in American society—which Parker describes as both conflict averse and low on big rituals—high-stakes events such as weddings are among the “last remaining collective mechanisms to help us have the fights we need to have to figure out who we are now.”
The Art of Fighting is predicated on Parker’s conviction that without confrontation, no group can work well. “Fighting,” she writes in her prologue, “is not the death of community. It is its lifeblood.” Parker considers Americans far too willing to focus on themselves rather than their communities, in large part due to a widespread fear of confrontation. A lot of loneliness, in her view, originates from the all-too-common decision to exit a challenging situation instead of dealing with its simmering disagreements. It’s a smart diagnosis, one that’s as relevant to small-bore social scenarios as it is to interactions within religious organizations, schools, and workplaces. The choice to hide from conflict is, to Parker, in many situations, a choice to be alone.
Parker’s idea that conflict is inherently a social good is intriguing and counterintuitive. But The Art of Fighting is not nearly as communitarian a book as its setup would suggest. Although its more abstract passages describe healthy confrontation as helpful and worthy, its examples tell another story. Parker presents The Art of Fighting as a “group-help book” but tends to take a side in her case studies—and in most instances, her side wins.
Her own life serves as illustration, too, and often provides the book’s most revealing moments. By way of arguing that everyone needs to get comfortable with disagreement, she mentions a clash she and her father had after the latter got upset that Parker hadn’t invited her stepbrother’s wife to her baby shower. As Parker relates it, their discussion of her reasoning—she and her stepsister-in-law just aren’t close—ends not with compromise or reconciliation but with the blunt lines: “He wasn’t getting it. And that was OK.” Such a one-sided resolution suggests a disinterest in compromise and an interpretation of fighting as an individualistic act. Facing conflict may very well be a social good—I believe it is—but her book more often seems to urge readers to wade into arguments to get what they want.
The Art of Fighting is full of stories of conflict. Some appear only once, and some are threaded throughout the book. The quarreling groups that Parker features, many of which she worked with in her role as a facilitator, range in size from an extended family to a percussion ensemble to a large architecture firm. Parker uses every case to ask a variation of her central question: “How do you fight with those to whom you want to belong?”
In the book’s most moving example, she writes about a church that, in the mid-1990s, deliberated about and then voted on whether it would perform and recognize gay marriages. Its pastor, Martin Copenhaver, understood that they couldn’t make a decision that might lead to division if his church were to survive. “In the political arena,” he tells Parker, “if you win by one vote, you win. In this arena, you win by one vote, you don’t win.”
Hoping to forge meaningful consensus, he hosted four meetings to discuss the subject; only those who attended were allowed to vote. After the election—the church decided, not unanimously but with “no great division,” to allow gay marriage—he asked everyone to reconcile in person with someone who voted differently. In essence, Copenhaver organized the entire conflict to prioritize congregants’ investment in the church, not to lead them toward a certain outcome.
I wanted to learn more about how other sorts of disputes, especially less orchestrated ones, might bolster a sense of community. But Parker is surprisingly blurry about the variety of incentives for confronting or ignoring tension that exist in one setting or another. Some strategies for managing conflict—waiting to engage until no one has steam pouring from their ears; ensuring that the arguing parties’ grievances and goals are clear; creating the right conditions for a tough conversation—may apply to all kinds of groups.
But the book doesn’t do enough to acknowledge that different sorts of conflicts have different stakes. Starting a fight for the good of the group may be wise among relatives but foolish if doing so could also mean losing your job. And a values-based argument may not be worthwhile in a corporate context where the overall goal is to maximize profit. One of Parker’s recurring examples is a debate that took place within a law firm about whether the TV in its common space should show World Cup games played in Qatar. It begins with an intern objecting, on Slack, to the “human rights abuses of workers in the lead up to the World Cup and the horrific status of rights for LGBTQ people and women in Qatar.” The managing partners invited employees to what Parker characterizes as a too-wide conversation about the World Cup. It was, she writes, “the wrong fight with the wrong assemblage of people in the wrong room.”
Parker uses this argument to underscore good and bad ways to navigate conflicts, especially ones that arise online—certainly an important issue in our screen-heavy times. But missing from this analysis is any real engagement on Parker’s part with the substance of the conflict itself. Readers never learn how the issue was resolved: Did the World Cup get shown or not? Was there ever a meaningful discussion about the objections the intern had raised? The book uses this example to describe strategies for handling internal dissent, focusing on how the managing partners could best have reestablished peace among their employees. It becomes a story about conflict management rather than conflict as a potential social good.
Some of Parker’s personal anecdotes more vividly illustrate her not-quite-communitarian approach to fighting. In one, she describes enrolling her children and their cousin in a small soccer camp one summer. Initially, the kids report hating camp and getting bullied by their counselors. Parker speaks with the camp director, who talks with his employees and establishes that Parker’s children and niece, who started on the eighth week of camp, are unfamiliar with both the established cohort’s “teasing culture” and the basic rules of soccer. Parker suggests that the camp’s coaches “give our kids a Week One experience, orient them, do the things you did with all the other kids when they were new.” They comply, and the camp—which Parker needs for child care—works out.
Parker’s reaction to the situation is entirely reasonable; what parent wouldn’t try to help a kid who’s being picked on, or scramble to rescue a child-care setup that seems about to fail? It is not, however, an illustration of confrontation as community service. She shows herself engaging in conflict to get her kids special treatment rather than nudging the kids to advocate for themselves or asking how the camp might better help them settle in despite their latecomer status. Another way to put this is that no compromise is on offer here, and we get no sense of a group working together. Parker, as the customer, gets to be right.
Throughout The Art of Fighting, individuals prevail in this way. A woman named Rebekah, exhausted by attending her family’s Passover seders—too much cooking, too much disruption to routine, too much airtime for her right-wing uncle—gives them up. But Parker never writes about what Rebekah’s parents, siblings, or children might lose when she and her nuclear family stop coming, or how her continued, if conflicted, attendance might have led her relatives to create more sustainable traditions. Just as some therapists prioritize clients over the other people in their lives, Parker prioritizes the subjects of her anecdotes over those with whom they fight.
What these stories add up to, ultimately, is a much less surprising take on conflict than the book tries to lay out. Parker provides a useful guide to having arguments in good faith without hurting anyone’s feelings unnecessarily or creating a corporate crisis. But arguments can be so much more than that. Alone in the book, the story of Copenhaver’s church demonstrates that even enduring and loaded disagreements can, if handled with enough care and respect, strengthen the bonds between parties—in other words, they can be productive, not just nondestructive. Many readers will have experienced this in intimate relationships. I, for one, have grown closer to some friends after air-clearing arguments and have drifted from others who weren’t willing or able to talk through issues when they arose.
But as Parker points out, public life in the United States isn’t set up for healthy conflict. Meaningful group fights are rare experiences. Aside from my wedding planning, I haven’t been part of one. I believe, in theory, that such a dispute could be transformational for both a community and its individual members. But in order for Parker’s book to have taught me how to navigate one, she would have had to truly let go of the old idea that the reason to fight is to win.

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

A maiden ODI century by Matt Renshaw and Nathan Ellis’ five-wicket haul powered Australia to a 59-run win over Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club on Tuesday.
With the win, the Mitchell Marsh-led side took a 1-0 lead in the three-match ODI series, with the second ODI scheduled to take place on Friday at the same venue.
Batting first, Australia managed to score 294/8, led by Renshaw’s century (109 off 94 balls) and a half-century from Cooper Connolly (51 off 46 balls).
For the host, Newham Nyamhuri impressed with a five-wicket haul (5/62), while Brad Evans chipped in with two wickets (2/51).
In the chase, Zimbabwe was rocked early as it lost opener Ben Curran for a duck. The Sikandar Raza led-side lost three more wickets in relatively quick succession, with Ellis contributing for two of the victims.
Then, Zimbabwe staged a brief resistance as Craig Ervine (59 off 60 balls) and Raza (57 off 76 balls) albeit well below the asking rate.
Once Ervine and Raza fell, the Australian bowling unit dismissed the rest of the batting lineup without wasting much time to secure a comfortable victory.
Renshaw, who scored his first international ton in ten years, was adjudged the player of the match.
“I just tried to rebuild the innings. We lost a few wickets (after) the boys started really well,” the opener said after the match.
“I did not feel under any scoring pressure. It was really nice. Pitch was nice. Ten years between international hundreds was not something I was expecting.”

Treasury secretary backs Trump’s $5,000 checks but refuses to say how the country will pay for it
Trump has faced bribery accusations after promising Americans $5,000 if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress during the midterm elections
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has backed the $5,000 checks Donald Trump wants to give Americans after the midterm elections, but has refused to say how the country would pay for them.
During the Republican convention held in Dallas last week to get out the vote for GOP candidates in the midterms, the president promised that his administration would pay a “Trump Dividend” to each American adult if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress.
“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said in his keynote speech Wednesday.
The idea sparked backlash, with critics accusing the president of bribery and others questioning where the money would come from. And Bessent did little to quell skeptics' concerns during a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee Tuesday.
When asked by Representative Juan Vargas, a California Democrat, if the $5,000 checks would increase the nation‘s $40 trillion debt, Bessent said, “I believe there are ways to do it without increasing the debt.”
Vargas then asked Bessent to elaborate, but Bessent just said the Treasury Department is in the process of figuring out how to pay for the checks without increasing the national debt.
“I’m not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury we’ve been working on it for quite a while,” Bessent said.
The Independent has reached out to the Treasury Department for comment.
Trump quickly said after he first announced the $5,000 checks that he didn’t think he needed approval from Congress, known for having the power of the purse.
“I think they will do it if we needed it, but we think not,” Trump told CBS News.
When asked about the “Trump Dividend” on Meet the Press Sunday, House Speaker Mike Johnson said he’d “work with the president hand in hand” on the matter but did not commit to being able to deliver on the checks.
The Independent’s Eric Garcia asked Johnson at a press conference Tuesday, “How is communism any different from what President Trump is doing getting equity stakes in tech and promising $5,000 checks to Americans and having equity in steel?”
Johnson and other Republicans have baselessly accused the Democratic Party of embracing communist candidates in the midterms.
Johnson sidestepped Garcia’s question, telling reporters that the president “comes up with creative ideas all the time” and that Republicans in Congress are "processing" the “Trump Dividend” proposal.
“What he is trying to articulate…if you want more money in your pockets, you gotta keep Republicans in charge,” Johnson said. “We have done that.”
But a majority of Americans don’t think Trump is doing a good job on the economy as they struggle to pay for everyday necessities like groceries and gas, partly due to the president’s war in Iran driving up energy costs.
Just 34 percent of Americans approve of the way Trump is handling the economy, compared to 66 percent who disapprove, according to a new CBS News poll.

"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

Content warning: The following article has references to suicide. Please avoid reading if you feel distressed by the subject.
The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.
If you are in distress, please reach out to national helpline 104 or any of these 24x7 helplines.
