Air Force Secretary Troy Meink made the first public declaration Monday that the United States has placed “space control weapons” in orbit, an announcement that will surely reverberate in the power centers of Beijing and Moscow.
Space Force officials have previously expressed their interest in acquiring space-based weapons, and Pentagon leaders have become more open to discussing space warfare in recent years. Therefore, Meink’s announcement Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference near Washington, DC, was not entirely unexpected.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats, wherever they exist. This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said in prepared remarks.
Meink did not reveal any details about the weapons, but the disclosure of their existence underlines a remarkable turnaround in the Pentagon’s thinking about orbital warfare, something no senior official wanted to discuss publicly until a few years ago. Military officials recently have openly discussed orbital combat, defensive countermeasures on satellites, and a new ground-based weapon designed to disable an enemy satellite in orbit.
“There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things,” Meink said. “We spend a lot of time talking about how we’re going to talk about these things. It is important from a deterrence perspective. But on the other hand, me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else.”
Meink also did not say when the Space Force deployed the space-based weapons. The development of space technology often takes years, so it is likely the weapons program, whatever it is, spanned multiple presidential administrations.
“I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the US can operate freely there,” Meink said.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Taking stock
The Pentagon’s acknowledgement Monday comes after US officials began highlighting Russia’s testing of an apparent anti-satellite weapon in orbit in 2020. Officials in the Biden administration accused Russia in 2024 of deploying operational anti-satellite weapons. Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), the former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, revealed a US government assessment the same year that Russia might put a nuclear weapon into space. A nuclear detonation in low-Earth orbit would jeopardize thousands of commercial and military spacecraft, including Starlinks, US spy satellites, Chinese satellites, and the International Space Station.
China, too, has deployed satellites that US military officials view with suspicion. Open source data indicate Chinese satellites routinely maneuver close to US military assets in orbit, likely for surveillance, similar to the way US satellites sometimes park themselves next to Chinese or Russian spacecraft.
“China continues to launch and operate highly maneuverable satellites, demonstrating an advanced level of technological and operational acumen that, if not already deployed for such purposes, could enable a formidable on-orbit counterspace arsenal,” analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies wrote in their 2025 Space Threat Assessment.
In press conference later Monday, Meink defended the US military’s deployment of space-based weapons by citing China and Russia’s own advancements in the field.
“Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” Meink said in response to a reporter’s question. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.”
Military commanders have routinely used satellites for communications, navigation, and missile warning for decades. Today, the list of applications is expanding, with space-based sensing and targeting, broadband connectivity through networks like Starlink, and perhaps soon, space-based interceptors for missile defense.
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
“With everything we’re talking about doing, from long-range fires to control of our forces, our maintaining and being able to count on those space capabilities is important,” Meink said. “It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space. So we’ve had to take steps to make sure that that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
President Donald Trump nominated Meink for the top civilian post in the Air Force last year. Before becoming secretary, Meink served as an Air Force officer, civilian program manager, and senior intelligence official in Democratic and Republican administrations.
The categories include directed-energy, such as lasers, radio frequency jammers, and kinetic weapons capable of physically destroying a target. These types of weapons could be positioned on the ground or in space. In 2025, Gen. Chance Saltzman, until earlier month the Space Force’s chief of space operations, said other countries, presumably China and Russia, are pursuing all six categories. “We’re not pursuing all of those yet,” Saltzman said at the time.
But Saltzman argued that maybe the United States should. “There are good reasons to have all those categories,” he said.
The Space Force revealed its first acknowledged weapon system in June, when it announced the operational acceptance of a ground-based mobile satellite jammer called Meadowlands. Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation think tank, speculated that the “space control weapons” announced by Meink on Monday could be jammers placed in orbit.
“China and Russia are both thought to have space-based jammers,” Samson wrote in an email to Ars. “I’ve always thought that the US must have them, too.”
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Credit:
NASA
US officials have repeatedly voiced a preference for “counterspace” weapons that do not generate space debris. A space-based kinetic weapon would leave behind a cloud of space junk jeopardizing countless satellites in orbit, including the US military’s own assets, and there’s no public indication that the United States has tested such a weapon (the US military has demonstrated a ground-based anti-satellite weapon), according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“Then there are non-kinetic weapons such as signal jammers and spoofers and laser dazzlers. From an under-the-hood hardware standpoint, such weapons are doppelgängers to technology already found at scale in orbit,” Swope said. “Any radio transmitter could be a jammer. Any inter-satellite optical link could be a laser dazzler. Certainly, a jammer or dazzler could be purpose-built, too.”
It is also not clear what the US military’s space weapons might target. Space control has a broad definition in US military doctrine, and term encompasses weapons that could be used against targets in space or on Earth, Swope said.
“For example, blowing up a satellite ground station to prevent an adversary from using a satellite is a space control activity,” Swope told Ars. “The fact that the weapons—plural—are on-orbit is a more significant data point and disclosure. This might be the first time a US official has spoken about the United States possessing on-orbit weapons.”
Swope said the lack of detail in Meink’s statement Monday raises questions about the Pentagon’s motivation for the disclosure.
“It is too vague to have a meaningful deterrent value,” Swope said. “Deterrence is not only about a weapon’s fact of existence but also about having an awareness of how the weapon will be used. For example, the concept of mutually assured destruction was based on the premise of how nuclear weapons would be used and not simply the fact of their existence.
“What also made deterrence work is an awareness of the destructive power of nuclear weapons,” Swope continued. “Both how and when the [space-based] weapon would be used and its destructive potential are ambiguous. Talking heads and pontificators like me are going to have a field day with the disclosure, but it’s not clear what Russia, China, and other potential adversaries are supposed to do with it.”
There was no immediate reaction Monday from the governments of China or Russia.
“Now that the United States has officially acknowledged it has those systems in space, it has opened the door for China and Russia to do the same, which people in the US will then use as justification for why we needed those systems there in the first place,” Samson said.
What is clear is there is now an arms race in orbit. The United States and China are leading the way by measures of volume and sophistication, while Russia appears to be the most aggressive in terms of tactics. But it matters less who started the arms race than how it ends.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Team Europe enjoyed a practice round at Adare Manor on Monday ahead of the Ryder Cup being hosted there next September; Several members of Luke Donald's side discussed the benefits of the team trip in their BMW PGA Championship press conferences
Tuesday 15 September 2026 23:21, UK
It may still be a year to go until Team Europe's bid for a historic Ryder Cup threepeat, but Luke Donald has already had many of his prospective line-up together at Adare Manor.
Although not quite a full scouting mission like Donald provided ahead of previous Ryder Cup wins at Marco Simone GC and Bethpage Black, it gave many of his potential players an early experience of tackling next year's Ryder Cup venue in Ireland.
A mix of established Ryder Cup members and likely rookie contenders made the trip after the Amgen Irish Open, with a team dinner followed by 18 holes on Monday

Sixteen players joined Donald and his vice-captains for the team session ahead of travelling onto the DP World Tour's BMW PGA Championship - 10 of last year's line-up, two more with past Ryder Cup pedigree and four potential debutants.
"Any time I'm asked to go to Adare Manor, I'm going to go happily and willingly," said Jon Rahm. "It's one of the best hotel golf course experiences there is in the world.
"It was a lot of fun. It was very enjoyable. I think those days are great for all of us to see each other and just in a way remember why we do what we do.
"For those players who have never been there before, I think it's just getting those first nerves out of the way of how they may feel.
Who made the trip to Adare Manor?
Only Rory McIlroy and Rasmus Hojgaard were missing from Donald's dozen that celebrated a 15-13 victory in New York. Alex Noren - a winner in 2018 and vice-captain last year - and Nicolai Hojgaard, part of the 2023 team, also made the trip.
Alex Fitzpatrick and Kristoffer Reitan both featured after impressive rookie campaigns on the PGA Tour, while Spanish duo Eugenio Chacarra and Ángel Ayora were the other newcomers involved.
Most travelled straight from the Amgen Irish Open, with Shane Lowry a later arrival after his record-breaking 11-shot win on home soil at Trump International Golf Links.
"It was a lovely boys' day out, in the sense we got together and had a nice dinner," Justin Rose told the Sky Sports podcast. "There was some intention-setting of what it means to be on the team and what the plans are going forward.

"The round itself yesterday was very casual, very fun and just a first look at the golf course. Having Adare Manor pretty much to yourself is a pretty special experience.
"For them [rookies], it lights the fire even more in them to want to be a part of that team. It gives them the comfort to feel like they're already part of the team, in the sense of [being in] Luke's thoughts, the way of doing things and how the captain goes about it.
"It doesn't necessarily feel like a game-changing trip and 'wow, we have an advantage' or anything like that, but I think it's very important in terms of culture setting and all that."
What were course conditions like?
The European players went out in groups of four for a round in calm conditions, with some playing the course for the first time and others refamiliarizing themselves with a venue that previously hosted the JP McManus Pro-Am.
"With the good weather they've had in Europe, in Ireland, it was in as good a shape as I've ever seen it," Rahm added. "It was actually firm. They could have had it as fast as they wanted to.
"It wasn't overly fast because obviously I think they want the public to still enjoy the week. It was in perfect condition. It was immaculate."
The last two Ryder Cups in Europe have been on venues used for regular DP World Tour events, with Le Golf National (2018) a past site of the Open de France and Marco Simone GC (2023) the Open d'Italia, giving Donald a different challenge in Ireland.
"The strategy around setting up the course is very different from when they have a lot of data from the [DP World] Tour," Noren explained. "It's a very difficult task to set that up, I think, to our advantage. We'll see how they do.
"It's the course and the resources where you can set it up pretty much however you want - you can grow in the rough, you can expand, and you can use tee boxes. It's like not particularly a blank sheet of paper, but you can do whatever you want."
Who else was missing and what happens next?
PGA Championship winner Aaron Rai was invited but unable to attend due to a close friend's wedding in Portugal on Sunday, while Tom McKibbin - who played two rounds with Donald in Ireland last week - was not involved.
Ryder Cup qualification is already under way, with points only available via the Race to Dubai standings for the rest of this season before including FedExCup points in January, with Rose expecting to see some new editions in Team Europe next September.
"I think freshening it up a little bit would be a good thing," Rose admitted. "You want your team to be experienced but to have some fresh energy is always great. Whether that be ideas, style of game, pairing options - to change is up is a good thing.
"There's plenty of opportunity for guys to break through. I think the transition from Whistling Straits (2021) into Rome was fantastic and I think that only strengthened into solidifying some of those players that stepped into that role at Bethpage.
There are so many good young players, like the Højgaards [Nicolai and Rasmus], Ludvig [Åberg], even Bob [MacIntyre]. Those guys are now real stalwarts of the team. There has been a great transition in Europe, so we can afford another new batch of youngsters."
Could consistency be key again for Team Europe?
Europe carried 11 of their 12-man line-up and four of the five vice-captains from their 2023 victory to New York in 2025, with the Molinari brothers - Edoardo and Francesco - already confirmed for a third consecutive stint in Donald's backroom team.
Padraig Harrington has been added as a vice-captain on home soil, while McIlroy anticipates the bulk of Donald's last two teams to be back together again in Ireland.
"If there's ever a place to blend rookies, it is in Europe," McIlroy told Sky Sports. "The thing that I preach around the European Ryder Cup team is there's this continuity.
"I think continuity between the captain, the players, the vice captains is a big thing in a team environment. Look, inevitably there might be some new faces on that team, but I don't think there's certainly not going to be wholesale changes.
"I think the nucleus of our team will remain the nucleus. You might have a couple [new] maybe, but I'd say for the most part, as long as everyone plays well and stays injury-free, you're going to have a very similar looking team to what we've had the last couple."
The Ryder Cup will be held from September 17-19 next year, live on Sky Sports. Donald will be looking to be the first captain in history to win three consecutive Ryder Cups.

How exceptional Garner became Everton's main man
- Published
Crunching tackles that help win hard-fought away points in an all-action performance are the kind of things Everton fans have become well accustomed to when watching James Garner.
Now the rest of the Premier League are starting to take proper notice.
Following Everton's goalless draw at Tottenham on Saturday, during which midfielder Garner bested a home line-up boasting the near-£200m midfield pairing of Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, Match of the Day pundit Thomas Frank hailed Garner's display.
It featured crucial challenges on Tonali and Fernandes to halt promising home attacks - by a player who missed a significant part of pre-season after hernia surgery.
"Garner today was extremely good," said Frank. "He is aware; he's talking; he's organising.
"In a high-press situation, he does the recovery, and that's just so exceptional and so important when you are playing against a team who are dominating you.
"He was running so hard, so that's one side of his game, but also so important is his touches. He is a lot on the ball. It's through him that a lot of things are happening."
Fellow pundit and former Everton defender Ashley Williams said: "He's really impressive. If you're a centre-back behind him, he's the type of midfielder you want."
The 'boy' who became a leader
Garner was signed for an initial fee of only £9m from Manchester United in 2022, having spent the previous season on loan helping Nottingham Forest get promoted to the Premier League.
The academy graduate did not make a Premier League start for United.
After taking two seasons to settle at Everton under Frank Lampard and then Sean Dyche amid a backdrop of financial problems and points deductions, the 2025-26 campaign proved to be a watershed moment.
Garner played all but six minutes of Everton's Premier League campaign to spearhead a European push that lasted for much of the season.
In December Everton travelled to Forest with a depleted squad and won 2-0 to move within four points of the top four.
Garner scored Everton's opening goal in a commanding display that underlined his development.
Following that win, manager David Moyes said: "When I came in, I still saw a bit of a boy and I think I now see someone who's turning into a really good leader as well, beginning to take a bit more responsibility and grow up and begin to start to act like a real midfield player."
The data backs up Garner's growing maturity.
He ranked top for a host of metrics for Everton last season, in terms of creativity and physicality, making the most successful passes, tackles and interceptions, but also providing the most assists and engineering the most chances.
Perhaps most impressively, he stepped up in the absence of key winger Jack Grealish - four of Garner's seven assists came after Grealish's season was ended by injury in January.
"He's been fantastic since I came in," said Moyes. "I didn't realise probably how good he was. He's been so good."
England's 'mini Valverde'
Garner's consistent displays last season earned him a first England cap in a friendly against Uruguay in March.
He produced a man-of-the-match performance, topping the game for tackles and chances created.
After the match England manager Thomas Tuchel compared him with Uruguay and Real Madrid midfielder Federico Valverde.
"He's our mini Valverde," said Tuchel. "He played very, very good. I was quite sure that he will play good because he has this natural confidence and he's just very physical. He won a lot of balls."
Garner missed out on a place in England's World Cup squad, but those physical attributes could result in more caps in the near future.
He covered the most ground of any Premier League player last season - and 6km more than England midfielder Elliot Anderson - while also topping the overall rankings for tackles and interceptions.
Garner signed a new Everton deal in January, keeping him at the club until 2030, but that did not stop a £65m bid from Chelsea on deadline day this summer, which was rejected by Everton - an important decision given that Garner's versatility is likely to be crucial to a threadbare squad this season.
Everton can currently call on only 17 fit senior outfield players, with Christian Norgaard and Merlin Rohl sidelined because of injury, meaning gaps may have to be plugged throughout the campaign.
Garner has played at right-back and left-back for Everton in addition to his usual central midfield role.
He also played at right-back when England Under-21s won the European Championship three years ago, while Moyes has said he can operate as a number eight or six – a valuable commodity after losing 254 Premier League appearances in the guise of departed midfielder Idrissa Gueye this summer.
If Everton are to push back towards European football this season, Garner may well be their most important asset.

State of U.S. democracy reaches new low, report finds
U.S. democracy has reached its lowest levels in 50 years, according to a new global report that tracks democratic performance around the world.
For several years, Dr. Seema Shah, who heads the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance's democracy assessment team, said their researchers have observed a global pattern of democratic decline: "Severe drops in scores that measure freedom of expression, freedom of the press, credible elections, effective parliament," she said.
Shah says that in the 50 years of compiling this survey, she's seen undemocratic trends like this correcting themselves.
But not this time.
"It's getting worse and worse," Shah says. "So that's really worrying, especially because we also see that people are more willing in some cases to consider non-democratic leadership or non-democratic governance."
The organization's annual Global State of Democracy report, which tracks democratic performance across 174 countries and draws on data going back to 1975, was released Tuesday. The latest report focuses on changes in democratic performance between 2020 and 2025.
And Shah says one country stood out for how far its democracy has declined. "The clearest example, unfortunately, is the United States," she says.
The report says that in 2025, "President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies. … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation."
Shah says the U.S. has historically served as a bastion of democratic governance, with strong performance in the rule of law and judicial independence and a prominent role in promoting democracy around the world. "But that's no longer the case," says Shah.
"Inside the U.S. and outside the U.S., we're seeing in the U.S. administration policies harming domestic democracy...but also really weakening global norms and actually providing fodder for other non-democratic leaders."
Democracy, she notes, is no longer the central focus of U.S. foreign policy.
Democratic values are also no longer the basis for new alliances globally, Shah says, noting that the democratic aid the U.S. used to provide to developing countries has been dismantled.
President Trump has hinted at this himself. At a summit last year in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, he criticized previous U.S. administrations as "interventionist" and said the U.S. would no longer give other countries "lectures on how to live."
Domestically, Shah says, the U.S. has seen declines in nearly half of the 30 indicators the organization measures. She says they've hit their lowest levels in 50 years of gathering data on democracies.
And it's not just the U.S. seeing these declines.
The organization's survey shows that 57% of countries surveyed showed declines in at least one key indicator of democratic performance, with the rule of law serving as the weakest-performing area of democracy globally.
But what about countries that have seen a resurgence of democracy — places like Poland, Hungary and Syria in recent years?
"What the research shows is that, depressingly, in 90% of cases, a democracy that has suffered decline and then comes back and what's called a U-turn in 90% of the cases, they suffer another democratic decline within five years."
Shah says candidates promising change typically find that when voters give them power, they often are not able to deliver on those promises because remnants of the old guard often prevent those changes.
"And unless," she says, "you're willing to break your own democratic laws to get them out, what can you do?"

The past few months have proved to be a microcosm of Sanju Samson’s chequered international career.
If his form at the business end of this year’s T20 World Cup — he won the Player-of-the-Tournament award with 321 runs in five innings — was a dazzling high, the tour of the United Kingdom just three months later was a debilitating low.
After just two games against Ireland and one against England, which yielded returns of 5, 0 and 1, he made way for teen prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. While Samson came back for the fifth and final T20I against the Englishmen, he had already been omitted for the subsequent tour of Zimbabwe.
Samson’s topsy-turvy ride hasn’t halted. At the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Tuesday, the 31-year-old was back to wielding his willow like a cutlass, scything the Afghanistan attack for a blistering 57 off 22 balls in a chase of 160. In the aftermath, Samson spoke with refreshing candour and endearing wit, and showed no resentment at recent developments.
“After a few failures, you definitely go through a lot as an Indian cricketer. It is not easy to face failures. But that is where my experience comes in. I try to shut out the noise and still try to keep scoring at a high strike rate. I take the chances knowing that if I fail again, I will be facing a lot of noise again. But that is the way we are built here in Indian cricket,” the opener said.

“As a captain in the IPL, I have been in that position where I have taken tough calls. That is where the communication comes in. GG [Gambhir] bhai’s communication was very important. He spoke to me a lot in England and before this series as well. It is not easy to make hard decisions, but as a leadership group, they have been taking tough calls, keeping the team in front. The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".
"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.
Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.
There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.
Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.
The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."
The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Formula 1’s 2027 calendar is out with next season again scheduled to run to a record-equalling 24 race weekends.
But the schedule features a number of points of intrigue including an increase in Sprints, headlined by the addition of Monaco, the continued presence of the sport's usual Middle Eastern rounds, and the return of two popular tracks...

Four more Sprints
As reported in July, Formula 1 is increasing the number of Sprint weekends on the calendar for 2027.
The final number of Sprints has been confirmed as 10, four more than the six which have featured in each of the past four seasons.
The alternative format, which was first introduced in 2021 and features an additional qualifying session to set the grid for a short-form 100km race, has led to increase in global television audiences, which F1 says are 12 per cent higher than on non-Sprint weekends which feature three practice sessions.
The 10 venues for 2027 are split evenly between tracks that have staged Sprints previously - Montreal, Silverstone, Monza, Interlagos and Qatar's Lusail - and newcomers to the format in Sakhir, Albert Park, Suzuka, Monaco and Abu Dhabi's Yas Marina Circuit.
The current Sprint format, which features points for the top-eight finishers, is thought set to remain the same for 2027.
Why Monaco is staging a first-ever Sprint
Certainly, many of the early headlines and debate around the 2027 calendar has centred on the fact Monaco has unexpectedly been included as one the 10 Sprint venues.
Not only has the Principality never hosted a Sprint before, its main 78-lap Grand Prix is already not known for overtaking around its narrow, twisty wall-lined circuit with the race often proving processional in dry conditions.
It is regularly Qualifying - and the flat-out challenge of threading an F1 car between the barriers - that proves the most jaw-dropping aspect of the Monaco weekend. F1 has pointed out that the addition of the Sprint means there will now be two such grid-setting sessions in 2027
It can also be argued that having only one practice session, rather than the usual three, offers the chance for more unpredictability in the pecking order given drivers will only have one practice session to build rhythm and confidence, a crucial element of a successful Monaco weekend.
"Traditionally Sprints have been held at tracks where it is easy to overtake. Clearly that's not the case at Monaco," said Sky Sports' Craig Slater.
"But the big bonus here we'll have two red-hot qualifying sessions. That's what that track is all about and the drivers will have the ultimate test on two occasions that weekend."
Season start and ending Sprint weekends
For the first time next year, the season will both start and finish with a Sprint event.
Bahrain opens the season with the format on March 12-14 while Abu Dhabi will close it on December 10-12.
The season-opening Sprint will certainly present a different challenge for teams and drivers given they will have just one practice session that weekend to prepare for the campaign's first competitive session, Sprint Qualifying, on the Friday evening.
However, pre-season testing at the same Sakhir circuit (February 24-27) will run to four rather than three days - one more day than is usually the case outside of years featuring big rule changes - meaning they will at least be familiar with the track with the new 2027 cars.
Still, the season-opening Sprint represents a new challenge and could offer some early-season surprises in the pecking order for one, or both, grids if teams are not on top of their cars and set-ups.
The fact that the season will finish with back-to-back Sprint events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi inevitably raises the possibility of the world title being decided in a Saturday race should the fight go down to the final rounds.
There is already precedent for this from Qatar 2023 when Max Verstappen clinched his third world title in the Sprint.
Middle East races scheduled as F1 waits on final 2026 decisions
The sport's four Middle Eastern races all feature on the 2027 season, bookending the 24-race campaign.
That also remains the case for 2026's final two scheduled races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi with just over two months to go until the sport is due to head there.
The conflict in the Middle East has already seen this year's Saudi Arabian Grand Prix cancelled and the Bahrain Grand Prix moved to Malaysia on October 4, having originally been scheduled for April at its own Sakhir track a week before Jeddah.
F1's intention and planning remains for 2026's concluding two rounds to go ahead as scheduled. Although Stefano Domenicali had previously indicated that there was a mid-September timeframe on making a final decision on whether the events could take place, there is thought to be no hard deadline as such with officials able to wait for longer before making a final call.
Italy's Imola circuit is understood to be the contingency to close the current season in December should the Middle Eastern rounds not be able to take place.
The early-season 2027 dates in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia are not scheduled for another five months, giving F1 and the FIA plenty of time to continue monitoring the latest situation.
Portugal and Turkey return
Formula 1's calendar first increased to a record 24 grands prix in 2024 and that number is again scheduled for next year.
Next year's calendar features no absolutely-new venues, but the sport will return to Portugal and Turkey for the first time since the popular European venues were called up to help out during the Covid-affected 2020 and 2021 seasons.
They replace the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, which starts a rotation with the Belgian GP and next returns in 2028, and Dutch Grand Prix, whose deal has ended.
Portugal's Portimao circuit takes over Barcelona's June slot, while Turkey returns at the start of October as part of a slightly rejigged run of races after F1's summer break, which will stretch to five weeks in 2027.
The season will finish on December 12, one week later than this year and the latest since 2020.

Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.
The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
The 24.2-megapixel camera features a retro redesign inspired by Canon’s old film cameras.
The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.
Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.
The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.
Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.
Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.
In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
- Published
Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.
The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.
It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.
The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday.
Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand.
"Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis.
Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed".
The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended.
There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen.
At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based.
The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects".
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict.

A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.
The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported.
Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m wonfine for the company.
The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.
He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.
Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.
Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.
Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.
Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.
Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.
Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.
The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.
Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.
They estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.
Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.
The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.
Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.

The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.
The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.
From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.
In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.
Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.
The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.
The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.
If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.
In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.
El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year.
Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme.
The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia.
More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it.
Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.

Beed: Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange Patil's health deteriorated on Wednesday while he was travelling towards Mumbai, with doctors advising immediate hospitalisation after his blood pressure and blood sugar levels reportedly dropped significantly.
Jarange, who is on the 19th day of his indefinite hunger strike over the Maratha reservation issue, reportedly developed acute dehydration after reaching Patoda in Maharashtra's Beed district at around 11 am.
He had reached Patoda nearly 14 hours after setting out from Antarwali Sarati village in Jalna district as part of his journey towards Mumbai.
'Tour taking toll on my health'
Addressing a press conference, the 44-year-old activist said he was experiencing a severe burning sensation in his stomach and feet and acknowledged that the long journey was affecting his health.
“If I take treatment, the government becomes completely carefree. If I stop treatment, they become anxious. This tour to Mumbai is taking a toll on my health. I can continue if I'm fine, but such a long travel is not good while on a hunger strike. The tour can also be cancelled if there is no option,” Jarange said, according to Hindustan Times.
Doctors advise hospitalisation
A medical team led by Beed District Civil Surgeon Dr Satishkumar Solanke examined Jarange in Patoda.
“Manoj Jarange's blood pressure and blood sugar levels have plummeted severely,” Dr Solanke said.
According to the medical assessment cited in reports, Jarange was suffering from acute dehydration and was minimally responsive.
He was administered intravenous (IV) fluids, but doctors reportedly cautioned that saline support alone would not make him fit to continue the long journey.
Doctors also warned that any further decline in his fluid levels could pose serious health risks and advised that he be admitted to an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for treatment.
Mumbai Police deny protest permission
Jarange's health scare comes after Mumbai Police denied permission for his proposed agitation at Azad Maidan.
Police cited law and order concerns amid the ongoing Ganeshotsav celebrations while rejecting the application.
Jarange has been demanding reservation for the Maratha community, including the issuance of Kunbi caste certificates to eligible Marathas. Despite uncertainty surrounding permission for the Mumbai agitation and concerns over his health, Jarange had set out from Antarwali Sarati towards Mumbai.

Legendary Nigerian actor Olu Jacobs dies aged 84
- Published
Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.
His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.
Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".
Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.
He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.
"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.
Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.
He became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.
His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.
In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.
Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.
In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.
In 2021, Silva disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy bodies.
"It's a degenerative disease that affects the brain and it's almost like a Parkinson-type of disease - it affects the brain and affects the person," she said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Chude Jideonwo.
On several occasions, there were rumours that Jacobs had died, but his family would promptly debunk them, the latest being in June 2024 when his eldest son, Soji, went on TV to say his father was still alive.

Jon McCracken is also playing regularly for Bradford City in England's League One, but Liam Kelly very much remains second choice at Rangers.
As for the backline, the new Scotland boss has predominantly played with a back three throughout his coaching career at both Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco.
He insists on his teams being aggressive in and out of possession, so will want defenders capable of picking brave passes but also with the pace to cover big distances when playing a high line.
Scott McKenna, Jack Hendry and Kieran Tierney all have experience of playing in a back three under Steve Clarke, albeit the approach will differ under Pocognoli. Captain Andy Robertson also clocked up a lot of minutes at left wing-back.
Aaron Hickey, Nathan Patterson and young Colby Donovan, who has impressed Pocognoli "but needs to improve on things like every young lad", are options for the opposite flank.
Uncapped trio Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and Luke Graham add more depth at centre-back.
Brondby captain Binks, who qualifies for Scotland through a grandparent, has had an interesting career. "The feeling and the timing about him was right," Pocognoli said of the former Bologna and Como man.
At the age of 25, the left-footed centre-back has already played in the MLS, Serie A, English Championship and now Denmark's top tier.
Meanwhile, Stoke's Graham - also left-footed - enjoyed a breakthrough spell at Dundee last season and continues to excel in England's second division, along with Swansea's Welsh, who proved he could thrive in a possession-based Motherwell side last term.
McPake included in familiar midfield
It is much of the same in midfield, although Scott McTominay is absent following a successful heart procedure and Udinese's Lennon Miller is back after being left out of Clarke's World Cup squad.
There is a welcome return for McTominay's Napoli team-mate Billy Gilmour, who suffered a crushing injury just before the start of the finals.
Arguably Scotland's most composed midfielder and best progressive passer, many expect the 25-year-old to thrive in Pocognoli's system. Miller, 20, could also fall into that category.
Experienced campaigners John McGinn, Ryan Christie, Kenny McLean and Lewis Ferguson - the Scots' standout performer earlier this summer - are all included in a seven-man midfield selection, which also features thriving Hearts player Josh McPake.
Signed this summer from St Johnstone, it has been a remarkable rise for the 24-year-old, who has been listed as a midfielder in the squad despite featuring on the left wing for the Tynecastle side. He was a Stirling Albion player just two years ago.
How excited should fans be by new-look attack?
While Ben Gannon-Doak, Findlay Curtis and McPake offer options in attacking wide areas, there is a centre-forward spot up for grabs in the absence of injured pair Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, plus the omission of Lyndon Dykes.
A free-scoring spell in Sweden earned Robbie Ure the number nine shirt at Sevilla, Oli McBurnie and his Hull team have made an impressive return to the Premier League and Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie scored in a win against Juventus on Sunday.
"Players who are performing well are in the new pathway," Pocognoli said when asked about Rangers academy product Ure, who is yet to score since his switch to La Liga.
"Robbie is adapting well to La Liga. He's put in some good performances, but he maybe needs to adapt to the intensity. Being selected gives him an opportunity."
On the return of McBurnie, who has received his first Scotland call-up in five years, he added: "It's regarding style of play, playing time and performance. I have to start on a new journey, a new book and it's a new opportunity for some players."
The head coach also spoke of his desire to mix youth with the "DNA and heritage" of his squad, evidenced by the inclusion of teenage James Wilson, who is showing signs of fulfilling his serious potential at Hearts.
By the end of the first week in October the Tartan Army, many of whom have been calling for what Pocognoli is preaching to deliver, will have a clearer idea of what that formula is going to look like on the grass, with a fascinating four-match window approaching.

Athletic Club forward Williams retires from Ghana duty
- Published
Athletic Club forward Inaki Williams has announced his retirement from international duty with Ghana.
The 32-year-old scored two goals in 28 caps for the Black Stars after making his debut in September 2022.
He featured for the West Africans at the 2022 and 2026 Fifa World Cups and the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Williams appeared twice at this year's World Cup as Ghana were knocked out in the last 32 by Colombia.
"I feel the time has come to bring my journey with the Ghana national team to an end," he said in a post on social media.
"I leave happy, proud and with the peace of mind of knowing that I gave everything every time I wore this shirt."
Williams, who was born in Bilbao to Ghanaian parents, chose to represent the Black Stars after previously playing for Spain at youth level and in a 2016 friendly at senior level.
His younger brother Nico, who also plays for Athletic Club in Bilbao, chose to represent Spain and has gone on to become a World Cup and European Championship winner with La Roja.
Inaki Williams' announcement comes a week after it was confirmed that Carlos Queiroz would return as Ghana coach in the build-up to the 2027 Afcon in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
He said his time with Ghana had given him "much more than football".
"It has allowed me to come back home, feel even closer to my roots and experience the enormous pride of representing my country and wearing this flag on my chest," he added.
"Thank you from the bottom of my heart to everyone who has been part of this journey and for all the love you have always shown me.
"Ghana will always be a part of me. I will continue supporting the Black Stars as one of you, wherever I am."

Indigenous leader Raoni receives palliative care in Brazil after cancer diagnosis
Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute says
SAO PAULO -- Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute said Monday.
The Raoni Institute said the cancer diagnosis in the chief's digestive system was confirmed after he was hospitalized in Sao Paulo in June due to a severe intestinal obstruction. He underwent surgery then and returned to the region of the city of Peixoto de Azevedo, in Brazil's Mato Grosso state.
“At this moment, our priority is ensuring that Chief Raoni is well cared for, comfortable, and close to his family and his people. We wish to share this information transparently, but we also ask for respect regarding his privacy, his need for rest, and his family’s decisions,” the institute said in a statement.
Raoni, one of the most renowned advocates for the protection of the Amazon rainforest and for Indigenous rights, traveled the world for decades to raise awareness about environmental preservation.
Doctors opted for palliative care given Raoni's advanced age, overall clinical condition, and the high risks associated with aggressive oncological treatments, the institute said.
“Palliative care does not mean an absence of treatment. The goal is to control pain and other symptoms, prevent complications, and ensure nutrition, hydration, medical supervision, nursing care, physical therapy, and the best possible quality of life,” it added.
Raoni is currently resting at home, surrounded by his family, community, and specialized health teams. The care plan also incorporates intercultural and spiritual support, the institute added, which honors his Indigenous heritage and allows traditional healers alongside medical professionals.

Hackers ripped down a Flock camera above a roadway, made a near-complete copy of the data stored inside it, and shared the files with 404 Media and WIRED, revealing in new detail how exactly Flock Safety’s cameras track the movements of both vehicles and people. The hackers say they are also publishing details on how they managed to obtain the software, in the hopes that other people may copy them.
The breach provides an unprecedented look inside a system that Flock has described as protected by on-device encryption. The hackers were able to copy the camera’s storage and recover an encryption key stored on the device, which unlocked videos of thousands of vehicle detections. The hackers shared the material with 404 Media and the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, which shared the data with WIRED. 404 Media and WIRED then analyzed those files as part of a joint investigation.
While much of the automatic license plate reader’s most sensitive storage remained encrypted and inaccessible, the joint analysis of the recovered data shows that software running on the device explicitly detects people as well as vehicles, license plates, and bicycles. The camera can produce dozens of images of a single passing vehicle and, according to several weeks of recovered logs, generated more than a million images. Its computer-vision software also sometimes isolated bumper stickers and other graphics, including, in one case, an American flag patch on a motorcyclist’s saddlebag.
The act of removing the camera and dumping its software shows that some people are not content with just destroying or removing the cameras. Across the country, multiple people have been arrested for allegedly tampering with or otherwise sabotaging Flock’s cameras. In response, some towns have announced that they are going to stop using Flock’s cameras altogether, and in one case, a police department even made a fake, 3D-printed Flock camera case in order to bait potential vandals.
“Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?” one of the hackers, from a collective calling itself stegan0gram, said in an interview. “We liberated hardware in the field, disarmed them, and proceeded with reverse engineering of the cameras and associated solar equipment.”
Flock’s cameras photograph passing vehicles and send the images and other data to the company’s servers. There, Flock’s system presumably reads the license plate and can identify characteristics such as the vehicle’s color, make, and model. Flock then makes these time-stamped records searchable by whichever local agency owns or has access to the cameras. But in many cases, Flock’s system also allows other police departments from all over the country to search those cameras too, as part of the company’s national network. In Alpharetta, Georgia, for example, WIRED found that records from the city’s Flock cameras were accessible to more than 2,000 agencies, including police departments, colleges, airports, and, inexplicably, the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration.
This national network has been a selling point for Flock but also a deep source of controversy. 404 Media revealed that local cops were performing lookups in the national network on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including in areas that banned working with immigration authorities or transferring license plate data out of state. 404 Media also revealed that a cop in Texas searched Flock cameras nationwide for a woman who self-administered an abortion. Those stories, among others, triggered a national conversation about whether people want Flock cameras, or automatic license plate readers more generally, in their communities.
And in the case of stegan0gram, the answer is clearly no.
The hackers said they were able to access the Android system on the camera and found two partitions—sections of its hard drive, essentially. A few of these were unencrypted, the hackers said, including one called “vendor” and another called “media.” The latter contained an encryption key that unlocked another part, which contained much of the media—the videos and stills—the camera took.
In early 2025, security researcher Jon “GainSec” Gaines reverse engineered a Flock license-plate reader and documented flaws that could be used to gain root-level access. After Gaines disclosed his findings, the company acknowledged the findings but downplayed their severity, writing that the flaws required physical access to the device and that even someone who gained access to a camera “would still not be able to gain access to footage,” because images remained on the device only briefly after being transmitted to the cloud.
404 Media and WIRED analyzed the camera’s contents. The device’s processor is similar to those used in midrange smartphones, and it runs about 20 Flock-built apps that handle everything from detecting motion and taking pictures to classifying objects, uploading data, and receiving remote updates.
According to the code, when something moves into view, the camera takes a rapid series of photos. A typical passing vehicle generated about 28 images, though some produced more than 100. The camera uses different exposures to capture both the license plate and the wider scene, then scans the images, selects and crops useful frames, and sends them with other data to Flock over the cellular network. The camera itself does not appear to read the plate or identify the vehicle’s make, model, and color. That appears to happen on Flock’s servers.
According to our analysis, the camera’s logs recorded about 21 days of activity across several periods. During those windows, the device photographed roughly 50,200 vehicles and generated about 1.6 million images. On a typical day, it logged around 3,300 vehicles, with a high of 4,454. Those figures would vary considerably depending on where a camera is installed and how much traffic passes in front of it. The camera was almost certainly operating outside those periods, but older logs had been overwritten or were no longer recoverable from the device.
The software running on the camera explicitly detects people, something which is typically overlooked in discussions around Flock cameras. When it spots a person, it records where they appear in the image and how confident it is in the detection.
To test what the software could actually see, WIRED extracted the models from the camera’s files and ran them against test images and footage recovered from the device. The models readily detected people, including a selfie of a reporter. WIRED then ran them across 27,321 short videoclips stored on the camera. The clips were MP4 files, each about one to two seconds long, recorded at 1,024 by 768 pixels without audio. They were separate from the rapid bursts of higher-resolution still images the camera also takes as vehicles pass. The models detected people in 11 of the clips, all of them riding motorcycles. The small number is likely due to the camera’s position above a roadway, pointed down at passing traffic where pedestrians were unlikely to appear.
The tests also showed how broadly the camera’s license plate detector could interpret what it saw. In some cases it mistook bumper stickers, dealership frames, and other graphics for license plates and cropped them out as if they were plates. In one video of a passing motorcycle, the detector cropped an American flag patch on the rider’s saddlebag as if it were a plate.
Flock insists its cameras do not perform face recognition. WIRED and 404 Media found no evidence of any face-recognition capabilities in the camera’s software beyond ones included by default in the Android operating system. Those capabilities did not appear to be enabled or in active use.
In August, WIRED obtained frontend code for Flock’s police software, now called OS Investigate and previously known as Nightshift, and reconstructed portions of the tool. That software showed how Flock can use the records generated by its cameras, along with police files and commercial data, to identify drivers, surface vehicles that repeatedly travel together, and search for people based on patterns of movement. The data provides a view of the other end of a system.
A Flock spokesperson said in a statement: “The unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal.” When asked specifically about the encryption key stored on the camera, the company added, “Flock takes security seriously and maintains a public Vulnerability Disclosure Policy for security researchers to report potential vulnerabilities directly to us. We received no report through that process, and based on the limited information provided, we do not have enough detail to assess the claims being made. If the individuals identified legitimate vulnerabilities, we encourage them to submit their technical findings through our vulnerability reporting process so our security team can review them and take any appropriate action.”
One of the hackers said, “Being investigated is a legit concern and something we are trying to avoid. I'm sure our actions have attracted some attention as it is, but we are careful and try to keep a low profile.”
Noel Pichardo, a former Pawtucket, Rhode Island, police officer who became an outspoken critic of Flock after challenging his department’s use of the cameras, says he understands the activists’ frustration but worries that sabotaging devices could ultimately strengthen the case for them. “I think that type of vigilantism will only crystallize the police and the state at large in their belief that this tool is necessary,” Pichardo says. “The longer the state continues to ignore the groanings of their constituents who are against this type of surveillance, the more this will happen.”
The camera’s logs also show the camera struggling with storage. Its logs recorded more than 27,000 “no space left on device” errors while trying to save full-resolution images, along with tens of thousands of related errors, crashes, and reboots. At the same time, about every two minutes, code checked that the camera was still running and logged the message, “Who’s a good boy?!” More than 12,000 of those messages appear in the recovered logs.
When the camera did restart, another service left a final message in the logs: “A reboot was requested! ¡Adiós, Amigos!”
