A shopkeeper’s alleged murder in West Bengal’s Titagarh on September 11 has triggered a controversy after Barrackpore BJP MLA Koustav Bagchi attempted to give it a communal spin by describing the victim as a ‘Sanatani’ murdered by ‘jihadis’.
In a 33-secong-long video that has now gone viral for over a week, the MLA’s claim was challenged on camera by the victim’s son, who interrupted Bagchi to say that there was nothing communal or political about his father’s murder.
The victim, Ramji Shaw, used to run a small corner shop from a portion of his home in the GC road area of Ward 18 of Barrackpore Municipality. He was allegedly killed after he refused to sell cigarettes on credit.
According to the locals, on September 11 afternoon, Shaw was trying to protect his son, who was allegedly being assaulted by three young men who were demanding to buy cigarettes from the shop without paying money on spot. As Shaw declined to sell cigarettes on credit, the men allegedly began attacking him and his son.
In the physical altercation, Shaw was pushed and heckled and lost consciousness. His family members rushed him to Barrackpore B N Bose sub-divisional hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries. According to locals, the three accused have been identified as Banti Ghosh, Sk. Sahil and Md. Nasir. Shaw’s wife had told Bengali news channel ABP Ananda that the accused had assaulted their son in the past.
Deceased’s Son Corrects MLA
As news of the alleged murder spread in the locality, Bagchi visited the deceased’s family the same day. Speaking to news channels while at Shaw’s home, he attempted to present the murder as communally motivated, specifically targeting the identity of the two accused who belong to the Muslim community.
In the viral clip, Bagchi can be heard saying (translated from Bengali), “This incident is not just related to an altercation over payment. Three Jihadis have killed a Sanatani. They wouldn’t have killed someone from their own religion.” However, even before Bagchi could finish his sentence, the deceased’s son corrected him, (translated from Bengali), “Sir, there is nothing related to religion in this case. The accused had come to my shop, looking to buy things on credit. When my father objected, they beat him up.”
The BJP MLA, seeming baffled by the interruption, responded: “I am speaking! Why are you not letting me speak!”. A few moments later, a person in purple shirt can be seen escorting the son to another room. While leaving the scene, the son stated, “This is not a matter of party politics.”
‘Politicians Inciting Locals for Electoral Gains’
Alt News visited the locality to independently verify the claims surrounding the murder and Bagchi’s allegation of a communal motive. While the bereaved wife and son both declined to speak, Shaw’s daughter Rikita confirmed to Alt News that it was indeed her brother who was seen correcting Bagchi in the viral video.
Sheikh Afroz (Ripon), who is Shaw’s immediate neighbour, said that the people in the area lived in communal harmony, as Hindus and Muslims co-existed there for generations. He added that politicians were, in fact, attempting to incite hostility between the communities. He also confirmed that Shaw’s son was seen in the video. “After the tragic incident, locals started to protest against the ‘gundagardi’ culture, and police officers had to come and pacify the situation. As the area is predominantly occupied by Muslims, most of the protesters were also Muslim. Does this not prove that this was not a communal incident?” asked Afroz.
A few metres from Shaw’s house, Md Mansoor, who runs a mobile repairing shop, said that Shaw’s shop used to have ‘ittar’ (perfume) and ‘surma’ (kohl) which were not found anywhere else in the area. “Every Eid, people from the Muslim community thronged to his shop to buy these products. Given that this was the reality which we saw every day, we don’t understand where this communal angle is coming from,” he said.
According to Mansoor, the accused youths were “known troublemakers”. “It is unfair to malign the name of an entire area and community for the wrongdoings of a select few. One of the accused is a Hindu, but the MLA still went on to claim that Shaw was murdered by Jihadis. Most of the shops in the neighbourhood, which is a predominantly Muslim area, were all shut in protest of Shaw’s murder for a few days after, only because there is no feeling of communal tension in this area,” Mansoor added.
No Communal Motive: Police
Alt News spoke to Titagrah officer-in-charge (OC) Atanu Chakraborty. The police station is located 1 km away from the crime scene. The officer confirmed that three people had been arrested in connection with the case. He said police did not find any communal motive behind the incident. The accused had pushed and beaten Shaw, following which Shaw suffered a stroke and died, he added.
“The accused are Sk Sahil, Md Nasir and Banti Ghosh. We have primarily booked them under sections pertaining to murder and further investigation is on. We couldn’t find any communal angle behind the crime,” he said, adding, the accused have been involved in public nuisance in the area in the past.
The police account, therefore, refutes Bagchi’s claims of a communal motive behind the alleged murder.
My Comments Twisted, Victim’s Son Apologised later, Claims MLA
Speaking to Alt News, Bagchi alleged, “There is no confusion. Some people are trying to do mischief with my quote. If I wanted, I could have done a lot of things over this issue, but I restrained myself considering the situation of the family. The area where this family lives are surrounded by Muslims — 90 out of 100 people living here are Muslims. The Hindu’s are constantly under a lot of pressure. So, whatever they said that day is due to fear.”
“I have a video of Ramji Shaw’s son. He had made a video and had sent it to me, clarifying their position. He also called me and apologised. Since my comments are being twisted, now I feel I have to publish the video that I have. I told his son that I can understand his emotions, his pain and fear. In the video, he also said that Hindus in that area are very few in number compared to the Muslims. However, they haven’t yet realised that the TMC government is gone and they [Hindus] are safe. I told him to be fearless,” Bagchi claimed, adding, “There definitely is a communal angle to this incident. The Muslims have kept the Hindus in that are terrorised.”
When asked about the one Hindu accused and how he could confidently claim that Shaw was murdered by ‘jihadis’, Bagchi said, “Banti Ghosh is a rowdy element and he mixes with them [the other two accused]. However, the main culprits are the two Muslims men. They have continued this for long, and you won’t find them attacking any Muslim.”
Alt News’ interactions with the locals and an observation of how they live, however, contradict Bagchi’s ‘fear of Muslims’ narrative. Shaw’s house is 550 metres from the Titagarh railway station. About 200 metres from the station, beside G C Road, stands a Muslim shrine (mazar), and next to it, a Ganesh Puja pandal has been erected. The two structures are separated only by a food stall.
A search on Google Maps of the area brought up an image from two years ago, in which a Durga Puja pandal was erected right next to the same Muslim shrine.
Further down the road, opposite to Mansoor’s shop, is Hasanjan Sporting Club, and a Hindu temple stands right next to it.
Pointing towards the narrow path beside the club, Mansoor said, “Ten families live there. Six are Muslim and four are Hindu.”

What Trump’s Bizarre Posts Are Teaching Us About AI
The president’s recent Truth Social barrage of fake images reflects the dangers—for all of us—of virtual self-aggrandizement.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Here is a selective list of the dozens of images the president has recently disseminated on Truth Social: Donald Trump on a horse next to George Washington on a horse, in the body of Hulk Hogan, beating Hogan in arm wrestling, standing between General George Patton and General Douglas MacArthur in a World War II uniform, hovering menacingly with a hockey stick over the Canadian prime minister, commanding the deck of an aircraft carrier, nuking parts of Earth from space, gleefully dancing to “YMCA” as he replaces a sign for Lake Ontario with one for Lake America. Maybe most surreal (though, admittedly, kind of funny), he posted a video of a squad of “Donald Ducks” with his signature hair, armed with machine guns, waddling in formation to protect said lake.
Trump has never been shy about his proclivity for self-aggrandizement (daydreaming about having his face chiseled onto Mount Rushmore or printed on a $250 bill). But his recent spate of social-media posts—almost all products of AI—has him living in an expanded fantasyland. His supporters are likely to just giggle; more fun and trolling—so what? His critics might roll their eyes at the extravagant immaturity but almost can’t be bothered anymore (unless they’re Iceland). After a decade of Trump shenanigans, getting worked up either way is hard. Also, these images might come across as just a little sad—the projections of a man who is losing power and virility but desperately needs to see himself as powerful and virile.
The absurd cartoons are worth pondering, though, and not for the sake of getting to know Trump better (I believe that onion has been thoroughly peeled). Because what AI can do to exaggerate and aggrandize Trump, it can do to everyone. For the president, this may be just one more level up on his escalator of self-regard, but for those without Napoleonic degrees of narcissism, the mental terrain opened up by these quick-prompt chimeras is new.
When the psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan wanted to understand how the ego takes shape, he thought of mirrors. Sometime from six to 18 months of age, he theorized, a baby begins to recognize their reflection, and experiences what Lacan—abstruse French structuralist that he was—described as the “jubilant assumption of his specular image.” In plainer words, the baby realizes, That’s me! This is significant because the child at this point is otherwise a fragmented mess, experiencing the world through disconnected sensation. Lacan thought the mirror provides an idealized perception of wholeness when, really, inside it’s all a scramble, and through this illusion of coherence, a proper ego—a sense of self—begins to bud.
Lacan didn’t believe that we ever really outgrow this reliance on our reflection, whether seen above a bathroom sink or in the ways other people look at us. But the mirror he had in mind could show you only the person who stands in front of it—the image is always tethered to physical reality. The AI mirror is something else. It asks what we’d like to see and produces it.
In the past, only kings and emperors could indulge their most exalted, exaggerated picture of themselves. They could commission heroic, larger-than-life representations—though even these were limited by available materials and plausible realism. AI image-making has now democratized this kind of statue-building. I know because I just asked ChatGPT to create an image of me astride a bronze horse in the center of a city, and I’ve never looked more commanding. But AI can do so much more: The ideal self has escaped the confines of the mirror and even the gilded sculpture; it can now inflate to unimaginable dimensions.
In this new world, our insecurities are not obstacles; they are starting points. Take my modest height. I can conjure up what I would look like in Victor Wembanyama’s stretched-taffy body—though I’d settle for something one foot shorter. I’m fully aware that this is just an image, and a bizarre one, but it engraves this taller me—a version who walks into a party and looks down, not up, at everyone—into my brain. It creates a gulf between reality and such a picture. This fantasy made manifest can either delude or taunt me. It exists, and I can’t forget it. Conversely, I should say, it also reveals what I’m most self-conscious about—exactly as AI does for Trump. The puffed up, dominating, victorious man with the six-pack is what the AI mirror shows the president, because that is what he prompts it to show him. (In most cases, of course, he is reposting images prompted by supporters, who are thereby exposing their own displaced fantasies.)
To give Trump a little credit, he seems vaguely aware of the idea that AI is, like the Mirror of Erised in Harry Potter, showing us what we most want. One of his posts has Barack Obama looking into a mirror and asking: Mirror mirror on the wall who’s the greatest president of them all. No surprise, it’s Trump, who is staring back at him.
What I see in the AI mirror is greater than I could ever be—and infinitely editable. Instead of feeding a desire for coherence, as Lacan imagined, it creates a bottomless hunger for the unachievable. I can keep tweaking it with more prompts: “Give me thicker hair. Make my jaw more chiseled.” Start down this road, I’m afraid, and you’ll encounter unhappy young men using hammers to shape their actual faces so that they can come closer to the digital simulacra.
Not all people are narcissists, and certainly not all are like Trump. But we are all susceptible. Who doesn’t dream occasionally of evading reality or the truth of the body you are stuck living in? On the scale of human history, it has been only about a second since we got photography (and the inevitable selfie) to augment what for so long only a pond’s surface or a piece of glass could show us: our own face. What will come from finding, instead, Supermen, kings, popes, and Jedi staring back at us?
Without AI, Trump might be forced to look around him, perhaps at the portraits of other presidents in the White House—just like Richard Nixon did. In their book The Final Days, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein recounted what became a famous story: As Nixon’s presidency was crashing down around him, he began talking at night to these dead former presidents. (One of his sons-in-law denied this claim.) Oliver Stone dramatized the moment in his 1995 film, Nixon: The defeated, haggard president focuses on a painting of John F. Kennedy and says, with startling self-awareness, “When they look at you, they see what they want to be. When they look at me, they see what they are.”
Fiction, I know. But this is the kind of reckoning that can happen when you have no choice but to see what is in front of you. Trump is also very aware of the presidents who came before him. In another recent post, he ranks them all in a tiered chart from Great (Lincoln, FDR, Jefferson, and so on) to Failures (Biden, Obama, Carter, and so on). And atop the entire graphic in a box roughly four times the size of all the others, Trump’s severe, unsmiling face looks out under a label that reads back to him: The Greatest.

When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

US defense chiefs warn of munitions shortfall as Iran war costs hit $33bn
President Donald Trump’s ‘Operation Epic Fury’ assault on Iran has cost $33.4 billion and has resulted in a strategic missile shortage, the Department of Defense’s inspector general finds
President Donald Trump’s “Operation Epic Fury” assault on Iran cost $33.4 billion in its first four months and has resulted in a munitions shortfall, according to a report by the Department of Defense’s inspector general.
The 44-page report to Congress states that, between February 28 and June 30, the joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran saw the Trump administration spend $22.3 billion on munitions alone.
The onslaught “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Inspector General Platte B Moring III concludes.
His report also lists the damage done to American military assets by Tehran’s retaliatory strikes, listing four F-15Es and and up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones as destroyed and one F-35A, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft and seven helicopters as damaged.
The F-35A plane is the first of its type to be compromised by enemy fire, according to CNBC, and would cost $92 million to replace. An F-15E, meanwhile, costs $31.1 million to produce, U.S. Air Force data indicates, putting the pricetag for replacing four at $124.4 million.
The U.S. also spent $79.2 million responding to emergencies arising from the conflict “such as evacuation-related expenses for State personnel and their family members, U.S. citizens, and eligible third-country nationals.”
Damage done to U.S. diplomatic premises in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. add another $184 million to the bill.
Even further expense was incurred by Iranian strikes on military buildings and infrastructure in the U.S.-allied Gulf states of Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan, although no cost is calculated in the report as it is not yet clear whether they will be restored and who would pay for the work.
The Independent has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies was asked by CBS News, in response to the report’s findings, whether he believed the U.S. still had a sufficient supply of munitions to call upon.
“For a war against Iran, the answer is yes,” he answered. “The problem is a war against China. We might be able to provide enough munitions for a month, but getting on to month two or month three or four, that’s a great challenge.”
Trump himself has repeatedly insisted the U.S. has no munitions supply issues but was angered when it was reported in early August that he had confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the matter at Camp David in Maryland, reportedly saying he thought the problem “had been fixed.”
The president took to Truth Social in anger over the story, threatening the “leakers” who spoke to the press with jail.
Reuters reported around the same time that the U.S. Army had significantly depleted its stockpile of long-range missiles, using up “virtually all” of its crucial surface-to-surface weapons.
Trump was back on his social media platform Monday to claim: “The United States is producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History.
“They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East, and beyond. Our Defense Company Factories are moving 24/7, while at the same time building, on average, 4 to 5 largescale brand new Plants, each!
“A primary focus of this production has been Patriots, THAAD Systems, Tomahawks, and other Standard Missile Systems, of which we already have large numbers in stock.”
His unpopular war has rumbled on for another 10 weeks since the period documented by the report and shows no obvious sign of coming to an end even now, although Trump has said he is “open” to negotiations with Iran while stressing the final decision rests with him.
At least 18 U.S. soldiers have been killed and more than 750 service members injured in the conflict.

Trump’s Kennedy Center sabotage is complete

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump can’t put his name on the Kennedy Center — so he’s closing it, effective immediately.
What’s happening? On Tuesday, the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted to close the building indefinitely, shortly after a federal judge rebuked efforts to engrave Trump’s name into the facade.

How did we get here? Trump has been obsessed with claiming the Kennedy Center — a memorial for an assassinated president — and its cultural cachet for himself ever since he returned to office last year. He quickly stacked the Kennedy Center board with his appointees, then installed himself as chair.
In December, he had his name added to the building’s facade and its official title, temporarily making it the Trump-Kennedy Center. A federal judge ordered him to undo the renaming in June, and the administration complied — but the facade has remained covered since then, obscuring the removal.
In August, Trump also threatened the center with demolition if he didn’t get his way; he sounded a similar note in a Truth Social post Tuesday, writing that “the Building is destined to doom.”

Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour.

"Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added.

Draper making changes as Murray remains part of team - analysis
Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm.

Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required.

More than 100,000 people in Japan are now aged 100 or older
- Published
The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry.
Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of whom 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto.
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology.
But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system.
Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.
The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets.
Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch.
Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade.
Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus.
For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14.
The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research.
Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070.
Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency".
In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating.
The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates.
Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children.
While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown.
When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998.
The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup.
Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures.
A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously.
The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions.

Multiple inmates stabbed during brawl at notorious New York jail housing Luigi Mangione and Nicolas Maduro
Several inmates’ injuries were so severe that they had to seek medical treatment outside of the jail, according to federal officials
Multiple inmates have been stabbed and slashed during a major brawl at the federal jail in New York City that is currently housing UnitedHealthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione and disgraced former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Federal officials confirmed to The Independent that the massive fight took place on the morning of September 6 at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York. The New York Daily News first reported on the brawl, which their sources said was gang-related.
Members of the Trinitarios gang fought another gang on the seventh floor of the jail’s west building, the Daily News’ sources said, adding that a total of at least 20 people had joined in the brawl.
“Several incarcerated individuals were medically assessed and treated for minor injuries at the facility, while other incarcerated individuals sustained injuries requiring outside medical treatment,” Donald Murphy, a spokesperson for the Federal Bureau of Prisons, told The Independent.
Murphy did not confirm the exact number of inmates involved in the fight and the number of those wounded remains unknown. The exact injuries that the wounded inmates sustained are also not clear.
Murphy told The Independent that jail employees were able to contain the incident without being injured themselves, adding, “At no time was the public in danger.” The incident is still under investigation.
MDC Brooklyn, as the jail is commonly referred to, is known for holding infamous inmates like Mangione and Maduro.
Mangione, 28, is currently awaiting sentencing in the jail after he admitted last month to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on the streets of Manhattan in 2024. Thompson’s murder shocked the nation as the New York City Police Department tracked down the Ivy League graduate, with some admiring the killer for what they saw as a stance against the health insurance industry.
“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died,” Mangione said in court on August 14. “I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”
Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 69, are currently awaiting trial at the jail on drug trafficking charges, following a stealth mission by American forces to capture the couple from their Caracas home in early January. Their trial is set for next June.
Both have pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from an alleged conspiracy to transport thousands of tons of cocaine to the U.S.
Maduro “and his co-conspirators have, for decades, partnered with some of the most violent and prolific drug traffickers and narco-terrorists in the world, and relied on corrupt officials throughout the region, to distribute tons of cocaine to the United States,” their indictment reads.
MDC Brooklyn has a history of violence, including the reported February 2025 stabbing of Karl Jordan Jr., who was convicted and then acquitted of the 2002 murder of New York rap star Jam Master Jay. Jordan survived the attack.
In September 2024, the Justice Department announced charges against nine inmates in five separate cases involving violence at MDC Brooklyn, including the murder of Uriel Whyte on June 7, 2024, and the murder of Edwin Cordero on July 17, 2024.
“Violence will not be tolerated in our federal jails,” Breon Peace, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said at the time. “As the only federal pretrial facility in New York City, MDC-Brooklyn houses pretrial inmates accused of some of the most serious crimes in our region.”
“Let these charges serve as a warning to those who would engage in criminal conduct behind bars, and anyone else who facilitates those crimes: your conduct will be exposed, and you will be held accountable,’ Peace said.

"The flag-off event in Vadnagar will be attended by Amit Shah, Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel, state unit BJP president Jagdish Vishwakarma, Maharashtra Deputy CM Eknath Shinde and Union Minister Anupriya Patel among others," said VD Sharma, the national in-charge of the Vadnagar-Varanasi bike rally.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu and Union Minister Chirag Paswan, among other leaders will be present for the Varanasi event.
"The rally starting from Vadnagar will traverse various parts of the country before reaching Varanasi, while the journey originating in Varanasi will proceed towards Vadnagar," said Sharma, according to PTI.

Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.
The defensive midfielder, 30, was out of contract following his release from Spurs in June but is now set for a return to football in the Netherlands.

The Mali international is currently in Amsterdam finalising the move to the Eredivisie club.
Bissouma joined Spurs in 2022 and made 111 appearances for the north London outfit following a high-profile move from Brighton.

The new Boox Palma 3 comes with stylus support and an aluminum build
Boox has unveiled three new E Ink devices.
Boox has unveiled three new E Ink devices that all run Android 16 and come pre-installed with the Google Play Store, including the latest version of its popular Palma palm-sized ereader. The Boox Palma 3 has an anodized aluminum frame, unlike previous models that have plastic casing. Similar to the Boox Palma 2 Pro, it supports the Boox InkSense Plus stylus, so you can annotate books or jot down notes saved on the cloud. It has a 6.13-inch HD E Ink screen with a dual-tone front light and 128GB of storage that you can expand with a microSD card up to 2TB in size to hold quite a big amount of books.
The device's 3,950mAh battery can power days of reading on a single charge, but it will likely run out sooner if you frequently use the reader's 16MP rear camera. Boox says you can use the camera, which comes with a flash, to scan documents. In addition, the reader has dual microphones for voice memos and speech-to-text. The Boox Palma 3 is already up on the company's website, but it's not available for sale yet. You will be able to get it in black or white when it does come out for $320, a full $60 cheaper than the Boox Palma 2 Pro. Boox is selling the stylus separately, however, and it will cost you an extra $46.
Aside from the Palma 3, Boox has also unveiled the 10.3-inch Note Air6 C. Its big, color E Ink display will allow you to read documents and take notes without having to jump between two screens. A new feature called Dual Notes will also give you a way to annotate two different documents side by side. The device supports the Boox Pen3 stylus and comes with a keyboard cover that connects to it via pogo pins. You can now get the Note Air6 C for $580 without the keyboard or for $657 bundled with the keyboard cover.
Finally, Boox has unveiled the Note Mini C for people who need to work in transit. It comes with an 8.52-inch color E Ink screen, a fingerprint-enabled power button and a stylus. The device can also access enterprise apps like Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Slack and OneDrive. It's listed as "available soon" on Boox's website for $550.

Poll data released Tuesday by the New York Times and Siena University confirms what we’ve already been seeing, and what politicians are responding to — AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular. Asked if they support or oppose the construction of data centers to power AI tech, 61 percent of the 1,503 likely voters surveyed in early September (ahead of the recent AI safety slowdown discussion) said they were opposed, with only 14 percent saying they strongly support. The split was about even among 2024 Donald Trump voters, at 49 percent support to 45 percent oppose, while people who had voted for Kamala Harris or who didn’t vote leaned oppose, at 74 percent and 67 percent, respectively.
AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular in every poll
61 percent of likely voters said they oppose the construction of AI data centers, but neither major party has much of an edge.
56 percent of voters surveyed who said they were opposed to data centers said they supported limits, while 38 percent instead preferred a total ban. The list of reasons for opposition is also revealing, with the environment/water usage most common at 32 percent, impact on local communities at 21 percent, general distrust or dislike of AI at 18 percent, followed by regulation concerns and the economy at 10 and 9 percent.
An NBC News poll in March showed AI polling lower than ICE, and a Gallup poll in May revealed seven in ten Americans opposed local construction of AI data centers.
Still, the data released today ranked AI and data centers low on the list of issues that voters saw as most important in deciding their midterm vote. Across the board, AI and data centers registered at less than one percent for most demographics, with exceptions for younger voters like the 18-29 group, where three percent picked that one instead of the most popular responses like the economy, foreign policy, inflation, and opposition to Trump/Republicans. Voters in either party still overwhelmingly picked their own party as the one they trusted to handle the issue, while overall the 554 respondents had 40 percent favoring Democrats, 42 percent favoring Republicans, and 18 percent saying they didn’t know or refused.

Almost every Indian payments giant delivered a similar pitch at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 organised last week: merchants no longer need to inspect settlements, chase failed transactions and untangle disputes. An AI agent will do it instead. Five of the country’s largest B2B payments platforms introduced agents that can recover lost sales, reconcile chargebacks, pursue refunds and execute transactions, turning AI from an assistant into a protagonist in the payments chain. For starters, BharatPe, a merchant payments platform, launched an Agentic AI assistant built on Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise that works across more than 60 systems to resolve complaints and chargebacks, while also recommending products such as credit cards on UPI and loans. Similarly, digital payments provider PayU launched Agent HQ, a store where merchants deploy one agent per job. Cashfree also rolled out an agent for payment operations, Relay. Razorpay put an AI account manager named RAY on WhatsApp with IndusInd Bank. Meanwhile, Pine Labs went a step ahead, allowing an agent to complete the purchase itself. Pine Labs is now powering an agentic marketplace for L&T Finance. Cashfree's Relay is live for all its merchants. PayU’s Agent HQ and Razorpay's Agent Studio stay in early access. Together, these launches suggest that AI is moving beyond assistance. The questions are: who needs them, what work they can take on, and how much control businesses are willing to give them. What Are These Agents Up To? Proving adept at recovering failed payments, confirming orders, filing disputes and reconciling chargebacks, payments giants are building agents to take work off a merchant’s plate. Describing the shift, Reeju Datta, the cofounder of Cashfree Payments, said that most merchant AI worked like a copilot a year ago, preparing something for a person to review or send. "Now, the brief has changed. Agents are being built to complete the task themselves,” he added. He explains a widening list of jobs an AI agent can now own: Recovering abandoned carts and retrying failed payments Confirming cash-on-delivery orders before dispatch Managing failed subscription renewals Filing disputes before the deadline Reconciling chargebacks, escalating refunds and following up on settlements Some have upped the ante. At GFF, Pine Labs demonstrated an agentic purchase with Big Basket, where a customer could ask an agent to track the price of an iPhone and complete the purchase once it fell by 40%. While it may look like a consumer use case, it benefits the merchant directly. Tanya Naik, who heads online and omnichannel business at Pine Labs, pointed out the commercial logic behind the push, noting that a human-run payment never quite reaches complete success, while an agent-triggered transaction is captured against an amount already authorised, so the success rate is structurally higher. The same mechanism opens a second use case: re-engaging dormant customers. A deal seeker who never returns to a storefront can set an agent to buy the moment a price condition is met, turning the agent into another channel alongside Instagram, Facebook and Google ads. Who Needs These Agents? Not every merchant needs an AI agent. The first market is likely to be businesses where there is plenty of payment-related work, but very few people to handle it. Cashfree, for instance, has built Relay with small and medium businesses (SMBs) in mind, particularly lean teams of around five people with no dedicated payments or finance function. PayU's chief product officer, Manas Mishra, points to the same group, naming SMBs and mid-market merchants as the most relevant segment. Early interest is from D2C brands automating chargeback reconciliations, refund escalations, settlements, and transaction follow-ups, while also using agents to stay discoverable where their customers now search. Cashfree estimates a single agent working across its merchant base could recover as much as ₹20,000 Cr in sales lost to failed payments every year. For now, however, these agents are mostly recovering money and handling routine work rather than running the business. This may change as they are given more autonomy. How Much Autonomy Should Agents Enjoy? The more work merchants hand to agents, the more important the boundaries become. This is why payments platforms take different approaches towards setting a control layer. Cashfree’s Relay, for instance, only accesses a merchant’s own transaction data. It also has two checkpoints that an agent cannot cross without approval: before money moves and before a customer is contacted. PayU’s Agent HQ sits within the merchant’s existing dashboard, with the merchant setting the operational limits. Its agents cannot act beyond those boundaries. Pine Labs has taken a different approach with Grantex, an authority and trust layer built into its payments protocol. It checks each transaction against the mandate given to the agent and creates an audit trail that can be used to trace a transaction or resolve a dispute. Razorpay’s Agent Studio follows a review-first approach. Large transfers and deletions require a second confirmation and cannot be approved automatically. Despite the differences, the principle is broadly the same: agents can prepare, decide and execute routine tasks, but actions that move money, contact customers or cannot be reversed remain subject to human control. However, these boundaries are already starting to stretch. Cashfree’s Relay can generate custom agents once a merchant defines the business logic and desired outcome, moving beyond a fixed set of pre-built tasks. Pine Labs, meanwhile, wants to extend this self-service model to banks, allowing merchants to ask about a payment problem and have an agent resolve it. In other words, the agent is evolving from a feature into a layer that merchants can build on. However, if an agent makes a mistake, who bears the loss? Will it be the merchant, the payments platform or the bank? For now, there is no clear answer. The Weekly Buzz: We Must Pace the Frontier Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a detailed public statement titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that frontier labs must deliberately slow the rate at which they improve model capabilities so that safety work can keep pace. He was careful to distinguish this from a full halt: training and technical progress would continue, but companies would take adequate time to align and safeguard systems, with independent confirmation required before further leaps. Two developments drove the shift. First, recursive self-improvement has accelerated sharply since summer, with AI systems increasingly helping build the next generation of models. Second, recent agent incidents, including OpenAI’s swarm that breached external systems — showed that misaligned collective behaviour is already possible. Amodei warned that a more capable version of such a swarm could, within 6-12 months, assemble a persistent botnet across large parts of the internet. His three-step plan begins with a unilateral commitment Anthropic is implementing immediately: giving third-party evaluators permanent, employee-level access (desks, badges, laptops) and the right to publish findings without editorial control. The second step calls for coordination among labs in democratic countries on common safety standards and limits on unchecked progress. The third, hardest step involves eventual global coordination, including with China, while democracies maintain their technological lead through export controls and security measures. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and later Satya Nadella publicly endorsed the call. Altman confirmed OpenAI would also adopt embedded evaluators. The unusual alignment among rival CEOs, coming amid researcher resignations and a string of agent incidents, marks the first time the leading US labs have so openly agreed that capability gains must be deliberately paced rather than maximised at all costs. The world’s most common childhood disability, cerebral palsy, has long been associated with birth complications like premature birth, infection, lack of oxygen, and perinatal stroke. But population studies suggest those factors account for only a fraction of cases. To fill this diagnostic void, modern medicine has routinely turned to gene sequencing to hunt for a root cause, and researchers have zeroed in on certain genetic variants in a substantial subset of children with cerebral palsy.
For families, gene sequencing offers a profound hope: of ending a gruelling diagnostic odyssey. Finding a definitive genetic root cause optimises patient management, reduces unnecessary testing, and finally gives parents concrete answers.
But a new study in The American Journal of Human Genetics suggests simply finding a pathogenic gene variant in a child is not proof that it caused their motor disability.
In resource-constrained healthcare systems like India’s, acting on a false alarm from a standard genetic panel can divert already limited medical resources away from treatments that actually work.
“The medical community previously has not comprehensively examined the statistical evidence in favor of a cerebral palsy association for genes flagged in large genomics cohort studies,” Peter N. Robinson, a computational biologist at the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine, U.S., and the study’s corresponding author, said. “Our study showed that there is convincing evidence for only a subset.”
Collapsing narrative
The researchers combed through 21 previously published genomic diagnostic studies involving 5,440 individuals diagnosed with cerebral palsy. Across these diverse cohorts, the original authors had pointed the finger at a staggering 515 different candidate genes, reporting them as the direct genetic cause of the patients’ symptoms.
But when Dr. Robinson’s team subjected this historical data to rigorous statistical analysis, the established narrative collapsed. Sufficient statistical evidence could only confirm a true association for 89 of those 515 proposed genes.
Sequencing the genomes of 460 patients across the Shriners Children’s hospital network in the U.S., the team also identified disease-causing mutations in 60 genes across 15.8% of children. Yet their stricter statistical paradigm whittled the list down to only 16 with significant evidence linked to cerebral palsy.
“What this paper is trying to suggest is some of the genetic variants may not be slam dunk,” said Kuntal Sen, a clinical geneticist and paediatric neurologist at Children’s National Hospital, U.S. “It might explain one problem, like intellectual disability, but it may not tie together everything. Which is a fair point to make, that some genetic test reports might be just a slight association rather than causal.”
False alarms
These false alarms can be traced back to a few traps. One is coincidence. Because roughly 5% of the general population harbours a rare genetic disease, sequencing a child with cerebral palsy frequently uncovers severe mutations entirely unrelated to the disability.
A previous large-scale study flagged the LIPH gene as a cause of cerebral palsy because an affected patient happened to carry it. However, mutations in LIPH actually cause a rare form of hair loss and possess no known neurological link.
Conversely, across both historical literature and the newly sequenced cohort, CTNNB1 mutations showed up far more often than random chance would allow, providing the proof necessary to confirm it is a real risk factor.
The confusion is also compounded by the fact that ‘cerebral palsy’ is a clinical catch-all rather than a single biological disease.
“For me, I think the term ‘cerebral palsy’ does not always make sense from a purely scientific perspective.,” Dr. Sen said. “The motor symptoms that the children have [severe muscle stiffness, and weakness affecting either one side of the body or all four limbs] are more scientifically informative.”
He noted the outdated label survives, rightfully, mainly because it guarantees patients access to specialised insurance and physical therapy in the western world.
But as an umbrella term for brain-derived muscle weakness, the diagnosis lumps a large variety of conditions together. While some stem from birth injuries, others are ‘mimics’: rare metabolic or genetic disorders masquerading as a muscle weakness.
Stakes of precision
This heterogeneous reality is why distinguishing a harmless genetic coincidence from a true biological driver carries large stakes.
If doctors accept an incidental mutation from a standard genetic panel as the final answer, they may halt their workup prematurely, leaving a true, treatable ‘mimic’ undiscovered. But accurately pinpointing the biological cause using strict statistical proof can fine-tune this personalised approach and open the door to highly targeted care.
“If the genetic test report gives you a slam dunk answer, you counsel them, you provide management guidelines, and you can also give a recurrence risk for other family members,” Dr. Sen said.
The researchers estimated that among 8.5% to 24% of individuals who receive a valid genetic diagnosis, the findings point to specific, available treatments. By catching mimics early, doctors can swap generic physical therapy for precise interventions, such as dietary changes for arginase deficiency or specific medications for vitamin-dependent epilepsies and hereditary dystonia.
For these families, getting the statistics right means much more than simply solving a mystery. It unlocks treatments that can alter the course of a child’s life.
For countries like India, where three in every 1,000 live births are affected by cerebral palsy and genetic testing is an emerging and rapidly growing field, studies like this offer an advantage. A severe mutation that breaks a specific protein and masquerades as cerebral palsy does so universally, regardless of ethnicity. And by identifying only the true genetic mimics, local clinics can skip the diagnostic trial-and-error phase of older, bloated sequencing panels, and pave the way to adopt highly accurate genetic testing, connecting families to precise treatments faster.
Cautious path
While the Robinson et al. study has set a rigorous new standard, the authors have also conceded their strict mathematical model might actually underestimate the true number of genes linked to the disorder.
“One must remember that the lack of statistical significance does not imply the absence of an association,” Dr. obinson said. “It is very likely that there are more genes with cerebral palsy association than the 89 we flagged.”
Realising the full promise of this approach will require the medical community to move beyond just sequencing DNA. Scientists need large, globally shared datasets of detailed patient profiles to finally calculate the exact degree of risk a specific genetic variant carries.
Ultimately, translating these statistical insights into daily practice will take time. “With appropriate caution, genomic testing can be a useful addition to CP diagnostics,” Dr. Robinson said. “Caring physicians will integrate many kinds of information when making the decision.”
Anirban Mukhopadhyay is a geneticist by training and science communicator from New Delhi.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

The Mr. Green bodega sits on a busy stretch of Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn, New York. Near the counter, you can buy the usual assortment of candy, gum, rolling papers, and soda. You can also purchase tiny vials of injectable peptides. So we did. And then we sent them to a lab.
Mr. Green is one of several shops that went viral this summer for selling peptides, a broad class of amino acids touted for their ability to aid in everything from weight loss to injury recovery. For $376.20, we acquired four varieties: PT-141, for low libido; BPC-157, for healing and muscle recovery; NAD+, for cellular repair; and retatrutide, for weight loss. The clerk packed them up in an unlabeled paper bag and sent us on our way.
WIRED sent the vials to Finnrick, an Austin-based startup that offers independent peptide testing. Consumers can request tests for purity and whether samples contain common contaminants, as well as whether they contain the quantity of the substance listed. The company doesn’t have in-house labs but instead acts as a middleman between labs and individuals. In a few weeks’ time, Finnrick told us, we’d know if our bodega peptides were the real deal.
In August, the results came in. The (relatively) good news: The samples contained low levels of heavy metals and endotoxins, meaning they likely weren’t actively harmful. The bad news: They weren’t peptides.
The testing for each substance found that they did not contain the active ingredients on their labels—the BPC-157, for example, had no BPC-157 within it. The negative results suggested that the vials were either mislabeled or, if they had at one point contained the correct ingredients, had been corrupted beyond recognition. Peptides are often sensitive to temperature changes and require refrigeration, so improper storage could degrade ingredients, for example.
What did they contain? Hard to say, according to Marco Krause, the chief executive officer of the laboratory that performed the tests for Finnrick.
“What we offer is simply a label claim analysis. So you send us what you claim to think it is, and then we run it against a standard and verify whether or not it's the right compound,” he tells WIRED.
Peptides have surged in popularity in recent years, powered by endorsements from figures like US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and podcaster Joe Rogan. While some of these substances are pharmaceutical drugs like GLP-1s and insulin, many of the buzziest peptides have not been put through the typical regulatory approval process for drugs. Despite the hype surrounding them, many of these substances are not legal to sell for human consumption in the US—some precisely because they haven’t gone through the drug approval pipeline—and evidence of their purported benefits is thin.
The sign at Mr. Green advertising the peptides noted they were for “research use only,” a term that labs can use in an attempt to shield themselves from legal liability. But as the test results show, there’s no guarantee what’s in the vials—and in some cases there are real dangers to those taking them.
According to Raphaël Mazoyer, Finnrick’s CEO, the samples WIRED tested appear to be “just duds.” Over the past three months, Mazoyer says, the company has seen an uptick in these kinds of results. Though he can’t say for certain what’s going on—in part, his company has been testing more samples as it has grown—he points to the popularity of so-called turnkey services, which help pretty much anyone open a peptide business.
“There are a whole bunch of labels popping up that have the same upstream vendor,” he says. Not all the peptides Finnrick tests are duds, but the nature of the industry means that businesses may use the same shoddy supplier across a number of different brands.
WIRED isn’t the only organization to receive abnormal lab results after sending in peptides sold over the counter. Jeff Colhoun, the founder of the research-peptide vendor directory Peptide Critic, purchased INDR Labs peptides from a smoke shop down the street from Mr. Green called Smoker’s World and sent them to a different independent laboratory for testing.
Colhoun purchased two vials of retatrutide and two vials of NAD+ and had all four analyzed by Texas-based Analytical Formulations. The lab could “not positively identify” the substances. This doesn’t mean that they didn’t contain any of the substances listed, but it does suggest that the samples may have been contaminated or were otherwise too corrupted to decipher what was in the vials.
Colhoun says that he has heard from research-peptide vendors who have had similar results while testing products prior to selling them, and notes that buyers are at a high risk level when sellers “skip meaningful batch testing” altogether.
INDR Labs did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, but shortly after we reached out, its website began requiring login credentials. It previously cut off public access to its certificates of analysis, which provide evidence that a product has met certain standards. The company claimed its certificates were provided by Vanguard Laboratory; a spokesperson for Vanguard denied issuing the paperwork, CBS News previously reported.
INDR Labs is just one part of this booming ecosystem that investors estimate is already worth up to $3 billion, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. While the FDA has taken recent steps to loosen regulations, and many large telehealth platforms like Hims and Mochi are preparing to start selling a broad array of peptides, many people who take these substances today are purchasing them through questionable channels.
“The FDA needs to shut down these black markets,” Fred Mills, a longtime pharmacist and an executive at the nonprofit Americans for Safe and Effective Medicines, tells WIRED. Mills, who is based in Louisiana, says he’s had discussions recently about the dangers of people purchasing peptide products at convenience stores and that he warns those who do so to consult with a physician first.
If a peptide vial actually contains little more than water or saline solution, the worst that might happen is that someone loses money on a useless product. But some mislabeled peptides can contain ingredients that cause harm; a woman died this year after receiving a peptide injection from an unlicensed medical spa in the Bronx.
“My concern with the peptide industry is, we're legitimizing products, and we have no idea what's in them. We have no idea about the safety, accuracy profile, or whether they're adulterated or misbranded,” says Darshan Kulkarni, an attorney focused on pharmaceutical regulatory compliance. In the traditional pharmaceutical sales world, steps are taken to ensure prescription accuracy and product safety, from visual inspections to barcoding.
“Someone selling a product at a bodega doesn't know how to do that,” Kulkarni says.
“The FDA has warned companies selling products labeled ‘for research purposes’ or ‘not for human consumption’ when those products are marketed directly to consumers for human use,” an agency spokesperson who declined to give their name tells WIRED in an email. “Additionally, the FDA has warned telehealth companies for marketing drugs directly to consumers and for making false or misleading claims regarding compounded GLP-1 products offered on their websites. The FDA will continue to take action, where appropriate, to protect public health.”
The agency did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it has contacted or taken enforcement action against brick-and-mortar sellers of peptides labeled research-only, like those sold by Mr. Green.
There have been some enforcement actions. Earlier this summer, a man in South Bend, Indiana, was sentenced to six years in prison for selling “research use” peptides that were illegally imported from China—a major source of peptide ingredients—and were adulterated with steroids. Still, the enforcement atmosphere is loose enough that it remains easy to buy unapproved peptides both online and at brick-and-mortar medspas and other locations.
Kulkarni believes that the relatively low number of enforcement actions taken against the research peptide industry is related to the Trump administration’s attitude that “regulation stifles innovation, and therefore they believe that it is in the interest of patients to allow them to decide what products to take.”
As for Mr. Green, it did not respond to a written list of questions provided by WIRED. When we visited in early September, the menu in the window was gone. But a smaller version was next to the counter, and the peptides were still for sale.
