China tightens travel restrictions for citizens
- Published
China has imposed a range of sweeping new rules restricting travel in and out of the country in a move that observers say will give the government even more control over its citizens.
Citizens deemed to have "harmed" China's national security or interests while overseas can also be barred from leaving China for up to three years.
But the law also says that it will apply to anyone considered a threat to the country's industrial or technological security.
China keeps close scrutiny on sectors like semiconductors and AI, as the race between Beijing and Washington for tech dominance heats up. According to reports, travel restrictions were earlier imposed on some executives from these industries.
In March, the co-founders of Manus - an AI company that had been acquired by Meta - were reportedly barred from leaving China.
Under the new rules, border officials are now also required to advise Chinese nationals against travelling to countries and regions deemed "high-risk".
But even prior to the rules being announced, some people were already restricted from going to certain countries. Civil servants were among the earliest groups subjected to these controls, which later expanded to include state-owned enterprise employees and ordinary citizens.
A retired grassroots civil servant in Anhui told BBC Chinese that around 2018, his workplace made employees surrender their passports. His passport remains in the custody of his former employer even though he retired last year.
According to the ex-civil servant, employees had to apply and explain their reasons for overseas travel, and not all requests were approved.
For example, trips to visit relatives were more likely to be approved than tourism trips, he said.
"It is mainly to prevent corrupt officials from fleeing or transferring assets abroad," he said. "For more senior officials, it may also be intended to prevent the disclosure of state secrets."
A man identified by his pseudonym, Xiao Wang, who works at a state-owned financial institution in Beijing, told BBC Chinese that his fellow employees have long been required to surrender their passports and get approval for overseas travel.
The 32-year-old said managers have verbally reminded staff that "sensitive countries such as Japan are definitely off-limits".
Professor Tom Kellogg, Executive Director of the Center for Asian Law at Georgetown University, told BBC Chinese that the expanding travel restrictions were "deeply concerning" and said they reflect a "growing ideological control under Chinese leader Xi Jinping", which is reminiscent of Mao Zedong's era.
China was largely cut off from the world under Mao's decades-long regime, and international travel only became a part of life for Chinese people in the 1990s, after China underwent a series of reforms and opening up.
Today's various travel restrictions, Kellogg said, "bring back memories of that painful era".
Piyao, a Chinese government "rumour-refuting" platform, posted a statement last week saying the new rules "do not restrict the travel of ordinary citizens, but rather serve as a preventative measure against high-risk destinations and individuals with unusual travel patterns".
The regulations were issued to address "problems" such as people being deceived into leaving the country or engaging in illegal gambling and scam activities abroad, the statement said.
According to publicly available information, Chinese citizens currently cannot check whether they are subject to exit controls on their own.
Unless official written or verbal notification is issued, people generally only discover they are restricted from leaving when applying for documents or attempting to depart.
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and immigration authorities did not respond to enquiries from BBC Chinese.
Chinese authorities have drastically stepped up exit bans on its citizens in recent years, according to data provided to the BBC from rights group Safeguard Defenders.
China's supreme court database showed only 89 records mentioning exit bans in 2016, but that figure had risen to 188,760 last year.
The percentage of civil verdicts that dealt with exit bans also surged more than 30 times between 2019 and 2025, from around 0.23% to 7.3%. The actual volume of such cases is believed to be even higher, owing to an increasing number of withheld judgments.
The rules could also affect citizens who work in areas such as human rights, say analysts.
"This is another tool designed to control what Chinese citizens do and say overseas," said Professor Kellogg.
"In some cases, in order to prevent individuals from criticising the Chinese government overseas or to punish their rights advocacy activities, state security authorities directly refuse to issue passports."
One 26-year-old Chinese citizen, who wished to be identified only as Pipi, told BBC Chinese that his passport application in 2023 was rejected and he believes it was because he attended the massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong in 2019.
According to Pipi, he was interviewed by Hong Kong media outlets during the protests. When he returned to mainland China, he was questioned by state security police.
He said one immigration official told him that he could not get a passport "because of the Hong Kong issue" – but this was not confirmed in writing to him.
"I don't know whether I'll ever be able to leave [China]," he said.

Arsenal teenager Max Dowman shone with two goals in the 4-2 Carabao Cup win over Ipswich Town - but boss Mikel Arteta warned they cannot rush his development.
The 16-year-old played 13 times last season, but has had to settle for a place on the bench so far this campaign - until now.

But Arteta warned: "He is 16 years old and we have to be really cautious.
"We don't want to stop him, we don't want to put the brakes on him, we need to develop him and we are fully aware what he needs. He will have opportunities."
His first was a fine solo goal as he ran through, leaving defenders on the floor before slotting in.
"Unbelievable, he's unpredictable, he can go either way, so fluid, so nice to watch," said Arteta.
And for his second goal, Dowman showed good composure to place the ball in the bottom corner.
He is just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side in any competition, after Wayne Rooney for Everton against Wrexham in 2002 - which was also in the League Cup.
"With the demands that we put in them, to be able to do that is extremely difficult and he's coping better and better and better," Arteta added.
"He's an unbelievable player because of the character that he has and how much he loves to play at the biggest stage.
"It's not easy [to contain the hype], I understand, but what we have to do is look after him. He's 16 years old. You don't see that in this league.
"In other leagues in Europe, that's a totally different context, but in this league, with the demands that the league has, the players and everything put on you, we really need to make sure every time we throw him in, he's in the right context with the right preparation."

He received his GCSEs from Brentwood School in the summer and left school to focus on his football career.
Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp said: "He is a wonderful player who will be able to do everything in the game.
"But just give him time and how they are handling him is perfect. What you don't want to do is not give him the amount of game time he needs. He is an elite player."
Will Dowman get his chance now?
Breaking into the Arsenal first team will be a tough task for Dowman especially when the Premier League champions are in such fine form.
Arsenal have won all seven games this season, across four competitions.
Dowman was an unused substitute in four of those games, and not involved for the other two, before playing all 90 minutes against Ipswich Town.
The Gunners have played the same attackers in each league game so far - Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz.
But Dowman, especially considering Arteta turned to him in key moments in last season's title race, will hope to gain more of a supporting role.
"He's an unbelievable talent," team-mate Mikel Merino told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He will be a star in the future if he keeps his eyes and ears open and keeps learning.
"He's just 16 so he needs a lot of coaching, especially tactically. But I can't take anything away from him. He's always keen to learn. We'll keep helping him."
Quite possibly the best 16-year-old in the world, it is not unthinkable that he could earn his way into England's Euro 2028 thinking.
In fact there was even a debate about whether he should be going to the World Cup earlier this year.
"He is a real superstar," said former England defender Conor Coady on Sky Sports.
"A 16-year-old boy should not be doing this. He has got no better manager than Arteta to look after him. You want him to be looked after properly. If he plays every game at this age, he won't be scoring goals like this."
And it comes on the day it emerged highly rated 15-year-old striker JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United.
Gabriel had been expected to make his debut in Wednesday's Carabao Cup tie with Brighton.
That will probably deny him the opportunity to break up the stat that the three youngest players to score in the League Cup for a Premier League side all did so for Arsenal.
They are Cesc Fabregas (16y 212d v Wolves, 2003), Dowman (16y 258d v Ipswich) and Jack Wilshere (16y 266d v Sheffield United, 2008).

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

In the last few months, Sumit Nagal has made gradual progress in his bid to return to the level he had shown in 2024 when he was at a career high of 68, and competing frequently at Tour-level events and the Majors.
In June, he clinched his first Challenger title in two years. In July, he made it to the semifinals in another Challenger in Czechia. Last month, he landed in New York with the possibility of getting into the US Open qualifiers even though he was outside the initial entry cut-off.
As it turned out, he did make it into the draw after some withdrawals but ended up facing top-seeded Frenchman Arthur Gea and lost in straight sets in the opening round. Nevertheless, it was a step in the right direction as he made his first appearance at a Grand Slam since last year’s Wimbledon.

I got here on Saturday morning. I got a hit yesterday and today, a very long one. I’m going to do that same thing tomorrow and get ready for Friday. The courts are not very bouncy but the speed is medium slow.

Everybody knows that the opportunity is very good to do something that we have never done since the format has changed.
But at the same time, we need to stay calm, focus point by point. We can’t be thinking so ahead. The first thing is to get ready in practice, feel and move well, play the way you want to play and then, just fight.

If you do everything right, it’ll favour you more than the opponents and personally, that’s what I’m going to do.

The struggles I had when I was a kid. For two years, I didn’t know what holidays were. I would wake up at 5 a.m., do fitness from 5.45 or 6 o’clock to 7.30, come back home, take a shower, get ready, go to school, come back at 2 p.m., eat and sleep a bit. And then, I would practice from 6 to 9.

Chilean documentary-maker Patricio Guzmán, whose landmark documentaries included The Battle of Chile and Cannes prize-winner The Cordillera of Dreams, died in Paris on September 15. He was 85.
Guzmán, who was born in the Chilean capital of Santiago on August 11, 1941, has been hailed as one of Latin America’s most important non-fiction directors.
His landmark works include the three-part 1975-79 The Battle of Chile: The Struggle of an Unarmed People, chronicling the final year of socialist President Salvador Allende; the 1973 coup d’état which put General Augusto Pinochet in power, and resistance in the early days of the latter’s dictatorship.
Guzmán left Chile in the 1960s to study Official Cinema School (Escuela Oficial de Cinematografía, or EOC) in Madrid. He returned home in 1971 where Allende’s government appointed him head of documentary at state cinema company Chile Films. He was chronicling the work of the socialist government when the coup broke out.
Watch on Deadline
The filmmaker left the country in the wake of the coup after being arrested and detained briefly. He settled in Madrid and then Paris, only returning to Chile sporadically to film, when the political situation permitted.
Guzmán’s more recent credits include a trilogy reflecting on the legacy of his country’s 40-year military dictatorship: Nostalgia for the Light (2010), The Pearl Button (2015), which won Berlin’s Silver Bear for Best Screenplay, and The Cordillera of Dreams (2019), which won the Golden Eye documentary prize at the Cannes Film Festival.
For his final documentary – the 2022 work My Imaginary Country – Guzmán explored his native country’s contemporary politics and the youth-led popular protests that erupted in Chile in 2019 around democracy and social equality.

Athletics coach Rakesh Kumar was slapped with a life ban for administering prohibited substances, while powerlifter Gaurav Vats was provisionally suspended for possession and trafficking of banned drugs in the latest list of sanctions issued by the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) here on Wednesday.
Rakesh was suspended last year in March and his ban will be effective from that period.
National Inter-State bronze-winning sprinter Prakruthi Roopa Rao has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for banned steroids Stanozolol and Drostanolone.
Khelo India Games gold medal-winning weightlifter Chelsi got a five year ban for failing a dope test.
Among the other provisional suspensions, a minor weightlifter is also in the new additions after testing positive for Oxandrolone.
Quartermiler Kaushal Kumar, steeplechaser Jujhar Singh, and long-distance runner Baljeet Kaur were among those suspended as doping continued to cast a shadow on Indian athletics.
In all, seven names from athletics feature in the provisionally suspended list.
Powerlifter Vats, whose nutritional supplements company’s premises were at the heart of a crackdown on banned drugs, is also among those suspended by NADA.
In April, a tipoff from NADA’s Intelligence & Investigations (I&I) unit had resulted in the confiscation of several prohibited substances, including anabolic steroids like methenolone and stanozolol, at Vats’ company premises in Najafgarh following a joint operation, that included the local police.
The joint task force was led by Central Food Safety Officers (CFSOs) and also featured Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) officials.
Approximately 2,800 capsules/tablets and 11 injectable units of prohibited substances, including anabolic steroids — Methenolone Enanthate, Trenbolone, and Stanozolol — were recovered.
Three hundred Methandienone and 850 Oxandrolone tablets along with 1,500 Selective Androgen Receptor Modulator (SARMs) capsules were recovered. All these substances are steroids banned by the World Anti Doping Agency (WADA) as they can be abused for building muscle mass to gain unfair performance advantage.
Injections of Adenosine Monophosphate, a prohibited hormone and metabolic modulator that helps endurance, were also among the recoveries.

Tbilisi, September 16, 2026: Iran’s Ambassador to Georgia Ali Mojani said Tehran reserved the right to make its own choices after Tbilisi announced that it would comply with US sanctions on Iranian airlines, Iranian media reported on September 14.
The move will shut down one of the few remaining direct air connections between Iran and Georgia, with the route currently accounting for about 10 round trips a week to Tbilisi and Batumi. It could also affect Iranian leisure travel to Georgia, which has emerged as a visa-free, short-haul destination for Iranian travellers.
The decision comes as Tbilisi faces scrutiny in Washington over its ties with Moscow, Beijing and Tehran, including the handling of Russian crude at the Kulevi terminal. Compliance with the airline sanctions gives the Georgian government an opportunity to demonstrate adherence to US measures at a comparatively limited cost.
Iran Signals Right To Choose
Mojani said Iran respected Georgia’s decision as the choice of an independent country. However, he noted that respecting the choices of others did not mean disregarding one’s own.
He said Iranian travellers consider security, cost, convenience and mutual respect when deciding where to travel.
Mojani also said Iranian tour operators had approached the embassy seeking clarity over the future of travel to Georgia.
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, meanwhile, defended his government’s adherence to international sanctions.
Georgia Backs Sanctions Regime
Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency said it would act in full compliance with the sanctions regime. The agency said it had used US sanctions lists as a monitoring tool for years and had previously restricted several airlines under the same mechanism.
The agency did not specify when the restrictions would take effect, while its press office declined to comment when approached.
The US Treasury announced the designations on September 8 under what it calls Operation Economic Outcast. The sanctions cover 27 Iranian carriers and nine service providers, with Washington citing support for an aviation sector allegedly used to transport weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned companies dealing with the sanctioned airlines that they risked losing access to the global financial system.
Iranian Carriers Continued Flights
Sanctioned airlines continued operating in the days following the designations. A Sepehran Airlines flight from Tehran landed in Tbilisi on September 9, while further services by Qeshm Air and Varesh were scheduled for the same day.
Six Iranian airlines operate flights to Tbilisi and Batumi.

Iranian Tourist Arrivals Already Down
The restrictions come as Iranian tourist arrivals in Georgia have already declined sharply.
About 29,300 Iranian visitors arrived in Georgia during the first half of 2026, a 49 per cent fall year on year. Revenue from Iranian visitors dropped 65 per cent to $19.9 million during the period.

There will always be a use case for owning both a laptop and a tablet as stand-alone products. But the 2-in-1 laptop is the utopian dream of combining these two into a single device.
Of all the models I've tested, no 2-in-1 laptop is equally good at being both a tablet and a laptop. They always lean toward one or the other. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't buy one, especially since the convenience of having both in one device makes it an easier pill to swallow, price-wise.
The products below should meet most people’s needs. But if none are a fit for you, check out WIRED's other computer buying guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Surface Devices, Best Cheap Laptops, the Best Tablets, and the Best iPad.
Updated September 2026: I've made the Surface Pro 12 my new top pick and rearranged many of the other recommendations on my list.
The Best Detachable 2-in-1 Tablets
You can't talk about 2-in-1 laptops without talking about Microsoft's Surface devices. These tablets have removable keyboards that attach magnetically, not unlike an iPad. This form factor lets you switch between tablet and laptop modes. It's just as functional as a tablet as it is as a laptop. As I said, the Surface Pro is the epitome of this design, pioneering the idea of a tablet with a built-in kickstand that runs a full version of Windows.
The best model to buy right now is the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Reviewed). The smaller screen and compact design befit a 2-in-1 tablet that's meant to be held in one hand (at least occasionally). This wasn't my favorite when it came out, largely because it was overpriced at the time. But with all the configuration changes and price increases in the Surface Pro lineup, this model has become my go-to recommendation.
This is the most successful small tablet Microsoft has ever made, and a big reason is that it doesn't cheap out on quality or shrink down the size too much. With a 12-inch screen, it still allows the keyboard to be large enough to type on comfortably. It doesn't have the option for an OLED screen, but the device still feels surprisingly premium, and it is even more portable than its older sibling.
Not only is the Surface Pro 12 cheaper overall, but it's also the only 256-GB storage model on offer, which gives you a more affordable starting configuration. Regardless, you get the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus, which gives the Surface Pro 12 excellent battery life and solid performance. And because Surface devices run a full version of Windows, they are the best 2-in-1 options to use as full laptop replacements. But be careful: Microsoft sells a $750 starting configuration with only 8 GB of RAM, which may limit multitasking and heavier applications.
An even better laptop replacement, however, is the Surface Pro 13.8 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). The larger screen gives you more visual real estate, and the larger touchpad on the keyboard cover is more comfortable to use. The keyboard cover also comes with fabric-like textured palm rests and a built-in spot to hold the Surface Slim Pen 2. I also like the option to upgrade to an OLED screen, which makes it a more capable iPad Pro competitor. The only problem is that price increases have made this larger Surface Pro feel overpriced. The 2026 Snapdragon X2 Elite or X2 Plus models have largely replaced the 2024 model I tested, priced at $1,600. For me, that's too expensive for something meant to be more of a compact travel device. That's especially true since you still have to buy the keyboard cover. That's why I'd recommend this older Snapdragon X Elite model, which gets you the OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate and also bundles in the keyboard and stylus. On top of that, it even includes a terabyte of storage. That's well worth it.
While the hardware makes for a good tablet, Windows still isn't a very touch-friendly operating system and lacks a touch-first app ecosystem to support it. That's where iPads come into play. The iPad Air and iPad Pro are the best tablets you can buy, largely thanks to the breadth of touch-first apps available in the App Store. In many ways, that's what makes an iPad such an ideal 2-in-1 laptop, especially if you actually want to use it as a tablet. They are also easier to hold in one hand because they are lighter than Surface devices. These days, iPads are increasingly becoming legitimate laptop replacements too. With the Magic Keyboard attachment, you can add an additional USB-C port and a full-size keyboard and trackpad. I also like that this design doesn't rely on a kickstand, which makes it easier to use on your lap than the Surface.
While iPadOS isn't perfect, the introduction of windowing and improved cursor support over the years have made iPads work more like laptops than ever. But which iPad should you buy? The latest model I tested, the M4 iPad Air, is immensely powerful, and with the Magic Keyboard attached, it's a solid 2-in-1 laptop that costs less than the Surface Pro with the keyboard included. It's plenty of performance for just about anything you'd want to do with an iPad, especially if you opt for the larger 13-inch model. My only real complaint is that the palm rests on the Magic Keyboard are quite small.
Lastly, I have to point to the Asus ROG Flow Z13, one of the most interesting detachable 2-in-1s. I don't know anyone who has asked for a gaming-based 2-in-1, but Asus went out and made one anyway that actually works. Although you likely won't use the ROG Flow Z13 much as a tablet, the form factor keeps heat away from your hands. Unlike almost every other portable gaming device you can buy, your hands on the keyboard stay cool and sweat-free. This 2025 model is still a good buy, since only a more expensive, special-edition version came out in 2026.
The Best Convertible 2-in-1 Laptops
A different breed of 2-in-1 is commonly called a convertible laptop. These look like traditional laptops, but they have two unique features: a 360-degree hinge that allows the screen to flip to the back of the device, and a touchscreen. Most often, people enjoy tilting the screen back and laying the keyboard upside down on the table to watch movies and videos. You can go into tablet mode by folding the screen all the way back against the bottom screen, but the thickness and weight of these devices make it fairly uncomfortable to use that way.
I'll admit these aren't my favorite laptop designs. While I appreciate a touchscreen, I rarely use the 360-degree hinge in these other poses, not to mention downsides like a wobbly screen, an unattractive hinge, and extra cost. Lenovo, however, has made a name for itself in this category with its Yoga line, creating the very best of this look (though even Lenovo has begun launching “Yoga Slim” models that ditch the 2-in-1 aspect). That aside, I really enjoyed the Lenovo Yoga 9i that I reviewed in 2025.
The 2026 version, the Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition, is largely the same laptop, except with a newer Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor. Bar none, this is one of the most premium laptops you can buy, sporting a classy design, a very sharp OLED screen, and a thin chassis. One interesting aspect of this design is that Lenovo added an extra benefit to the 360-hinge by building a loudspeaker into it that delivers higher-quality audio, regardless of the mode you're using it in.
The other convertible 2-in-1 I'd point you to is the Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). I'm a big fan of Framework devices because of their great repairability, which lets you replace or upgrade nearly every internal component. You can even upgrade the processor and motherboard, which Framework sells separately. In theory, that means more years of use and less e-waste. Admittedly, it has a fairly thick chassis. But it's affordable, and the 2-in-1 hinge makes it a great, versatile family or student computer. To save money, you can opt for the DIY Edition, which requires assembling the laptop from its components. Framework's elegant, well-documented system makes the building process much more enjoyable than you might think. It would also make for a fun education project for a kid.
I've also tested many convertible Chromebooks over the years, but my favorite is the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Not only is this the best 2-in-1 Chromebook, it's also the best 2-in-1 you can buy for under $600. It uses a powerful (and efficient) chip from MediaTek that gives it competitive battery life, something Chromebooks have lacked for years now. It even comes with a higher-resolution screen and 12 GB of RAM; it's pretty stacked for a Chromebook. Googlebooks are coming soon to take the baton from Chromebooks, but for now, the selection of 2-in-1 Chromebooks is dwindling. Hopefully, we'll see a surge of interest in Googlebooks that brings more 2-in-1 laptops to market.
Other 2-in-1 Laptops to Consider
Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $259: The Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) was one of my favorite pieces of tech when it came out for one reason: its size. This diminutive detachable laptop is only 11 inches, which sounds painful at first. But this isn’t a productivity machine. Rather, it’s better viewed as a companion you can take anywhere for light web browsing, writing, and watching videos.
Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus for $630: We’ve long been fans of the Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus (8/10, WIRED Recommends), though it's beginning to show its age next to newer models. This one used to sell for as low as $500, which made it a solid budget alternative to the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 mentioned above, but these days the prices are on par. The Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 is better on every front, though, so depending on the current discount, I’d recommend that one over the older Flex 5i.
Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 for $750: You might think a 16-inch 2-in-1 laptop sounds silly. It's not portable enough to use as a tablet, that's for sure. But if you need a large touchscreen on your laptop, there's reason to pick up something like the Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Review). The flexibility of having a 360-degree hinge is useful in all sorts of scenarios. This 16-inch 2-in-1 balances price, portability, and performance with just enough finesse to be worth it—but only consider it when on sale.
Asus ProArt PZ13 for $1,250: Another detachable, the Asus ProArt PZ13 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) takes inspiration from Microsoft’s Surface Pro 13 design at a much more affordable price. For $1,250, you get a detachable 2-in-1 that can go up to around 19 hours on a single charge—and importantly, the keyboard comes bundled. Unfortunately, the performance leaves much to be desired, and its three-piece design is confounding. Still, it’s a nice alternative to the 13-inch Surface Pro if you’re dead set on the style.
What Is a 2-in-1 Laptop?
A 2-in-1 is a laptop that can go from a standard clamshell laptop configuration to a tablet setup. Two main designs fall into this category: detachable tablets and convertible laptops.
Detachable tablets are Windows tablets meant to be used with magnetic keyboards, not unlike an iPad Pro. These let you completely separate the screen from the keyboard, using a kickstand on the back of the display to keep it upright. Microsoft’s Surface lineup popularized this design, and it's still going strong more than a decade after its introduction. We’re even starting to see dual-screen laptops arrive, adding even more flexibility (if you have the cash to spare). The main benefit of the detachable 2-in-1 is the portability. While they aren't as good to use on your lap, they are thinner and lighter, making them better stand-alone tablets and travel devices.
Laptops with convertible displays, on the other hand, use a 360-degree hinge that can position the screen flat, in “tent” mode, or flush against the laptop's underside. Think of this as a touchscreen clamshell laptop with a fancy rotating hinge. This flexibility makes them great for everything from signing documents to streaming TV shows and movies—and you can switch back to a standard laptop orientation when it’s time to work.
Should You Buy a 2-in-1 Laptop?
The big draw of 2-in-1 laptops is that they can be used as both a laptop and a tablet. While in laptop mode, they’re generally comparable to any other clamshell laptop you’ll find. However, Windows and ChromeOS aren’t exactly the best touch-oriented operating systems out there, so you may find the touchscreen experience lacking when using it as a pure tablet.
If you already use a recent iPad or Android tablet regularly, you may not get as much out of a 2-in-1. But if you don't, these 2-in-1 laptops can give you the functionality of both devices in one—hence the name. Beyond that, convertible laptops use 360-degree hinges to offer even more capabilities, such as flipping the laptop upside down in various modes.
The only real downside to choosing a convertible 2-in-1 over a clamshell is the design tweaks needed to incorporate the hinge. Sometimes the weight balance can feel off, and the heftier hinge can look ugly and sometimes require a larger bottom bezel under the display. They're often more expensive too.
Why Not Just Buy an iPad?
It's a good question. All in all, it remains difficult to beat the iPad or iPad Pro for pure tablet use. From a software and third-party app perspective, iPadOS is far more robust without a keyboard, though that may change with Apple's multitasking improvements in iPadOS 26.
Windows tablets are the opposite, benefiting from the full Windows 11 experience. That means you can get all your work done, in theory, on one device, while still having something highly mobile. Some people can even do all their work on an iPad Pro, for example, but others prefer (or require) a desktop computing environment such as macOS or Windows.
I still wish Microsoft would improve Windows' touch experience, though, which would make 2-in-1 laptops much more enticing than iPads.
How I Test
I test 2-in-1s much like how I test clamshell laptops. Before you add in the 2-in-1 element, laptops are already incredibly complex devices, and I test every possible aspect of them. That means I measure display quality, benchmark CPU speed, run it until the battery dies, and type on the keyboard—a lot.
With 2-in-1 laptops, though, there's more of a physical element that needs testing. If it's a detachable, I extend the kickstand and use it in a variety of scenarios. How does it balance on your lap? What's the adjustability of the angle of the kickstand? If it's a convertible 2-in-1, does the touchscreen feel responsive? Does the screen wobble like crazy when you tap it? These are questions only hands-on time with the 2-in-1 laptop can answer.
All the products I recommend were provided by the manufacturers. However, our opinions and test results are completely independent. I don't guarantee positive coverage (or coverage at all) when I agree to accept a review unit from a company. I often send units back once I'm done testing unless I need to do long-term testing.

Fears that advanced artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity have dominated global headlines, but in Japan the technology is being used for a sweeter purpose — developing never-before-seen convenience store desserts.
For customers tired of the usual egg sandwiches and rice balls, major chains are turning to AI to develop products, including some unexpected flavors.
Lawson, one of the country’s biggest convenience store operators, said on Tuesday it will roll out three new food items, including a pickle-flavored lemon tart and a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yogurt cream.
These products, to be launched this month in Tokyo and neighboring regions, were created using AI around the theme “What on earth is this? But it’s delicious.”
“To generate ideas unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends, we used AI during brainstorming, without relying on past sales figures or market data,” a company press release said.
Meanwhile, rival FamilyMart said it fed sales data into AI to help develop a new dessert — a French-style canele pastry made with dough containing sweet potato puree and topped with caramel sauce.
The dessert will hit shelves nationwide next week, a spokeswoman said, adding that the company had wanted to create something new but likely to sell.
Like Lawson’s products, AI was used primarily for brainstorming, while human specialists were still involved in product development, according to the company.
It will not be FamilyMart’s first dessert product suggested by AI.
In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment — a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream.
It proved a success, so the company decided to properly pursue AI in product development, and plans to launch more of the items in the coming months, the spokeswoman said.
The rapidly advancing capabilities of AI have sparked a global panic in recent days, as researchers warn of the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems that could evade human control.
Leading U.S. AI labs have called for a coordinated slowdown of their cutting-edge work, while debate rages over how governments should regulate the technology.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Saudi Arabia’s interception of a Houthi drone south of Mecca has brought the Yemen war dangerously close to Islam’s holiest city.
Saudi air defences intercepted and destroyed what Riyadh said was a Houthi-launched drone south of Mecca on Tuesday, September 15, before it entered the prohibited airspace over the holy city.
Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said the security of the Two Holy Mosques and pilgrims was a “red line” and warned that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the Houthis.
The Houthis, in a post on X, denied that they had targeted Mecca, calling the Saudi claim false.
The incident comes barely a month after Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, under which an armed attack against any one of the three countries is to be regarded as an attack against all three. The agreement was also signed in Mecca on August 7.
And that is where the latest Houthi escalation creates an uncomfortable test for Islamabad.
The language of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement is broad. An armed attack against one signatory is to be regarded as an attack against all, similar to NATO's Article 5.
But the agreement does not publicly spell out an automatic military response, nor does it specify what form assistance must take in every circumstance. Reuters noted at the time that the responsibilities under the pact remained vague.
The Houthis have expanded attacks on Saudi territory, including cities and energy infrastructure, while the conflict in Yemen has simultaneously moved closer to the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
So far, Islamabad has been careful not to cross that line.
Earlier, Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif recently suggested that the pact could become operational if Saudi Arabia faced “unprovoked aggression” or the Yemen conflict spilt into the kingdom, as he was quoted by Geo News.
But later, Islamabad backtracked and sought to narrow expectations.
On September 10, Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said there was no military response under discussion in connection with the Houthi attacks. At the same time, he maintained that Pakistan would act “when the time comes” under the agreement.
Afterwards, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif came in a damage-control mood and called Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and condemned the Houthis' attacks on Saudi civilian and economic infrastructure. Sharif stressed Pakistan's solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Islamabad would continue efforts to “defuse” regional tensions.
Pakistan has substantial military ties with Saudi Arabia. The new agreement builds on longstanding defence cooperation between the two countries.
Under a separate bilateral framework, the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed in September 2025, Saudi authorities confirmed in April that Pakistani troops, along with fighter and support aircraft from the Pakistan Air Force, had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base amid heightened regional tensions.
The Houthis are not just a conventional state adversary. They are a powerful armed movement operating from Yemen and backed extensively by Iran.
American think-tank Council on Foreign Relations says Iranian assistance has included weapons, training and intelligence support, helping the Houthis develop capabilities that allow them to project force into the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab.
That makes any Pakistani military intervention potentially more complicated than simply defending Saudi territory.
The Houthis have moved beyond sporadic attacks and are now threatening the security architecture surrounding the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Recent Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast have heightened concerns over the strategic maritime chokepoint, while attacks on Saudi infrastructure have added a direct economic dimension.
CFR describes Bab al-Mandab as a crucial chokepoint for global energy flows and notes that Iranian support has helped the Houthis build the ability to project power into the strait and the wider Red Sea.
Iran has already used the geostrategic leverage of its geography during the Iran war, choking the Strait of Hormuz and creating an energy crisis.
After being ditched by the Pakistan-led alliance, the clearest sign that Riyadh is not relying exclusively on the new trilateral arrangement is the emergence of reports about Saudi efforts to obtain outside intelligence and security assistance.
The Jerusalem Post report citing diplomatic sources say Saudi Arabia and Israel have held discussions, mediated by US Central Command, about intelligence assistance against the Houthis.
The reported cooperation is focused on intelligence. Neither Saudi Arabia nor Israel has publicly confirmed the arrangement.
There have also been reports that Riyadh sought British assistance in dealing with the Houthi threat to Bab al-Mandab and Saudi energy infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia appears to be building a wider security network rather than waiting for help from the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement alone to determine its response.
Given the developments after the attack, Pakistan’s balancing act is now under the spotlight

Iran-US war latest: Blow for Trump as Congress votes again to curb his powers over $38bn war
Saudi Arabia draws 'red line' as Mecca put on air raid alert for the first time in history
Saudi Arabia's air defences destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Wednesday.
The coalition claimed that the drone intercepted on Tuesday evening was the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca after a ballistic missile launch in July 2017.
The Iran-backed group strongly denied targeting "Mecca or any other holy sites", calling it a "worn-out lie that has been used before".
Meanwhile, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran for the third time late on Tuesday, approving a war powers resolution that would halt president Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president's desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
China defence minister urges an end to 'provocative acts'
Chinese defence minister Dong Jun urged nations to avoid provocative acts and curb the resurgence of regressive historical trends.
Dong's comments at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on security come at a time of roiling regional tension in Asia since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran.
Warning that the world had arrived at a "fragile moment", Dong called for a fresher, more equal approach to resolving international tension, but offered few specifics or direct criticism of rivals.
"We must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against all latent manifestations of hegemony, militarism and historical revisionism," he said in an opening speech.
Some 2,000 military officers, diplomats and academics from 100 countries are attending the three-day event set to run until Thursday, with delegates including some regional defence ministers, a senior Pentagon official, Russian academics and Taliban representatives.
US state department issues travel advisory for Saudi Arabia
The US state department has issued a travel advisory for Americans, urging them to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing conflict with Iran-backed Houthis.
The state department said Iran has launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
It warned that the Houthis have threatened further attacks on the kingdom.
The state department advised US citizens to avoid travelling to areas near the Yemen border.
Houthis claim to have downed Saudi F-15 fighter jet
The Houthis claim to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over the Marib governorate in Yemen, Al Jazeera reported.
The Iran-backed group's spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the US-manufactured jet was downed using a "locally manufactured surface-to-air missile".
“In the face of this brutal aggression against our country and people, the Yemeni armed forces – with God’s help and grace – were able to shoot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was conducting hostile operations in support of its military buildup in the airspace of Marib governorate,” he said in a statement.
Iranian military official says Tehran ‘fears no war'
Iran does not fear war when it comes to safeguarding its sovereignty and security, claimed Habibollah Sayyari, the Iranian Army’s deputy commander for coordination.
Sayyari was speaking at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on security this morning.
He said the long-term interference of external forces in the Middle East have torn apart regional unity and called on global powers to condemn the "unilateral hegemonism and law of jungle", in a reference to the US.
US defence chiefs warn of munitions shortfall as Iran war costs hit $33bn
President Donald Trump’s “Operation Epic Fury” assault on Iran cost $33.4bn in its first four months and has resulted in a munitions shortfall, according to a report by the Department of Defence’s inspector general.
The 44-page report to Congress states that, between 28 February and June 30, the joint US-Israeli attack on Iran saw the Trump administration spend $22.3bn on munitions alone.
The onslaught “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Inspector General Platte B Moring III concludes.

Iran claims to down another US MQ-9 drone
The Iranian Revolutionary Guards this morning said they have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over Qeshm Island at around 2.29am local time.
The Guards said it was the 52nd MQ-9 drone destroyed by the Iranian forces using advanced air-defence systems.
Militias in Iraq remain defiant as the last US troops pack up to leave
As the end of the month approaches, Iraq faces two major deadlines: the conclusion of a decades-long US military deployment and the required disarming of non-state paramilitary groups.
With the US draw-down already in progress, officials confirm that the remaining hundreds of troops stationed in northern Iraq will depart prior to the Sept. 30 cutoff.
The government in Baghdad tied the US departure to a demand that militias give up their arms, though a majority of these factions have signaled no intention of complying. This defiance raises profound questions regarding the future stability of Iraq once American forces depart.

OIC condemns Iran-backed Houthi 'attacks' on Mecca
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation has condemned alleged attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Mecca.
The OIC said: “These attacks instil fear in innocent civilians, violate the sanctity of holy sites and mosques, and provoke the sentiments of Muslims around the world.”
Mecca was placed under an air raid alert for the first time in history on Tuesday evening. Saudi Arabia said it downed a Houthi drone near the holy city. The Houthis have denied attacking Mecca.
The OIC added: “The General Secretariat affirms that the acts committed by the Houthi terrorist militia against holy sites, mosques, and civilian infrastructure constitute terrorism that runs counter to Islamic values and to international norms, principles, and law."
India condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
India has expressed serious concern over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's civilian infrastructure and economic assets.
Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar held talks to discuss the Middle East crisis with his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on the sidelines of the Brics summit in India, a spokesperson told reporters in Delhi."
The issue of the Houthis was also discussed. As you know, recently there was an attack on Saudi Arabia which we have condemned. We are deeply concerned also with the escalation in the situation in the Red Sea region," spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.
"We have condemned the attack on the Saudi sovereign territory, including on the civilian infrastructure and economic assets. I would say that such attacks undermine regional stability and threaten freedom of navigation through the Bab-el-Mandeb," he said.
Iranian state actors targeting UK dissidents, activists and journalists with spyware
British intelligence has issued a warning after finding that Iranian spies have targeted dissidents with spyware that can enable tracking of their movements.
Dissidents, activists and journalists were targeted by state actors that impersonated their contacts on messaging apps to trick them into downloading spyware called Chosen Brick, the National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, warned.
The malware gave agents access to the person’s contacts, emails and social media messages as well as a device’s microphone and content on the screen.

Elon Musk is seemingly done attacking Apple over its decision to integrate ChatGPT into iPhone features.
Back in 2024, when the partnership was first announced, Musk slammed the integration as an agreement from Apple to let OpenAI install “creepy spyware” on users’ devices. The next year, he sued, claiming the partnership gave the firms a “monopoly” on Apple users’ AI prompts, which allegedly harmed competition in both smartphone and chatbot markets.
For Musk, the fight with Apple seemingly escalated after he believed that his chatbot, Grok, was perhaps being illegally blocked from topping Apple’s App Store rankings. Last August, he claimed that “Apple is behaving in a manner that makes it impossible for any AI company besides OpenAI to reach #1 in the App Store, which is an unequivocal antitrust violation.”
However, on Monday, Musk confirmed in a court filing that he has resolved all claims against Apple. The filing does not indicate if there were any negotiated settlement terms or otherwise explain why X would suddenly seek a voluntary dismissal. What is clear is that Musk agreed to never raise the claims again against Apple, while notably refusing to drop the same claims against OpenAI.
Now, it seems that Musk plans to advance claims that OpenAI relied on the deal—which Apple emphasized was never exclusive—to monopolize the chatbot market.
OpenAI has already slammed Musk’s lawsuit as another attempt to harass the AI company as Musk’s rival AI firm, now called SpaceXAI, races to catch up. Last fall, OpenAI mocked Musk’s claims as baseless, emphasizing that Musk won’t even “hazard a guess” at what portion of the chatbot market is being foreclosed by the OpenAI/Apple deal. Instead, Musk claimed it could be anywhere from 0 to 55 percent, based on “back-of-the-envelope math” that OpenAI thinks the court should reject.

Three dead after NBC News helicopter crashes in Los Angeles while covering bus accident
Aircraft goes down between two commercial buildings in Chatsworth neighborhood
At least three people have died and another is injured after a local NBC News helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood on Tuesday while reporting on a bus collision earlier in the day, according to officials.
The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighborhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson said.
Five patients were assessed, with one person transported to a local hospital in an unknown condition while three others were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the fire department.
NBC4 Los Angeles said it was their news helicopter, NewsChopper 4, that crashed in the city during a live broadcast. Several television news helicopters covering the bus collision were operating in the area, according to media reports.
"We've been telling you that we've been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o'clock tonight in Chatsworth," NBC anchor Colleen Williams said.
NBC said the helicopter was operated by Angel City Air, which is affiliated with the station.
The helicopter crash happened after a vehicle collision in the area in which a Los Angeles Metro bus and a passenger vehicle met with an accident, killing at least two people.
Footage from the scene showed two shipping containers and several vehicles burning and firefighters working to douse the blaze, which has been extinguished.
The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said the helicopter crashed at around 6:58 pm and its officers responded to the area of Lurline Avenue and Nordhoff Street in Chatsworth.
It said it was not confirmed how many people were on board.
At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, Capt Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the LAFD, said during a news conference. It was unclear if the other two who were killed were on the ground or inside the aircraft.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was "devastated" by the loss of life in the helicopter crash and the bus collision in Chatsworth.
“I’m absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash,” she said, thanking emergency responders for their swift response.
California governor Gavin Newsom also shared his condolences and said "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground caught fire from the burning helicopter wreckage, which was quickly put out, according to officials. More than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the Fire Department.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate the crash, the Fire Department said.
About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half of the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.
The helicopter crashed about a mile and a half from the bus crash.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York), the modest, two-person musical that charmed critics last season and scored eight Tony Award nominations, will play its final performance on Sunday, November 29.
At the time of its closing, Two Strangers will have played 21 previews and 428 performances at the Longacre Theatre. The First National Tour of the show will launch in Providence, RI., with an expected start date in fall of 2027.
Written and composed by Jim Barne and Kit Buchan, and directed and choreographed by Tim Jackson, Two Strangers stars Sam Tutty and Christiani Pitts (both Tony noninated) as two young strangers who meet when he is visiting New York (from England) for the wedding of a father he never met. Pitts plays the bride’s sister, and in opposites attract style the two bond, sometimes reluctantly, as they carry out the wedding task described in the title.
While the musical received favorable reviews and solid word of mouth, it did not become a major hit at the box office. In recent weeks attendance at the show was typically on the lower end of the Broadway grosses roster: Last week, attendance was at 70% of capacity at the Longacre, with a middling gross of $519,236.

The US war against Iran has cost the Department of Defense more than $38 billion through August 1, with the conflict potentially adding another $2 billion to $3 billion or more each month, depending on the intensity of fighting, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said on Tuesday (September 15).
“As of August 1, 2026, the armed conflict with Iran has cost (the Department of Defense) approximately $38 billion,” the CBO said in an assessment, referring to the war that began after US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran on February 28.
The agency warned that the monthly cost could increase further if the conflict escalates.
“These expenses could be higher still if the violence escalated further,” the CBO said.
The CBO said the estimate largely reflects the cost of replacing munitions expended during the conflict and equipment lost in battle, along with higher fuel costs for the US military and other expenses.
The estimate does not include costs related to US military personnel killed or injured in the conflict, or longer-term veterans' healthcare and disability compensation.
The analysis was prepared following a request from Rep. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, along with other Democratic lawmakers.
The estimate broadly aligns with an earlier assessment by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who told the Senate in July that the Iran war had cost the Pentagon about $37.5 billion.
The CBO said the conflict's broader economic impact is being felt through higher inflation, primarily because of disruptions to oil and natural gas shipments.
Iran's retaliation included blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global energy transit. The disruption, along with shipping problems in the Red Sea, has reduced energy flows and pushed up costs.
The CBO estimates that inflation in the first quarter of 2027 will be about 0.5 percentage points higher than it had projected in February, based on the personal consumption expenditures price index.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is also expected to be 0.3 percentage points higher than previously forecast.
Higher inflation could, in turn, push up interest rates on US Treasury securities, adding to the government's borrowing costs.
The findings come as the Iran conflict enters its seventh month, with the war and elevated prices emerging as major issues ahead of the US midterm elections.
The White House requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding in June, largely to support the war effort. Congress has not yet approved the request.
The CBO noted that its estimates are subject to considerable uncertainty because the Defense Department declined to provide information requested for the assessment. The budget office instead relied on government databases and publicly available reports.
The cost of replacing weapons and equipment is also raising concerns about US military stockpiles.
A Pentagon inspector general report released on Monday said the war had resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls.”
“This nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs,” Boyle said.
He also criticised President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans over the spending, arguing that the administration was willing to spend tens of billions of dollars on the conflict while warning about the cost of domestic programmes.
(With AFP, AP inputs)

Aurobindo Pharma has received final approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) to manufacture and market Beclomethasone Dipropionate HFA Inhalation Aerosol, 40 mcg and 80 mcg.
The product is a generic equivalent of QVAR Inhalation Aerosol, 40 mcg and 80 mcg, marketed by Teva Branded Pharmaceutical Products R&D LLC. It is Aurobindo’s first metered-dose inhaler and marks the company’s expansion into complex respiratory therapies. Beclomethasone Dipropionate HFA Inhalation Aerosol is indicated in the maintenance treatment of asthma.

The product will be manufactured at subsidiary Aurolife Pharma’s Raleigh facility in North Carolina and expected to be launched in upcoming quarters. The U.S. market for the approved product and newer versions of the reference product was estimated at $301 million for the 12 months ended July 2026, Aurobindo said citing IQVIA numbers.
