The All India Petroleum Dealers Association has appealed to the Union Finance Minister for an immediate waiver of Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges on UPI payments exceeding ₹2,000.
In a formal letter sent on Wednesday, Association President Ajay Bansal urged government intervention regarding high payment processing fees.
The association emphasised that because dealer earnings are based on fixed per-litre margins rather than overall transaction values, percentage-based transaction levies directly deplete their net income.
Quick answers to key questions
The proposed UPI transaction charges for payments exceeding ₹2,000 include a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.4%, capped at a maximum fee of ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above.
Petrol pump dealers argue that high MDR charges deplete their earnings since their commissions are fixed per litre, not as a percentage of transaction value, putting financial strain on their operations.
The new UPI MDR framework could discourage petrol dealers from facilitating UPI payments over ₹2,000, which may undermine the government's goal of expanding digital payment adoption.
Consumers should not be concerned about paying UPI transaction fees, as the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has clarified that consumers will continue to make UPI payments without charges.
The Association has called for either a complete exemption from all MDR and transaction fees for UPI payments or specific exemptions for payments over ₹2,000 to maintain business viability.
Highlighting their financial strain, the association pointed out that dealer commissions have not been updated since October 2017. Over the same period, key operational overheads—including electricity bills, staff wages, and compliance expenditures—have surged significantly.
Although pump owners have repeatedly engaged with oil marketing companies to resolve the matter, these negotiations have yielded no results, leaving operators with increasingly razor-thin profit margins.
"Dealer margins are determined by the Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) under the guidance of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas and are primarily fixed on a per-litre basis, rather than as a percentage of the transaction value. Dealers therefore have no mechanism to increase their earnings in proportion to the value of a transaction," the association said in the letter.
"Even a seemingly modest fixed charge of ₹5 per UPI transaction above ₹2,000 would have a substantial cumulative impact. Petrol pumps process a very large number of transactions every day, and the multiplication of even a small charge across thousands of transactions would create a significant recurring financial burden. A percentage-based MDR of up to 0.4% would be even more disproportionate to the economics of petroleum retailing," the letter added.
Fuel retailers argued that the payment channel a customer uses does not change the basic nature or profitability of a fuel sale.
They pointed out that the government has previously recognised the unique economics of petroleum retail by granting special card-payment exemptions—a policy framework that dealers contend should logically apply to high-value UPI transactions today.
The association warned that unmitigated processing fees might force dealers to cap or discourage UPI payments above certain limits simply to safeguard their livelihoods. Such restrictions would directly undermine the central government’s larger mission to expand digital payment adoption, enhance transaction transparency, and improve consumer convenience.
To maintain business viability across retail outlets, the association submitted two specific solutions to the Centre:
Alternatively, if a standard industry threshold is maintained, provide petrol pumps with explicit exemptions from both percentage-based MDR and fixed fees for UPI transactions above ₹2,000.
"Digital payments have significantly enhanced customer convenience, transaction transparency and operational efficiency in fuel retailing. Petroleum dealers should therefore not be financially penalised for facilitating and encouraging such digital transactions," the letter said.

Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life.
The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning.
According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach.
Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement.
The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.
“Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read.
“From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.”
The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling.
The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident.
“Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said.
Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate.
A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians.
“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement.

Let them ref the games and be humans - Andrews
- Published
Brentford head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.
As his Bees progressed to the Carabao Cup fourth round with a battling 2-1 win at League One side Reading, Andrews said he was not happy with the officiating.
Reading defender Paudie O'Connor had a goal for a first-half overhead kick ruled out by referee Tom Nield for a high boot, prompting Royals boss Leam Richardson to say it was "possibly in the top three [wrong] decisions that I've seen in my career - and I've seen thousands of games and played in hundreds".
With no VAR used at this stage of the EFL Cup, Andrews added: "It's been a tough week for officials as everybody is probably aware.
"I think we just need to let them ref the game and be human beings and make decisions.
"We have gone through a period in the game where I feel like they weren't actually making decisions in both boxes because of the technology we have in the game and I feel like that is a real shame."
His comments followed the admission of Pro Ref to an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's winning goal for Manchester City in their Premier League encounter at Manchester United on Sunday.
There was intense debate over whether the goal should have been disallowed for City midfielder Enzo Fernandez - who was in an offside position - interfering with play as he dived, attempting to head the ball in a central position before Haaland's finish.
Andrews, whose Brentford side are seventh in the Premier League, said referees were no longer allowed to "make mistakes".
"I always felt as a player, when there was a relationship with an official that was built on respect and being able to speak to each other in a certain way," he added.
"We've gone away from allowing them to officiate and allowing them to make mistakes and I think it is a real shame.
"Now they are having to go back to that and it's not the habits they have had in recent years."
On Sunday's refereeing error in the Manchester derby, Andrews said it was "pretty alarming" Haaland's goal was allowed to stand.
"The first thing was whether [Erling] Haaland was offside and then obviously [Enzo] Fernandez was. It's a shame," he admitted.

Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.
“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.
The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published two days after one of its researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.
Among the findings in the company's report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.
“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.
Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”
Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”
“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models — which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”
Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
As companies introduce increasingly powerful AI models, experts have called on governments to regulate the technology, rather than relying on the industry to police itself.
John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, said it is an uncomfortable position for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to be in when they are expected to determine what is safe vs. unsafe behaviour and make "value judgments at societal scale without any kind of democratic or deliberative oversight.”
Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”
Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he's resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon's post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said.

In June 2026, numerous Chinese news media outlets reported on updated international guidelines advising researchers not to independently respond to extraterrestrial signals. English-language news outlets also reported on these updated guidelines, which came from an international scientific organization. It was not possible to find any evidence of the Chinese government sending a nationwide alert telling people not to communicate with aliens, nor of the existence of a U.N. "alien hotline."
In September 2026, a rumor circulated online that the Chinese government broadcast a warning to the country's population of roughly 1.4 billion people, instructing them not to communicate with aliens and to instead contact the United Nations if extraterrestrial life reaches out to them.
For example, one Instagram user posted a video making the claim (archived), during which the user said the alleged warning was distributed through several channels:
Broadcast was made as if it were a giant emergency. They did it through the radio, they did it like the way that you get Amber Alerts on your phone, they did a television broadcast and they had messengers going into rural communities to tell people this and give them this information.
The supposed announcement said, "If you are contacted by aliens, do not attempt to communicate with them. Call this phone number, which will send you to the United Nations desk of the alien communications specialist, and they will take care of it for you." The Instagram user later referred to the supposed number as an "alien hotline" and said similar messages circulated in Japan and South Korea.
The claim spread spread elsewhere on Instagram as well as on Reddit and Facebook. Readers also contacted Snopes to ask whether it was true.
In short, it was not possible to find any evidence the Chinese government issued the nationwide warning described in the posts, and a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C., said no Chinese government agency issued such a warning. The real guidance behind the rumor also did not instruct ordinary people to call a U.N. "alien communications specialist" if extraterrestrials contacted them. As such, we have rated the claim as false.
Warning did appear in Chinese media
There is a real story behind the rumor. On June 1, 2026, the International Academy of Astronautics, a Paris-based nongovernmental scientific organization, published updated guidelines for people and organizations involved in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI. The document says possible signals should be independently verified and that researchers should not send a reply before international consultation.
These guidelines did receive attention in China. For instance, on June 7, IT Home, a Chinese technology news website, published an article titled (translated using Google Translate) "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! The International Academy of Astronautics updates eight guidelines." China Science Daily, Shanghai-based digital newspaper The Paper and national television broadcaster CCTV News also reported on the updated declaration.
The article on The Paper's website appeared in its "Government Affairs" section, which could make it seem like an official government message.
English-language news media outlets similarly reported on the IAA's updated guidelines.
Graphic may explain how rumor spread
A blue graphic with yellow text in Chinese circulated alongside the rumor in some social media posts. Jingchu Network (荆楚网) — which is part of CnHubei, a news website in Hubei province — posted the graphic on its Douyin account (shown below). The message, translated using Google Translate, reads:
Do not reply to extraterrestrials on your own initiative; the International Academy of Astronautics recommends immediately notifying the United Nations upon the discovery of extraterrestrial life.
(Jingchu Network Douyin account)
The Douyin post cites Red Star News as its source and explains that the message concerned the IAA's guidelines. On June 7, Red Star News published an article about the IAA update.
Jingchu Network is a state-backed news outlet. According to its website, it is supervised by the Hubei Provincial Party Committee Propaganda Department and the Hubei Provincial Cyberspace Administration. "It is the only national key provincial news website in Hubei Province approved by the State Council Information Office," the website reads.
The graphic later circulated on English-language social media platforms, where users described it as an announcement posted in China. This may have contributed to claims that the Chinese government itself issued the warning.
Government website also links to the story
The story also indirectly appeared on at least one official Chinese government website.
On June 10, Fushun Municipal Science and Technology Bureau — a government department of the city of Fushun, in Liaoning province — listed (as shown below) a webpage titled, "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! Why did the International Academy of Astronautics call for a halt?" in the "Science and Technology Work Updates" section of its website.
(fskjj.fushun.gov.cn)
However, that webpage originated from outside the department's website. It was not presenting the message as a new government policy or warning.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C. said via email that the Chinese government issued no such warning:
Based on publicly available information to my knowledge, no Chinese government agency issued such a warning, distributed it through national alert channels, or instructed the public to contact the U.N. about extraterrestrial contact.
The claim may stem from confusion over a revised SETI protocol issued by the International Academy of Astronautics and reported by Chinese media. It was not a Chinese government notice.
Snopes also contacted the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Guidance is for researchers, not ordinary people
The IAA document explicitly says it was written for people and organizations taking part in scientific SETI research. It does not tell ordinary people what to do if an alien personally contacts them.
The declaration says that after a confirmed detection, researchers should take part in international consultations over whether a response should be sent. Until those talks are finished, "no reply should be sent." It also says those discussions should include the United Nations and other international bodies.
Chinese Science Daily interviewed Zhang Tongjie, a Beijing Normal University professor who took part in discussions about the revised declaration. He reportedly said the cautious approach was based on uncertainty about whether an extraterrestrial civilization would be friendly, hostile or neutral. He was also quoted as saying the declaration was not legally binding.
There is no UN 'alien hotline'
Social media posts also claimed Chinese citizens were given a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist," but no such a number is in the IAA declaration. The document directs questions about its principles to the IAA itself.
Searching Google for a United Nations "alien communications specialist" returned no results (archived) suggesting that such a role exists.
Though the declaration says consultations about whether to respond to confirmed extraterrestrial intelligence should involve the United Nations and other international bodies, it also says the specific procedures for such consultations still need to be established in a separate agreement or arrangement.
The idea of an official U.N. representative for alien contact has appeared before. In 2010, a report in British newspaper The Times claimed astrophysicist Mazlan Othman, then-director of the U.N. Office for Outer Space Affairs, was appointed as Earth's contact person for extraterrestrials. Othman denied this and said no specific U.N. response role had been decided, while further action would be up to member states.
Therefore, the IAA declaration's reference to international consultation through the United Nations does not mean there is a U.N. "alien hotline."
Snopes has contacted the U.N. and, specifically, its Office for Outer Space Affairs to ask whether such a hotline exists. We will update this article if we receive any responses.
Bottom line
All in all, there is a kernel of truth behind the story. In June 2026, Chinese news media outlets did publish messages saying people should not "respond to aliens" without authorization, and an official municipal government website did link to a webpage on the topic.
However, that information came from guidelines for SETI researchers issued by the International Academy of Astronautics. The guidelines say a possible extraterrestrial signal should first be verified and that no response should be sent before international consultation.
Finally, it was not possible to find any evidence that China sent a nationwide emergency alert or gave people a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist."

Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
- Published
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.
The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.
Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.
BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.
The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.
Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.
If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.
However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.
With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.
Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.
She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.
The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.
London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.
Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.
When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.
"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."
Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.
"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."
Inspired by Ronaldo, dancing her way to the top - analysis
Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.
She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.
By October of that year, Luvanga headed for Saudi Arabia to join Al-Nassr, a move that would prove transformative for her career.
Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.
Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.
"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.
There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.
Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.
Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.
Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.
She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.
For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Hello, I’m Amanda Erickson! For the past year, I’ve been editing Morning Rounds. Now, I’ll be writing the newsletter twice a week, on Mondays and Tuesdays. I’m very excited to share the latest health and science news. I’m also eager to hear from you: tell me what you like about the newsletter, what’s not working, and what you want to see more of. (If you have any favorite medicine memoirs, send those over as well! I’m still working on my fall reading list.)
In the meantime, read on for a fascinating new poll on trust in science, a story on heart health in space, and a big number that highlights how President Trump’s immigration policies may be impacting kids’ health.
RFK Jr. will speak at conference by anti-vax group
Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will deliver a keynote address at the Children’s Health Defense conference in Washington, D.C., this week. It’s something of a full circle moment for Kennedy, who ran the anti-vaccine organization from 2015 to 2024 before leaving to campaign for president.
Since joining the Trump administration, Kennedy has tried to distance himself from the organization. As my colleague Isa Cueto explains, “the CHD conference will serve as the secretary’s first public embrace of the group since he took the helm of HHS — a marked shift from January 2025, when Kennedy promised senators he would not do anything to discourage Americans from getting vaccines.”
What patients want to hear from their doctors
In exploring why trust in science has declined, one question looms large: What can medical professionals actually do when patients choose to follow unscientific advice? Having those conversations is not easy – science is complicated, and primary care doctors typically get just 20 minutes with a patient. As a pediatrician in Florida recently told public broadcaster WLRN: “What’s happening now is kind of like being a pilot, and every passenger on the plane wants to know what every button on the console does.”
New polling data from the Edelman Trust Institute and the Yale School of Public Health underscore why those conversations are so crucial. The poll asked people across 13 countries what would be important to them if a medical expert wanted them to follow a recommendation about which they had doubts. The top five answers people most often ranked as critically important or very important included some things you’d expect a doctor to do, like explaining risks and benefits and using language patients can understand, but also listening “to make sure they understand me and my life situation” and welcoming doubts and addressing them “patiently and without judgment.”
Trust, in other words, isn’t just about reciting the facts. It comes from the types of exchanges that emerge during a long-term relationship. As the CEOs of the Greenwall and Dana foundations put it in a new First Opinion on this subject: “Messaging can’t substitute for the relational infrastructure needed for building and sustaining trust.” Expect to hear more from me soon on how I’m approaching my new trust in science beat. In the meantime, story suggestions are more than welcome at [email protected]. — Nick Florko
40%
That’s the proportion of doctors who say children in their care have skipped medical appointments over the last 12 months due to fears about immigration status, according to a survey of about 2,600 pediatricians by the American Academy of Pediatrics. Another 38 percent of respondents said they weren’t sure if immigration played a role in missed appointments, “suggesting an underestimation of the families affected,” the authors wrote.
As my colleague Daniel Payne laid out earlier this year, the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement actions have resulted in patients from immigrant communities — including mothers and parents with sick children — avoiding care. Across the country, no-show rates for appointments are rising, and the number of vaccines given to immigrant populations has declined. In Dallas, for example, the local health department’s clinics gave 50% fewer back-to-school vaccinations to Hispanic children in August 2025 compared to August 2024.
Why you shouldn’t skip leg day, even in space
Space isn’t easy on the body. The lack of gravity changes the heart’s shape, the flow of fluid, and even how blood is pumped. So what’s an astronaut to do? That question has long animated Benjamin Levine, NASA’s top consulting cardiologist. In a new paper, he explores how the heart could be impacted by a six-month trip to Mars. (This is especially important since, as Levine put it: “I love the crew and the astronauts; they’re wonderful people, but they’re not particularly remarkable physical specimens.”) In an interview with STAT, Levine laid out what he learned about keeping astronauts healthy on possible journeys to (and from) the red planet.
Businesses can now apply for NIH funding
Last week, the National Institutes of Health announced an expansion of the kinds of organizations eligible for grant funding to bolster research facilities. Previously, only institutions of higher education and nonprofits could apply for this money. But now, local governments, other federal agencies, community based organizations, and, notably, for-profit businesses may access facilities funds as well.
This is part of a larger push from the Trump administration to decenter academia in the conduct of scientific research. In a May Senate hearing, NIH director Jay Bhattacharya talked about finding ways to diversify the types of institutions that receive such funding. Generally, money to support research overhead is tacked onto grants as “indirect costs.” But, as Bhattacharya put it, in the current system, institutions need to have top notch equipment to attract talent that can then win grants. “This catch-22 guarantees that our investments in institutions will be concentrated,” he said at that hearing.
Beyond NIH, the National Science Foundation has also embraced a program, called “X-Labs” that prioritizes independent research organizations, and launched a Ph.D. program that combines academic experience with experience in industry. You can read more about that program from my colleague Jonathan Wosen here, or about the administration’s broader vision for science here. — Anil Oza
A new leading cause of death for Hispanic people in the U.S.
The “Hispanic paradox” has long held that Hispanic adults in the U.S. were less likely to die from cardiovascular disease despite a higher burden of higher risk factors. Not anymore, according to a statement from the American Heart Association published this morning.
In 2022, cardiovascular disease displaced cancer as the top cause of death among U.S. Hispanics. Risk factors such as obesity, diabetes, and high blood pressure emerge at younger ages compared to other populations, the new call to action emphasizes.
“Although some CVD outcomes historically appeared favorable, a phenomenon referred to as the Hispanic paradox, emerging evidence indicates that rising cardiometabolic burden and acculturation-related risk factors may attenuate these advantages, particularly among U.S.-born individuals,” the AHA asserts.
Why was this missed before? Treating Hispanic people — who are not always well represented in research — as a monolithic group obscured differences across heritage groups, including limited access to care that might mean underdiagnosis, the AHA said. Other explanations include selective migration to and from the U.S., differences in social support, and data limitations. — Elizabeth Cooney

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

After an aggressive run at Mumbai's food sector, Maharashtra Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has now turned his attention to medical devices and their exorbitant price in the state.
Mundhe has written to the Department of Pharmaceuticals and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), after a survey by the state government found that some hospital surgical consumables and medical devices were being sold at markups as high as 2,841% over their procurement prices, according to a Mint report.
The Maharashtra FDA commissioner has sought a review of the findings from the survey and an appropriate action. In his letter to the NPPA, he proposed capping trade margins and bringing essential categories of medical devices under structured price monitoring.
"Our survey has revealed an extraordinary disparity between the trade procurement price and the printed maximum retail prices (MRP) of medical devices used in inpatient care, reaching as high as 2,841% in some cases, including IV sets, syringes, nebulizers and oxygen mask products," Mundhe told Mint over phone.
According to the survey, private hospitals procured some of the medical devices at prices below their printed MRPs. For instance, catheters were procured at ₹29.41 against an MRP of ₹310, while IV infusion sets bought at ₹11.05 were billed to patients at ₹325.
The survey covers surgical items used in inpatient departments (IPD), including products such as IV sets, syringes, nebulizers, oxygen masks and catheters.
According to Mundhe, such medical products remain outside the direct ceiling-price mechanism under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 (DPCO).
The DPCO empowers the NPPA to regulate and enforce statutory ceiling prices for essential medicines and notified medical devices. However, Mundhe's survey found that many hospital surgical consumables are not covered by these strict price controls.
In his letter, Mundhe called for margin rationalisation, an inter-agency review and guidelines to regulate the permissible gap between trade procurement costs and declared MRPs.
"Unlike scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, many categories of medical devices fall outside strict statutory price controls, allowing unchecked pricing practices to persist," he wrote.
The NPPA is examining whether manufacturers and intermediary supply channels are adding large markups between wholesale procurement prices and the prices ultimately charged to patients.
Mundhe said the pricing disparity requires examination, including whether the differences could be linked to margins, product quality or other factors.
He added that the issue goes beyond pricing because patients often have limited information about the actual procurement cost of medical devices used during hospitalisation.
"This is not merely a pricing issue; it is a patient-protection issue," Mundhe said, adding, "There is a significant asymmetry of information in healthcare, with patients often unable to assess whether the price they are charged is reasonable."
He further said when a product procured at a low trade price carries an exceptionally high MRP, "it is the patient that bears the financial burden".

Meta may be ready to reveal a new pair of smart glasses with no camera at all, amid a PR crisis for the company caused by the video recording capabilities of its flagship smart glasses. A new report from The Information claims the camera-free glasses, codenamed Luna, could be revealed as soon as the Meta Connect event next week.
Meta is reportedly ready to launch less pervy smart glasses
New camera-free frames might avoid the ‘pervert glasses’ nickname, The Information reports.
Instead of a camera, the Luna glasses will reportedly include six microphones that allow users to chat to Meta AI and the new Muse AI agent, along with speakers for audio playback. Stripping the camera out has apparently made it possible to make the glasses’ arms smaller, and closer to ordinary frames. Meta is reportedly targeting to ship the new glasses in October in two styles: Clubmaster and Burbank.
It’s a delicate time for Meta’s smart glasses. While its existing frames have proven popular, they’ve also sparked a privacy backlash caused primarily by the camera. Bad actors have used the glasses to surreptitiously record people, in some cases intentionally harassing them in pursuit of social media virality, and the glasses have been banned everywhere from New York courtrooms to Britain’s largest pub chain. While the glasses are equipped with a recording LED, and Meta says the camera will stop functioning if this has been tampered with, the company has been caught in a cat-and-mouse game with a small group of users developing workarounds to record with the LED off.
The Information reports that the camera-free Luna glasses will be joined at Connect next week by new augmented reality glasses, codenamed Phoenix, capable of bringing up a virtual workspace or movie screen in AR. Those are set to release in 2027, and follow a similar AR concept device from 2024.
Removing the camera may not entirely solve Meta’s privacy woes. The new Apple Watch models announced last week drew some criticism for their always-on audio recording capabilities. Meta’s new glasses could still trigger their own concerns thanks to the combination of microphones and a design that makes them harder to distinguish from regular glasses. And when it comes to trust, Meta rarely gets the benefit of the doubt.

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

British tourists escape ‘wall of flames’ by fleeing into the sea as Croatia wildfire tears through holiday island
Dozens of tourists were evacuated from the Brač island on Croatian navy and fishing boats
Hundreds of people including British tourists have evacuated a Croatian island after a major wildfire broke out, with one recalling fleeing “as a wall of flames closed in”, according to reports.
Around 500 people were evacuated from the island of Brač near the popular coastal city of Split, firefighters told the Hina news agency, many of whom were guests at the Gava Waterman Milna Resort, including several guests.
Britons at the resort told how they were forced to flee into the sea on a paddleboard to escape the flames, with some alleging they were “abandoned” during the evacuation effort in an interview with The Times - an accusation the resort has denied.
Josh Robbins, 26, said he and his fiancée Shelby A’Court left their room to find the resort’s car park “surrounded by a wall of fire as firefighters tried to hold back the flames”. The pair had to “run for our lives as a wall of flames closed in as we were showered by burning embers”, he told The Times.
They first noticed something was wrong when the power went out. The hotel’s reception told them “everything was fine” but to pack their bags just in case, Mr Robbins told Croatian broadcaster RLT Danas according to net.hr.
“We went to our room, but about 10 minutes later the fire was already close to the room, maybe 20 or 30 meters away,” he said. “We went to the reception, but it was empty. There was only one member of staff left. The electric doors wouldn't open, and guests were trying to get out. We had to force them open.”
Boats were sent out to rescue those trapped on the island, including speedboats, fishing boats, and boats belonging to the Croatian navy and port authorities.
Ms A’Court gave more details of the harrowing evacuation effort: "It was terrible. We were in the water, on a stand-up paddleboard and trying to get to the boat that was leaving.
“We were screaming, crying, begging. Luckily, they stopped and we were able to get on board. It was a matter of life and death. We're safe now and that's what matters.”
She added in a separate interview with The Times: “Josh lost his shoes as we swam and I had to abandon stuff in my bag because it was soaked through and dragging me down. Others swam for it and it’s amazing no one was lost or drowned in the darkness.”
Electrician Steve Saunders, 57, from Kent, told the British outlet that he and his 52-year-old wife, Anna, were “abandoned and given no instructions whatsoever”.
Mr Robbins said the hotel “handled the situation very poorly”, adding: “They didn't give us any warning, they didn't tell us in time to evacuate.”
The Independent has contacted Waterman Hotels for comment, but a spokesperson previously denied that the staff abandoned guests in a response to The Times.
“This was an exceptionally fast-moving wildfire, driven by very strong winds. Power was lost across the resort, heavy smoke severely reduced visibility and conditions changed dramatically in a very short period of time. We completely understand why guests caught up in those circumstances were terrified, and we do not seek to diminish or challenge their individual experiences.
But the spokesman added the resort is “extremely proud of the responsibility and courage shown by our employees that night”.
The mayor of Milna, a village in Brač, described the wildfire as a “disaster”, adding that it was “simply impossible”.
Speaking to Net.hr, mayor Frane Lozic added on Sunday: "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9pm and out of nowhere, there is a monster.”
Authorities believe around 3,500 hectares have been burned by the fire, according to the AFP news agency, although a full damage assessment is still underway.
Croatia has suffered the its worst year for wildfires since 2022 in terms of burned area, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), the forecasting system for the EU’s Copernicus climate change service.
More than 20,800 hectares have burnt across 59 wildfires in the country so far this year, EFFIS data shows.
It is unclear whether this includes the Brač fire, but it remains short of the record of 67,666 hectares across 108 wildfires in 2017, the worst year for wildfires in the country since EFFIS started recording data.
It comes towards the end of a devastating summer for wildfires across Europe. Malaysian boy acquitted for murder of schoolgirl on grounds of insanity
- Published
A Malaysian teenage boy charged with the high-profile murder of a female schoolmate has been acquitted, with the judge finding the boy was mentally unsound during the incident.
He had fatally stabbed Yap Shing Xuen in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur.
The killing of the 16-year-old girl had shocked Malaysia and sparked debate about the effects of social media on children.
Police previously had said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy, who was 14 at the time. The case was seen to have spurred authorities to limit children's access to social media, which began earlier this year.
The boy - who cannot be named under Malaysian law as he is still a minor - had pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
During the trial defence lawyers did not deny that the boy killed the girl, but argued that he had suffered from poor mental health for years and asked for his acquittal on the grounds of insanity.
An expert witness, a psychiatrist, testified that the boy had schizophrenia, and had suffered from mental illness and experienced delusions since he was nine years old.
The boy's condition was said to have worsened during the pandemic and when he eventually returned to school. Lawyers had said that the boy would need medication for the rest of his life to manage symptoms.
On Monday the judge ruled that the boy would be acquitted, but also ordered for him to be detained and to receive treatment at a psychiatric hospital.
He will stay at the hospital until he is deemed fit to be released back to society, and would likely be subject to yearly assessments.
A defence lawyer told reporters on Monday that upon hearing the verdict, the boy appeared "neutral in emotion, but he understands what is going on, [that] it's a very serious matter".
The trial and verdict hearings were held in a closed court, which meant that the public and media could not attend.
- Malaysian boy on trial for allegedly murdering girl in school 
  - Published3 August
The case has profoundly shocked Malaysia and sparked a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children.
Much of this conversation was triggered by the contents of a note that police had found on the boy at the time of his arrest, which was leaked online and widely circulated.
Some people had compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which featured a storyline about a young boy killing a female schoolmate and explored the theme of online radicalisation.
Last year, the country's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools.
He was quoted by local media as saying that "almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media", and vowed to look into stricter measures.
Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content.
Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.

DOJ says companies used Binance to funnel $1.5 billion in crypto to Iran
President Trump pardoned the exchange's founder last year after he pled guilty to violating anti-money-laundering laws.
The US Department of Justice is accusing several companies of using the crypto exchange Binance to send money to Iran to fund its military, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. Federal prosecutors disclosed Binance's alleged role in the scheme in a forfeiture complaint that looks to seize $61 million of cryptocurrency. In total, they say that around $1.5 billion was sent to the country via a series of interrelated digital wallets.
This scheme involves two Hong Kong-based companies called Hexa Whale and Blessed Trust, which acted as intermediaries to sell black-market Iranian oil to Chinese buyers. Binance itself confirmed this, as the company's internal investigators found that the two entities, among others, had moved heaps of money through the exchange to a network that was funding Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The US Attorney's Office has said that the companies used "Binance to conduct cryptocurrency transactions representing the proceeds of black-market sales of Iranian oil to buyers in China." The complaint goes further and says that some of the money was sent through the US financial system before ending up in Iran. These transactions were allegedly designed to hide the original source of the funds.
The crypto exchange removed both Hexa Whale and Blessed Trust from the platform, though it's worth noting that the latter was an actual Binance business partner that provided payment services. It also fired some of the investigators that found the suspicious transactions, which seems like an odd move. The company says these investigators were fired because of "individual circumstances."
This is just the latest Binance-affiliated scandal. The company actually pled guilty to violating anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws back in 2023, agreeing to pay billions of dollars in fines. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao spent four months behind bars on related charges, though was later issued a full pardon by President Trump.
The exchange has recently been accused of allowing an Iranian financier named Babak Zanjani to send over $850 million over two years to help fund the country's war chest, though Zanjani denies the allegations. Investors also lost millions during a system outage, which led to a class action lawsuit.
Other than speculation, I'm still not entirely sure what legitimate uses there are for cryptocurrencies. Sending money to a foreign government via shadowy means seems like a feature more than a bug. As far as I can tell, the key use case here is funding organizations in secret (see above), buying drugs and weapons on the dark web and scamming people. What a technology!

In an interview, Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe discussed his findings regarding steep markups on hospital consumables and the recent regulatory action against Mumbai's Cafe Mondegar. Person-to-person transfers and merchant transactions up to 2,000 rupees remain entirely free, alongside exemptions for small vendors receiving up to 1 lakh rupees monthly. Indian police detain driver who hit female biker in viral video
- Published
Police in India have detained a man after footage appearing to show a car striking a female motorcyclist in the city of Gurugram near India's capital Delhi sparked national outrage.
The incident took place on Sunday when Shivani Chauhan was riding with a group of motorcyclists.
A video recorded by a camera mounted on her bike appears to show a white car moving close and hitting her motorcycle. Chauhan falls on to the road as her motorcycle skids away, while the car continues moving.
The clip, shared by Chauhan on Instagram, has gone viral, prompting police to open an investigation. The driver, identified as Kalyan Bainsla, has denied hitting her deliberately.
On Tuesday, Gurugram police spokesperson Sandeep Kumar confirmed to the BBC that Bainsla, a gym owner from Palwal in Haryana state, had been detained. Police said he had borrowed the car from another man.
The case was initially registered under sections of the law which deal with rash driving and acts endangering life or personal safety. Police later added "attempted murder" to the charges.
In an interview with Aaj Tak news channel, external, Bainsla claimed that members of the biking group had repeatedly overtaken his car before slowing down in front of it. He said he lost control near a U-turn while trying to avoid Chauhan's motorcycle.
Bainsla also said he did not initially realise that Chauhan was a woman and maintained that he had asked her and another rider to slow down.
He claimed he drove away because the motorcyclists were shouting abuses and he feared that he and his relatives would be attacked.
"Had I stopped right then, those people would have beaten us up," he told the channel.
Chauhan has disputed his account. In a video posted on Instagram after the crash, she said the car had begun following her group shortly after they started their ride.
She alleged that its occupants became hostile and asked her to stop after she told the driver to keep a safe distance. Chauhan said she continued riding because she feared the car might block her, while a friend riding behind tried to shield her motorcycle.
She also alleged that the men in the car appeared to be intoxicated. The police have not said whether alcohol tests were conducted.
But Bainsla's lawyer, Naveen Bainsla, denied the allegation, telling the ANI news agency that his client had not been drinking and was travelling with relatives. He also rejected the description of the incident as a deliberate "hit-and-run case", arguing that it was a case of negligent driving.
After Bainsla publicly denied hitting her deliberately, Chauhan posted another video on Monday night challenging his version of events.
She said the footage showed which vehicle had been moving towards the other. She also rejected his claim that he had not realised she was a woman.
Chauhan also questioned why Bainsla had not stopped to check on her. "I could have been gravely hurt or broken my bones. I could've died on the spot," she said.
Chauhan sustained minor injuries, according to reports, but her protective gear is believed to have prevented more serious harm.
The footage has prompted widespread anger online and a broader discussion about the harassment and hostility female bikers say they face on Indian roads.
Several women riders shared their experiences of being followed, filmed without consent or challenged to race, particularly when they were riding high-powered motorcycles.
Divya Sandhu, a riding coach who was involved in a similar collision a decade ago, told NDTV, external channel that attitudes had changed little since then.
"It's very common for people to joke about women's driving skills," she said.
Another motorcyclist, Pallavi Singh, said some women concealed their hair and wore full protective clothing partly to avoid being identified and harassed while riding.

Saudi Arabia has warned Yemen’s Houthi group against attacks near the holy city of Mecca after its air defences intercepted and destroyed a drone south of the city on Tuesday.
The Saudi-led military coalition said the drone was brought down before it could enter prohibited airspace over Mecca. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said the security of Islam’s two holiest sites and pilgrims was a “red line”, warning that necessary deterrent measures would be taken against the Houthis.
Mecca is Islam’s holiest city and home to sites visited by millions of Muslims during the annual Hajj pilgrimage.
Al-Malki described the incident as the second alleged Houthi attempt to target Mecca, following what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch towards the city in July 2017.
The Houthis, however, rejected the Saudi claim. Houthi spokesperson Hazem al-Assad said on social media that allegations of targeting Mecca were a repeated claim that “no longer fools anyone”.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) condemned what it described as an attack targeting Islam’s holy city and blamed the Houthis. The 57-member grouping also denounced what it called continued aggression against Saudi Arabia.
Saudi authorities issued security alerts across several parts of the kingdom on Tuesday, including Mecca, amid a series of attacks by Iran-aligned fighters that have increased tensions in the region.
The US Embassy subsequently advised Americans to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia, citing risks including drone and missile attacks, armed conflict and terrorism. It also warned against travel to areas near the Yemen border.
The latest incident comes as the Houthis have expanded their operations around the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key global shipping route.
The group has claimed several attacks against Saudi targets in recent days, including a strike on an airbase on Monday, which it said was retaliation for Saudi-led airstrikes in Yemen.

I have similar feelings about the very large glass trackpad. For things like photo editing, the trackpad's size is great, but I found my palms occasionally clicked the buttons at the bottom of the trackpad when I took a break from typing. It didn't happen often, but I learned to be careful about where I put my palms.
The 2-MP 1080p webcam is fine for casual use, chatting with family and friends, but if you do a lot of Zoom meetings in a professional context, you may want an external webcam. Also, open-source purists should note that Coreboot still does not support AMD Ryzen chips (or AMD does not support Coreboot, depending on how you want to look at it), so the Pangolin Pro does not use open firmware.
Finally, the Pangolin Pro is easy to open up to replace or repair components. There are nine screws on the bottom of the chassis, and none of them are hidden under the rubber feet or other shenanigans. Unscrew them all, and the bottom lifts off, giving you access to the SSD slots, RAM, WiFi card, and the rest of the internals. You'll have no trouble upgrading components down the road if you decide to, say, upgrade your memory when RAM prices come back down. (Is that actually going to happen? Who knows.)
Pop!_OS Linux Integration
System76's Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you're using Linux.
As a long-time Linux user, I'm probably biased, but I find Linux to offer a better user experience than MacOS or Windows. I never feel like I'm fighting the operating system to get things the way I want them. I mainly run a terminal for writing, email, reading RSS feeds, etc, and a web browser. When I need to edit photos, I open Darktable; videos in DaVinci Resolve. None of that should require much from an operating system, but for some reason it's all easier for me in Linux.
Pop!_OS is particularly good in this regard, as it manages to feel familiar enough for Linux newcomers to find their way around, while still offering a good amount of power-user features. For instance, if you don't know what tiling windows are, you never need to be bothered about them, but if you want them, you can enable them with a toggle switch in the settings app. There are loads of (customizable) keyboard shortcuts for developers who eschew the mouse, and there are plenty of trackpad gestures to control workspaces, window focus, and more.
Should You Buy It?
At the beginning, I said the Pangolin Pro is overkill for most peoples needs, which is true. Although the Pangolin is actually cheaper than the smaller System76 Lemur Pro (review coming soon), the more portable Lemur Pro might be a better fit for many. However, if you're doing highly intensive things with your laptop, building local AI models or training custom agents, compiling software, or just want a powerful, future-proof machine, Pangolin is one of the best Linux laptops I've tested.
If you're a Linux user looking for a 16-inch laptop with all the bells and whistles, and one that isn't crazy expensive or crazy heavy, this is the machine I would get.

‘Feminism Is the Consequence of the “Man Problem,” Not Its Cause’
Readers respond to our June 2026 cover story and more.
The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote
Helen Lewis’s “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” is the most important thing I have read this year. My husband has said that Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election because of the misogyny that exists in America; Lewis’s article proved him correct, with just a teaspoon of humor mixed into an otherwise very frightening topic.
Amy Crist
 Gettysburg, Pa.
Upon finishing “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote,” I found myself equal parts stunned and galvanized. Lewis has an extraordinary ability to illuminate what so many of us feel but struggle to articulate, and this article was no exception.
The MAGA movement contends that feminism is to blame for American decline. But feminism didn’t emerge from nothing. Feminism is the consequence of the “man problem” Lewis identifies, not its cause.
The Bible passage that anti-feminist commentators love to cite is from Ephesians: “Wives, submit to your husbands.” But that’s where they stop reading. The verse goes on to say that a husband must provide for his wife, and love her as he loves his own body. This is not a “do as I say or else” arrangement; it is a covenant of mutual care—her health and happiness are meant to be as important to him as his own, and vice versa. When men forget the instruction to care for their wives as they care for themselves, women have no choice but to learn to care for themselves.
I was recently at the pharmacy, and the man ahead of me—trying to pick up a prescription for his sick wife—answered the pharmacist’s questions with “I don’t know; my wife takes care of that.” When a husband utters, “My wife takes care of that,” the word that means “everything.” It means knowing the passwords, the medications and dosages, the appointment schedules. It means knowing what to say to assuage a teenager’s broken heart, whom to call at the school, how to manage a crisis. It means caring for sick husbands and aging parents—sacrificing for the people you love.
I am the breadwinner in my family. My husband stayed home and raised our three daughters. The plan was for him to return to work once the girls were in elementary school. But we all know what happens when we make plans—God laughs. My husband now lives with a neurological condition that complicates our lives in ways neither of us anticipated. Does working to provide health care for my children and husband make me less of a woman? Would my husband be mocked in the manosphere for not working? Is staying home to raise children noble only when a woman does it?
Erika Jackson
 Gilbert, Ariz.
I worry that “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” misses a crucial component of the rise of masculinism. I stand in vocal opposition to misogyny and the idiocy of the far-right masculine media sphere. I teach my daughters that they control their bodies and that they should never miss a vote. But I do think that a large cohort of men is struggling with issues that have been ignored, or sometimes even mocked, by the mainstream media. Many men try to be good husbands and parents, only to hear mantras like “We don’t need men” and “There are no good men out there”; on social media, people discuss whether they’d prefer to be trapped in the woods with a man or a bear. Meanwhile, American men are nearly four times more likely than women to die by suicide. The manosphere discusses that issue frequently, as Lewis notes; the mainstream media do not. When men hear negative messages about being a man from the mainstream media but see the manosphere addressing their struggles, they will gravitate toward it. I hope society can learn to address male issues without mocking them. Otherwise, I fear, the extremism will continue.
Ben Rodriguez
 Suffield, Conn.
A significant number of men are never fully socialized. These men have few if any friends—and certainly no female friends. Deep down, they may not hate or fear women; they just don’t know how to interact with them. They never learned how to work with or cooperate with them. If one accepts that, then quixotic attempts to repeal women’s suffrage or strip women of social and political freedoms should not surprise anyone.
Virgil Jose
 Apple Valley, Calif.
Helen Lewis makes a convincing argument that the noisy, often lewd misogyny of the MAGA right is no longer fringe and presents a real danger to women. This sexist worldview reflects and interacts with patriarchal systems across the world.
Examining more than 350 variables across 176 nations, the scholars Valerie M. Hudson, Donna Lee Bowen, and Perpetua Lynne Nielsen have demonstrated that “the fate of nations is tied to the status of women.” Their 2020 book, The First Political Order: How Sex Shapes Governance and National Security Worldwide, shows that nations that subordinate women tend to be more fragile, autocratic, corrupt, and impoverished. Helen Lewis replies:
As you might imagine, this article prompted a large and varied mailbag. I heard from grandfathers—happily married for decades—who couldn’t understand how society seemed to have gone backwards, from middle-aged men who felt overlooked because their problems weren’t fashionable, and from parents who worried about what their sons were watching online. I came away thinking that screen-time limits are good, that schools should do more to accommodate rambunctious boys as well as conscientious girls, and that the Democrats need to develop their own, positive visions of masculinity to compete with those of Andrew Tate and Nick Fuentes.
Some of the likely 2028 presidential contenders have started to do that: Gavin Newsom talks regularly about men’s problems, and signed an executive order aimed at improving mental-health services and reducing male suicide rates in California. Pete Buttigieg has learned how to bro out on podcasts such as Andrew Schulz’s Flagrant—the kind of spaces where Donald Trump did so well during the 2024 campaign. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez waded into the debate over the looks-maxxer Clavicular (the guy who claims to have achieved a better jawline by hitting himself with hammers) by highlighting the pressures on young men to conform to unrealistic beauty standards. The conversation is definitely shifting.
Behind the Cover
In this month’s cover story, “Empire of Grift,” Anne Applebaum examines how hardened ideologues and opportunistic profiteers are bending American diplomacy to advance an antidemocratic agenda—and their own financial interests. For our cover, the illustrator Ben Hickey created an ominous image of figures in shadow arrayed around a map of the world, evoking the war-room scenes from Stanley Kubrick’s 1964 film, Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb.
Corrections
“The Great Romance Slump” (September) stated that birth control was legalized for married couples in 1965. In fact, in 1965 the Supreme Court held that the government couldn’t restrict a married couple’s access to birth control. “Confessions of a Token Black Professor” (September) described a sign affixed to the wall of a former mill in Lewiston, Maine, as neon. In fact, it is a marquee sign.

6 other ways Trump is meddling in the midterms
The Supreme Court ruled against Trump’s mail voting rules, but the president is still trying to mess with the election.
The recent history of mail voting in the United States has more twists and turns than an Emmy-winning drama. But for the cause of democracy, at least, yesterday’s ending is a happy one.
On Monday, the Supreme Court definitively blocked President Donald Trump’s many attempts to sabotage voting by mail — opining, in a three-sentence brief, that Trump can’t implement his new rules for the 2026 midterms. Or for any election, probably.
Those last-minute rules, you may recall, would have required states to adopt new ballot envelopes and upload absentee voters’ names and envelope barcodes to a still-nonexistent online platform. Many officials argued they couldn’t possibly adopt the new measures before midterm voting starts, which would essentially cancel mail-in voting in their jurisdictions.
The Supreme Court, of course, has been broadly sympathetic to Trump’s legal antics, even when they appear to clearly flout law or precedent. But shutting down voting just before the midterms? That’s one bridge too far for them.
Go a little deeper
Hobbling vote-by-mail was just one of Trump’s plots to meddle in the midterms, however — and several of the others are still underway. Here’s where some of the president’s most significant election maneuvers stand today:
How worried should you be going into the midterms? That, my friend, is a question to answer in your own little heart. But I’m taking my cues from Vox’s politics editor, Benjy Sarlin, who recently reminded listeners of our America, Actually podcast that there are many, many institutional and logistical barriers to many of Trump’s more concerning legal machinations.
“We’re taking it very seriously here…and nothing’s guaranteed,” he acknowledged. “But it is still a very difficult path [where] so far he has had zero success.”
