NEW YORK — Pennsylvania officials have reported a fourth measles-associated death.
The latest death involved an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state, the county coroner’s office said in a Facebook post. The cause was acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of measles, it said.
On Saturday, a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania, died of measles complications. And last month, two measles-infected infants died in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state.
None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with nearly 700 illnesses reported so far this year across 38 counties, including about 100 cases in the last seven days. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say.
“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” the state’s health secretary, Dr. Debra Bogen, said in a statement Tuesday, referring to the two most recent deaths — those of the adults.
“We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine, which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades.”
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, health care access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates.
— Mike Stobbe

- The claim that the Flight 93 National Memorial changed the time of its 2026 9/11 observance to accommodate a visit from U.S. President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance but neither showed up is unproven.
- Though event pages for past Flight 93 National Memorial ceremonies showed the 2026 event started around an hour and 15 minutes earlier than in previous years, the 2026 program (archived) also was longer than previous years. Moreover, we found no evidence that Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the event at the memorial but failed to show.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the National Park Service regarding the reason for an earlier start time in 2026 and the White House to find out whether Trump and/or Vance were supposed to attend, and are waiting for responses.
After the U.S. commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that the Flight 93 National Memorial changed the time of its 9/11 observance to accommodate a visit from U.S. President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance but neither showed up.
United Airlines Flight 93 was one of four planes hijacked on 9/11. It was the only one that did not hit a building, instead crashing in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers attempted to retake control of the plane from the hijackers.
In sharing the claim about Trump and Vance, one X user wrote: "The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up. Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead."
The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up.
Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead. pic.twitter.com/SVhVbLaY6s
— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) September 14, 2026
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claim is unproven. Though event pages for 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial from 2020 to 2026 showed the 2026 event started around an hour and 15 minutes earlier than previous ceremonies, the program (archived) also was longer than in previous years.
We found no evidence that Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the event at the memorial but did not show. Trump attended a commemoration ceremony at the Pentagon with military leaders on Sept. 11, 2026, while Vance attended a commemoration event in New York City at the site of the former Twin Towers. Trump travelled to Dublin, Ireland, in the evening for a two-day visit that included attending the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club on Sept. 13.
We contacted the National Park Service, which manages the Flight 93 National Memorial, to ask why the 2026 observance started earlier than in previous years. We also asked the White House press office whether Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the Flight 93 National Memorial observance and await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, because the NPS had not confirmed why the 2026 event had a different start time than previous years, we leave this claim unrated.
Longer 2026 event also memorialized other 9/11 flights
According to event programs for the 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 events, previous 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial started at either 9:45 or 9:50 a.m., which could be in order to coincide with the exact time Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, at 10:03 a.m. Sept. 11, 2001. The 2026 event started at 8:30 a.m.
The event programs from 2021 to 2024 generally started with welcome remarks, the Pledge of Allegiance or national anthem, followed by a reading of the names of the 40 passengers and crew on board Flight 93 who died when the plane crashed.
The event programs then listed bells of remembrance, a moment of reflection and conclusion and a wreath-laying. Some events also featured speakers such as former President George W. Bush and then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2021 and then-first lady Jill Biden in 2022. Trump attended a smaller, live-streamed ceremony during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The 2026 program appeared longer than in previous years, and included remembrances for the three other hijacked flights on 9/11 that struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The 2026 program added musical selections and also included bell tollings and wreath-layings for American Airlines Flight 11, which hit the North Tower on 8:46 a.m., United Airlines Flight 175, which hit the South Tower at 9:03 a.m., and American Airlines Flight 77, which hit the Pentagon at 9:37 a.m.
If the 2026 event intended to honor the other three flights at the times they crashed, it would have needed to start earlier than the previous 9:45 or 9:50 a.m. start times.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a series of other rumors about where Trump was or what he was doing on or around Sept. 11, 2001.

Hague court to deliver verdict in war crimes trial of Kosovo’s former President Thaci
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci will learn his fate on Wednesday as international judges in The Hague deliver verdicts in his war crimes trial
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci will learn his fate Wednesday when international judges at a court in The Hague deliver verdicts in his war crimes trial.
Thaci is facing multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity including murder, torture and persecution alongside three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army who fought Serb forces in the 1998-99 war. They are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
Thousands of people rallied in Pristina over the weekend in support of the four men. The protesters filled a central square in the capital, many carrying red and black Albanian flags.
Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city along with a huge digital clock counting down to Wednesday's verdicts.
“In the name of the people, declare them innocent," one banner read.
Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague have asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaci and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi. They have all denied the charges against them.
“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaci told judges in February at the end of his nearly three-year trial.
According to prosecutors, the men targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA.
The staff at the European Union-backed court are largely international due to fears about witness safety and security. In 2022, the court convicted two leaders of a Kosovo war veterans’ association for intimidating witnesses by publicizing leaked confidential documents.
Thaci also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin later this month.
He was a student who returned from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence. He earned the nickname “the Snake” for his ability to evade Serb forces during the conflict.
He was embraced by Western leaders, who invited him to the 1999 peace talks in France in his role as political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army, and was seen as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.
Thaci rose to political power after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the court in The Hague.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognize. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

Paediatric heart surgeries that can cost families anywhere between ₹5 lakh and ₹20 lakh each at private hospitals, were provided free of cost to children at the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad. As part of its fifth paediatric cardiac surgery camp, NIMS performed 19 complex heart surgeries on a cashless basis on children aged between two months and 13 years. The week-long camp concluded on Saturday (September 12, 2026)
The surgeries were carried out by the NIMS Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery in collaboration with Healing Little Hearts, with a specialist team led by paediatric cardiac surgeon Ramana Dhanapuneni from the UK. The NIMS team was headed by M. Amaresh Rao, Head of Cardiothoracic Surgery.
From screening to surgery
The camp’s impact extended well beyond the 19 operations. Around 1,000 children were screened as part of the programme. Of these, few were found to require minimally invasive intervention rather than open-heart surgery. The surgical team, meanwhile, selected a mix of complex congenital heart cases for the camp, prioritising children who required specialised cardiac surgery. More than 100 children who require surgery are still waiting, with dates already allotted for their procedures, said Dr. Amaresh.
“Congenital heart disease is common and the cost of paediatric cardiac surgery in private hospitals can be prohibitive for many families, ranging from ₹5 lakh to ₹20 lakh. Hope for the poor is public sector hospitals like NIMS,” said Dr. Ramana.
80 surgeries through five camps
The latest camp is the fifth such programme conducted through the collaboration between Dr. Dhanapuneni’s team and NIMS. The partnership began in 2023, when two camps were conducted. One camp was held in 2024 and another in 2025.
NIMS Director Rahul Devraj said the five camps had resulted in about 80 surgeries so far. “NIMS would like Dr. Ramana and his team to visit twice a year, assuring continued institutional support to the visiting specialists and the cardiac department,” he said.
Around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases
Dr. Amaresh said there are around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases, while NIMS currently performs around 400 paediatric cardiac surgeries annually. The department needs to reach 1,000 surgeries a year, he said.
ECMO support under Aarogyasri
Another significant development pertaining to the camp was the availability of ECMO services at NIMS under the Aarogyasri scheme for the first time. “No patient needed it during this camp,” Dr. Amaresh clarified. However, he said the significance was that ECMO would now be available to eligible patients free of cost for as long as it is medically required, subject to the scheme’s provisions.

Meta has removed several Instagram and Facebook accounts and content related to the Jantar Mantar protest that Alt News had flagged as AI-manipulated visuals.
On September 2, a Meta spokesperson confirmed to Alt News that following a review, all the accounts and content were found to be violative of the platform’s policies and had been removed.
These posts included several AI-generated and AI-manipulated photographs and videos of women protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest in July. Alt News flagged Instagram and Facebook accounts and posts to Meta, in which real visuals women had been altered using AI, purportedly in an attempt to outrage their modesty.
In these posts, women’s clothes, bodies and poses had been altered in such a way that they looked starkly different from the original videos or photographs. Alt News’ investigation found that many such visuals were either entirely AI-generated or altered using AI. In some cases, techniques such as face swaps or body swaps were used.
Targeting Women CJP Protesters
Women protesters who participated in the CJP protests in Delhi were particularly targeted on social media. For several days, women faced online harassment and trolling, doxxing, rape threats and the public disclosure of personal information. These AI-visuals formed part of this larger pattern of attacks against female protesters.
These fake visuals were shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, among other platforms, claiming that they were real footage from the Jantar Mantar protest. Users then mistook the AI characters for real women partaking in the protests which was followed by objectionable and misogynistic comments targeting their identities, physical appearance, clothes and character. A few of those comments are displayed below:
Alt News identified several Instagram accounts which circulated such malicious content, including @kauronfire, @sirfseerat, @tia_kaurr, @hey.siya_2.0, @kavya_homevibes, @annika0022, @divyankaha and @its_anushkaa69.
Right-wing Users Share AI Image
During the protest, several right-wing users, including RSS supporters Acharya Ankur Arya and Vikram Pratap Singh, shared an AI-generated image claiming that it was a real photograph from the Jantar Mantar protest.
The purported image showed a young woman wearing a crop top and jeans. Users who shared the post made objectionable comments about the woman’s clothing and character. Alt News fact-checked this viral image and found that it was entirely AI-generated.
However, in some cases that surfaced on social media during the final days of the protest, besides entirely AI-generated images, real photographs of women were being altered, making it difficult to determine its authencity.
Visuals Of A Woman In White Saree
An user, @divyankaha, shared a photo and video on their Instagram account and YouTube channel respectively. These showed a woman wearing a white saree and navy blue blouse, linking her to the Jantar Mantar protest. (Archive link-1, Archive link-2)
Alt News found the original video of the post uploaded on an Instagram page @khoji_reporter24news.
Comparing the viral clip with the original video, we found that the body and clothing of the woman were entirely different, thus confirming that the image had been altered using AI. The background and original footage of the viral video remained the same, but the appearance of the woman had been completely manipulated. After Alt News flagged this to Meta, they removed @divyankaha‘s account.
We found several such posts and videos on @divyankaha‘s page. In another post, a woman wearing a white saree is seen sitting on the road wit posters infront of her. Alt News found this photo was also an AI-deepfake. (Archive link)
Several different versions of the viral post, with a woman in a white saree, were also found circulating widely on social media. All of these were AI-deepfakes.
Visuals Of A Woman Standing With A Poster
Another photograph went viral showing different women near the stage at the Jantar Mantar protest, holding posters that read “Resign De De Bhai PUNE SE Aai hu..and Hum jeet gaye”.
In the different iterations of this photo being shared, the woman as well as the design of the poster kept changing. These photos were shared by right-wing handles and those opposing the CJP protest, with objectionable comments and captions. (Archive Link-1, Link-2, Link-3, Link-4)
We found that this photo had been altered using AI. The original photoe was posted on July 22 by an Instagram account named @nanddhini.
A comparison of the original and viral photos clearly showed the difference in the woman’s face and body. The design of the poster also appears to have changed across different viral versions. Thus, the face and body of the woman in the original photo were swapped using an AI editing tool.
Similarly, several AI-generated and manipulated photos and videos were shared on the Facebook and Instagram accounts of @sirfseerat. These posts either altered real visuals related to the Jantar Mantar protest or created entirely new AI visuals. Some of these posts, displayed below, were later deleted.
Woman Speaking To Journalist
An Instagram AI-digital creator page named @kauronfire shared a video on July 23 in which a journalist can be seen interviewing a woman participating in the protest. (Archive)
We found the original video posted on journalist Muskan Bhagat’s Instagram account. (Archive)

Woman Raising Slogans
@kauronfire shared another video showing a woman protester wearing a yellow crop top and shorts, raising slogans during the protest. (Archive)

These accounts misused AI, not only as a means to spread misinformation, but also to depict women in an objectionable manner, exposing them to online, and even real life harassment and abuse — all of which amount to punishable offences under the IT Act and the IT Rules of India.

BJP partners in Uttar Pradesh yet to open cards on Uniform Civil Code
For the BJP, UCC is part of its core ideological troika, besides the Ram Temple and the abrogation of Article 370.
The ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) partners in Uttar Pradesh seem to be treading with caution in declaring their support to the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), especially ahead of the assembly polls in the country’s most populous province.
The contentious issue has returned to the state’s political discourse after Union home minister Amit Shah, on September 13, asserted that the UCC would be implemented in all NDA-ruled states before 2029.
For the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), UCC is part of its core ideological troika, besides the Ram Temple and the abrogation of Article 370.
Deep Dive
“The UCC has always been part of BJP’s core goal and election manifesto like the abrogation of Article 370 in J&K. The party is committed to bring UCC,” said Dinesh Pratap Singh, state BJP’s chief spokesperson. “Now, after Union home minister’s statement, the state government will move in this direction.”
Also Read | Will Uniform Civil Code be an issue in poll-bound Uttar Pradesh?
A section of the BJP believes the UCC might help the party in countering the opposition’s poll plank in the caste-sensitive state ahead of the 2027 assembly polls.
“The narrative around UCC will help the party counter the opposition’s poll plank on caste to some extent,” said a senior BJP leader, requesting anonymity.
BJP’s allies in Uttar Pradesh, however, are yet to disclose their official stand, while treading the issue with caution.
“I will not comment on the issue at present. I will get back after consulting the party high command,” said Rashtriya Lok Dal (RLD) national general secretary Anil Dubey. Led by Jayant Chaudhary, the RLD is part of the NDA at the Centre and in the state, with its core base being Jats and farmers in western UP.
Another alliance partner, Apna Dal (Soneylal), which has a core base of Kurmis and non-Yadav OBCs in eastern Uttar Pradesh, is also yet to formally announce its support to the UCC. Party’s state chief RP Gautam refused to comment, saying the party high command will comment on the issue. Party chief Anupriya Patel is a junior minister at the Centre.
Also Read | Uniform Civil Code bills await President’s nod in Assam, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh
Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party (SBSP), led by Om Prakash Rajbhar, has also not made its stand clear on the UCC.
To be sure, none of the BJP’s allies in UP have openly opposed Shah’s assertion on the UCC.
Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav in a post on X on Tuesday said: “Public understands that the UCC [that] BJP is talking about actually has a different full form: UCC = Underground Communal Conspiracy. First fulfil previous promises, then bring UCC. Transfer ₹15 lakh into accounts, then bring UCC. Provide 2 crore jobs, then bring UCC.”

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

Wired vs wireless speakers: What are the pros and cons?
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi make different compromises, and a wired connection alone doesn't guarantee better sound.
Wireless speakers are often treated as the convenient option, while wired systems get cast as the choice for better sound. The connection alone doesn't settle this question, though. Speaker design, amplification, source material and room acoustics all affect what you hear.
It also helps to separate the connection from the way the speaker is powered. Traditional passive speakers need a separate amplifier, which sends the amplified signal through speaker wire. Powered, or active, speakers have amplification built in. A wireless speaker receives audio over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or another wireless connection, but that doesn't necessarily make it cable-free. Many home models still plug into an outlet, while portable speakers run on batteries.
What wired speakers still do better
One clear advantage of passive wired systems is modularity. Because the amplifier and speakers are separate, you can replace or upgrade one without rebuilding the whole setup. That matters when you're putting together a stereo or home theater system you expect to keep for years.
A wired connection also removes Bluetooth transmission from the latency chain. Bluetooth can introduce a delay between the source and the sound reaching the speaker, with the amount varying between devices. Video playback can often compensate by delaying the picture to keep it in sync, but it's harder to mask in video games since the sound needs to react to what you're doing. The Bluetooth Special Interest Group's explanation of LE Audio describes buffering in Bluetooth Classic Audio as one source of that lag and explains how LE Audio can reduce it.
That doesn't mean a cable automatically makes music sound better, though. If the source is a lossy audio file, some information has already been removed during compression. Switching to a wired connection can't put that information back. The quality of the speaker, amplifier and recording still matters, as does the room you're listening in.
Cables are the obvious trade-off. A basic stereo pair is usually easy enough to wire, but setting up surround sound can mean running speaker cables to several points around a room. That can limit placement or leave you figuring out how to hide wires along walls, under rugs or behind furniture.
Where wireless speakers have the advantage
Wireless speakers are easier to place when you don't want to run audio cables across a room. Bluetooth models connect directly to a phone, tablet or laptop without relying on home Wi-Fi, which makes them especially useful for portable listening. That's the core appeal behind the models in our best portable Bluetooth speakers guide: flexible options you can easily carry anywhere you need them.
Wi-Fi speakers are better suited to a permanent home setup. Compatible models can use the same network for synchronized playback across several rooms, often through a companion app. The Denon Home 200, 400 and 600 speakers we reviewed, for example, use the HEOS app to group speakers or control rooms separately.
The trade-off is that wireless systems replace some cable management with network and software dependence. Wi-Fi speakers still need power, and multi-room platforms can work best when you stay within one ecosystem. Bluetooth range and reliability can also vary with distance, interference and the devices involved.
Bluetooth doesn't automatically mean poor audio quality, either. Many codecs use lossy compression, but Qualcomm's aptX Lossless is designed to deliver CD-quality lossless audio with compatible hardware, a lossless source and suitable wireless conditions. Wi-Fi systems can support lossless and high-resolution streaming too, so the connection type alone doesn't determine how good a speaker will sound.
Some portable models support Wi-Fi, as well. As our Sonos Play review notes, that device can use Wi-Fi at home or Bluetooth for a direct connection while you're out.
Which setup makes more sense for you?
Wired speakers are the stronger fit for a permanent stereo or home theater system if you don't mind running cables. Passive models give you more freedom to replace the amplifier or speakers later, and the wired connection avoids Bluetooth latency.
Wireless speakers make more sense when portability, easier placement or multi-room playback matters more than component-level upgrades. Bluetooth is best-suited for speakers you want to move around, while Wi-Fi works better for several speakers spread through a home.
Sound quality alone shouldn't decide it. Start with where the speakers will live and whether you care more about upgradeability, portability or multi-room playback. Then compare the actual speakers that fit that setup to get the best audio quality for your situation.

What Comes After America
Emily St. John Mandel’s latest work of science fiction considers the tenuousness of any possible future.
Emily St. John Mandel writes science fiction, with the accent firmly on fiction. Imagination, not technical verisimilitude, is her strength; she wisely disregards the scientific in favor of the human. Her indifference to plausibility is a measure of her confidence as a storyteller, and helps snare readers like me, who have a mild allergic reaction to postapocalyptic settings and outer-space odysseys. Her previous novel featured time travel, interplanetary travel, and a cosmic glitch; now, in her challenging new novel, Exit Party, we have accidental teleportation between parallel universes. The underlying theme, though, is irresistible: how shockingly little humanity understands about the sudden swerves and reversals that shape a life—or end it. The new book also offers a prescient invitation to consider the human toll that a world of chaos or repression can exact.
Exit Party’s stunning first sentence leaps ahead to 2031 and peeks into a woman’s soul: “In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace.” Newly released after 18 years in prison, 48-year-old Ari Waker is just getting used to a Los Angeles that has seen vicious internecine violence. Although international peacekeeping troops have been withdrawn and the city’s curfew has been lifted, nothing like normalcy prevails. Ari walks with her roommate from their apartment in Echo Park (note the locale) to a party in Silver Lake. There, the incomprehensible happens: Two people from a parallel world materialize at the party, and another person (the host) is teleported in the opposite direction—all by accident.
The inexplicable appearances and disappearances are as disorienting for the reader as they are for Ari, who wonders whether she has a brain tumor or is having a stroke. For the three teleported individuals, the experience is a disaster: instant, complete, and irreversible dislocation. In the alternate universe, we soon learn, the “United State” has become a fortress, “closed like a fist,” where the national doctrine is “Harmony at any cost.” There we encounter, among other characters, Ibari, an enforcer of the brutally repressive social order.
Abrupt cataclysm is a signature of Mandel’s recent work. Before Exit Party came Sea of Tranquility (2022), The Glass Hotel (2020), and Station Eleven (2014)—all of them ingeniously splintered narratives involving many protagonists, zigzagging timelines, and some kind of shattering event. It’s never clear until the end that the shards of narrative can be assembled to form a coherent story. The big picture that at last emerges in Exit Party features paired life stories of doppelgängers, genetically identical sets of characters who have made decisions in their divergent worlds that move them along radically different paths. Ari and Ibari are the principal “twins.” Though at first they seem utterly dissimilar, they are, as Ibari recognizes late in the novel, “two sides of the same coin.”
Repeatedly drawn to criminality (which she associates with freedom), Ari has had more than her share of “hinge moments,” the term she prefers for dramatic, world- and life-changing twists. She launched one criminal enterprise—selling luxury goods bought with stolen credit-card numbers—as a teenager, while living in Brooklyn with an aunt and uncle who dealt in stolen antiques. Soon enough, helped out by her cousin, she was selling U.S. passports. When the Russian Mafia lured her into smuggling people, her cousin, beset by moral qualms, balked. So she hired an assassin to kill him. That’s how she landed in prison.
Sprung from jail and hoping to find her footing, Ari drifts instead. She works as a dishwasher and in warehouses, and then becomes, in dizzying succession, a gunrunner, a trophy wife, a philanthropist, an art collector. Arriving in Paris in a car with bulletproof windows (another hinge moment), she wonders, “How many completely separate lives am I going to get to live before I run out of chances.” Mandel makes this resilient character—a serial transgressor with a pragmatic code of ethics, uncannily accurate premonitions, and a touching capacity for regret—sympathetic and compelling. Her last name, Waker, is a clue to her essence: She’s awake, aware. She will always notice the jacarandas.
A meticulous observer by profession, Ibari is 79 when we meet her, and has risen to a high rank in the Internal Security Service. She’s as frank about her complicity in the disappearance of rule-breaking fellow citizens as Ari is about her weakness for criminality. Ibari has nonetheless imagined a scenario in which, instead of running surveillance operations for the State, she became a criminal; like her twin, she felt there would be “freedom in that.”
The door that swings open at the party remains thereafter obdurately shut. Appalled, puzzled, fascinated, Ari and Ibari (in their parallel worlds) try their best to comprehend what has happened. They investigate, quizzing the accidentally teleported. Eventually, they (and the befuddled reader) learn enough about each other and the different worlds they inhabit to have some thoughts about “entanglement”—about how doubles in their respective universes intersect. Which they do, eerily. Even before she knows anything about Ibari and her career in the secret police, Ari wonders why she herself hadn’t “just become a detective, instead of turning to crime.” She can see the appeal of a life played out in the ranks of the NYPD. She yearns for a homeland where she would be spared the “permanent unease” of encroaching anarchy, where armed fighters aren’t forever shooting at one another on the edge of town.
In Exit Party, those who diverge nearly converge, and every echo resonates.
When they were young girls, Ari and Ibari each read the same children’s detective novel and both latched on to the same sentence: “True diligence means following the improbable path.” While in prison, Ari had TRUE DILIGENCE tattooed on her left wrist; to judge from the improbable path that Ari and Ibari’s creator has followed, it’s Mandel’s motto too.
After growing up in western Canada, mostly homeschooled, Mandel graduated in 2000 from the School of Toronto Dance Theatre. Nine years later, at 30, having abandoned her dream of dancing professionally, she published her debut novel. Like her next two books, it was a noir thriller; all three slipped by more or less unnoticed. Her fourth, Station Eleven, about a flu pandemic “that exploded like a neutron bomb over the surface of the earth,” killing almost every human, won prizes and much-deserved critical praise, and sold remarkably well—before getting a big bump six years later during COVID. Sales of the book passed the 1 million mark shortly after the first episode of an HBO adaptation aired, in late 2021.
Station Eleven was Mandel’s own hinge moment. In addition to introducing what has since become her fiction’s hallmark fracturing of time and lives, the novel displayed her calm authority and her easy way with ambitious imaginative gambits—one world erased, another fighting to be born—carried off with barely a trace of writerly flourish: “The caravans had once been pickup trucks, but now they were pulled by teams of horses on wheels of steel and wood.” In Mandel’s work, unadorned realism is at the service of baroque invention, and everything, including the prose, is subordinate to the story.
Like all the best stories, hers are character-driven. In Station Eleven, Kirsten Raymonde, a child actor before the pandemic and afterward a skilled warrior, is canny and resourceful in the face of catastrophe. Eight years old when her familiar world ended, and a semi-feral teenager when she hooked up with a ragtag troupe that stages Shakespeare plays and orchestral concerts, Kirsten is permanently traumatized, ferocious when necessary, and somehow still capable of tenderness. She’s a sturdy hook for the reader.
Mandel holds tight to some of her characters: She teleports a few between the parallel worlds of her novels. Ari made her debut in The Singer’s Gun (2010), where she was already mercilessly pragmatic and minimally sentimental. An important prop in the new novel is a painting by a minor but vivid character in The Glass Hotel, Lucas Alkaitis, a heroin-addicted artist, talented and doomed, “on the run from mediocrity and Brylcreem and grey flannel suits.” Lucas himself also reappears, still an addict, still committed to his art, in a curious coda to Exit Party set in his Manhattan studio in 1960—a final, wrenching narrative swerve.
In Sea of Tranquility, you’ll find a Mandel stand-in: a newly famous writer in the year 2203 who has left her moon-colony home for planet Earth to embark on a globe-spanning book tour. Separated from her family, she finds herself unmoored, homesick. An interviewer in Estonia asks her what it’s like to have published a tremendously successful book. She answers, “I wrote three books that no one noticed, no distribution beyond the moon colonies, and then … it’s like slipping into a parallel universe.” She continues, “I somehow fell into a bizarre upside-down world where people actually read my work. It’s extraordinary. I hope I never get used to it.”
One of the projects of modernism (and postmodernism) is to unsettle our confidence in the coherence of the self and thereby reveal the truth about our disjointed identity, so often sabotaged by an unruly unconscious. The so-called neomodernist novelist Rachel Cusk has declared that she is “not interested in character because I don’t think character exists anymore.” It seems to me that Mandel, who merrily jettisons narrative conventions and plays cunningly with timelines, nonetheless insists on the essential coherence of her fictional creations. How many completely separate lives can Ari live and still track as a character? “I took out a contract on my cousin,” she says to the host of the Silver Lake party. “It was a mistake and I’m not that person anymore.” I don’t believe her. Though she probably would not now pay to have a close relative murdered, she remains the ruthless person who once did.
All of the doubling that powers the plot of Exit Party prompts us to consider how we recognize ourselves and others—whether we believe in the integrity of our persona and theirs. What is the essential stuff of our identity? What makes us whole? In The Singer’s Gun, Mandel has Anton Waker, the cousin Ari thought she wanted dead, provide an answer: It’s details, “small and personal and utterly beautiful and mundane, that make up the fabric of a person’s life.” Hinge moments may matter less than humdrum daily doings. We change tack, break free, and start over, yet we carry with us the stubborn imprint of all our old habits, the jumbled storehouse of memory, and a long trail of sensory data so familiar that it goes unnoticed. We endure.
And we suffer, due to circumstances beyond our control. This is where the doubling of the radically different nations comes in. Which is less awful, the calm and sinister surveillance state that Ibari serves with growing reluctance, or the “fracturing continent” that Ari yearns to escape? At first Ari reacts to chaos with a rueful calm—“You don’t notice the supply chain till it collapses”—but after years of “flashes of gunfire at night” from militia skirmishes that “stopped just short of all-out war,” a bone-crushing weariness sets in. As she knows, “Societal breakdown is exhausting.”
The “malevolent weight” of a tyrannical government is similarly sapping. When the secret police is everywhere, Ibari wryly notes, “anyone can be surveilling you at any time, including the person whom you are yourself surveilling.” To live peacefully, you make believe everything’s fine, ignoring “black cars moving too slowly down sunlit streets, unsmiling plainclothes agents in pairs, drones gliding quietly through the air.” At the academy where she trained to join the secret police, Ibari was told, “A harmonious society comes at a price.” The instructor added, “And we are not just the ones who exact that price, we are the ones who pay it.”
Mandel declines to identify any specific ideology in either world. No dictator is referred to in the totalitarian regime; no feuding warlords are named in the failed state. In both places, the status quo has evolved without recognizable human agency. That’s simply how it is—for now.
Ibari comes to treasure the phrase “No country lasts forever,” because “there was such hope in that.” A bitter sort of hope, but one that chimes with the spirit of the novel as it winds down, attuned to fluid time as well as fluid space. With Edna St. Vincent Millay’s “famous little poem” about burning the candle at both ends in mind, the artist Lucas Alkaitis (soon to die of a heroin overdose) reflects, “The point isn’t that the candle won’t last the night. Everything is temporary. The point is that the light is gorgeous while it lasts.”

An Indian firm and an American defence major on Tuesday announced a collaboration to support the development of India’s high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), news agency PTI reported.
Bharat Forge and Pratt & Whitney Canada said in a joint statement that they will evaluate the integration of advanced turboprop engines into a HALE UAV being designed and developed under a Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) programme.
The collaboration brings together Pratt & Whitney Canada’s propulsion technology and Bharat Forge’s engineering and systems integration capabilities as India seeks to expand its indigenous UAV ecosystem.
India’s unmanned aerial vehicle programme is expanding towards indigenous development, heavy-payload logistics and advanced strike capabilities under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
The Bharat Forge-Pratt & Whitney Canada partnership is focused on one of the critical elements of a HALE platform: propulsion. The evaluation of advanced turboprop engines could support the development of a long-endurance platform designed for sustained operations at high altitude.
“Bharat Forge Aerospace business is proud to collaborate with Pratt & Whitney Canada to advance India’s indigenous aerospace and defence manufacturing capabilities,” Amit Kalyani, Vice Chairman and Joint Managing Director of Bharat Forge Ltd., was quoted as saying by PTI.
“By combining Pratt & Whitney’s globally proven propulsion technologies with Bharat Forge’s engineering and systems integration expertise, we aim to support development of a world-class HALE platform that strengthens India’s strategic self-reliance and defence preparedness,” he said.
Ashish Saraf, Vice President and Country Head, Pratt & Whitney, said the collaboration reflects the company’s continued commitment to supporting India’s aerospace and defence ambitions.
“Pratt & Whitney Canada’s turboprop engines have a proven legacy of reliability in demanding operational environments, which is exactly what’s needed for India’s HALE programme,” he said, as per PTI.
The collaboration comes as India seeks to build a larger indigenous drone manufacturing ecosystem and reduce its reliance on imports.
India is also moving towards greater domestic production through initiatives such as a ₹1,577 crore contract involving Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE, as well as a planned military drone procurement worth more than $2 billion from domestic firms.
India is increasingly viewing drones as an integral part of its defence strategy, with recent conflicts highlighting their use in reconnaissance, strike operations, logistics and counter-drone missions, according to think tank Sphrical Insights.
The expansion is also reflected in the growing number of companies operating in the sector. According to the think tank, India now has more than 600 drone-related companies, including over 100 defence-focused firms, creating a larger industrial base for military UAVs, components and related technologies.
Earlier this year, in March, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said India must work in mission mode to emerge as a global hub for indigenous drone manufacturing in the coming years.
Addressing the National Defence Industries Conclave in New Delhi, Singh stressed the need to build a drone production ecosystem to ensure strategic autonomy, enhance defence preparedness and make the country Aatmanirbhar amid geopolitical uncertainties.
The push for high-altitude, long-endurance drones has gained importance following prolonged military standoffs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China.
HALE platforms can provide persistent, high-resolution surveillance over mountainous terrain, making them relevant for monitoring difficult and remote areas.
India is also looking at unmanned systems for logistics. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has issued a Request for Information (RFI) to procure 2,715 logistics drones for the Indian Army.
If the proposal moves forward, it would be the Army’s largest-ever procurement of logistics drones and could mark a significant expansion in the use of unmanned systems for military supply operations.
Recent military operations and conflicts have also shaped the expanding focus on UAVs.
Unmanned aerial vehicles played a foundational role in Operation Sindoor, India’s tri-service military response launched on May 7, 2025, following the Pahalgam terror attack.
Pakistan used drones targeting Indian cities, which were effectively neutralised.
India, meanwhile, used kamikaze and suicide drones, including Harpy, Harop and Sky Striker platforms, to hit tactical positions, aircraft hangars and radar sites, according to a Press Information Bureau (PIB) release.
The release said loitering munitions were used to target high-value assets, including enemy radar and missile systems.
In August 2026, India signed a $203 million, 30-month agreement with General Atomics to lease two MQ-9B Sea Guardian drones for the Indian Navy’s maritime surveillance operations.
The government said the deal would “significantly enhance” the Indian Navy’s maritime domain awareness capabilities and strengthen its “ability to monitor and respond to developments across the Indian Ocean Region”.
The agreement comes at a time when India and China are engaged in a strategic tussle for influence in the Indian Ocean region.
Against this backdrop, the Bharat Forge-Pratt & Whitney Canada collaboration on the DRDO’s HALE UAV programme represents another step in India’s expanding unmanned systems ecosystem.
While the immediate focus is on evaluating propulsion integration, the programme comes amid a broader push to develop indigenous capabilities for drone production.

You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.
Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
The PV7 is longer than Kia’s previous electric van and comes in two versions: one for passengers and one for cargo.
One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.
All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!
The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.
This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.
While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”
PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.
I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

Japan to charge rescue fee on Mount Fuji during off season
- Published
From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses.
The hearing is part of a broader push launched in April, when Trump ordered the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to focus on qualifying psychedelic drug programs for its priority-voucher program.
The order also directed the FDA to work with the Drug Enforcement Administration on a pathway for some patients to obtain investigational treatments under a law, which allows certain seriously ill patients to seek experimental therapies, and to increase collaboration with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Since then, the FDA has issued priority vouchers to three companies developing psychedelic-based treatments, one for psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, another for psilocybin for major depressive disorder and a third for methylone for post-traumatic stress disorder.
The hearing focuses on practical issues that could shape how psychedelic therapies are tested and delivered, including provider training and credentials, patient screening and monitoring, access and reimbursement, clinic capacity and the collection of long-term safety data.
The FDA said it was not seeking views on individual drug applications, the scheduling of controlled substances or the legalisation of psychedelics.
Doctors, veterans, pharmacists and therapists during the hearing urged the regulator to establish clear safety and access standards for psychedelic-assisted therapies.
Experts said any approved psychedelic treatment must include trained staff in the room during sessions, along with proper screening, follow-up care and community support.
Robert Barrow, CEO of Definium Therapeutics, which is developing an LSD-based therapy, told Reuters that the hearing offers "a nice opportunity for that continuing public dialogue" among regulators, clinicians and patients.
He said regulators and industry should treat psychedelics "like it's normal drug development, normal science, normal medicine," rather than as an unusually novel category requiring special treatment.
Just days before the hearing, senior FDA officials, including Michael Davis, head of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine outlining a framework for developing and approving psychedelic drugs and saying the agency was "meeting this moment" on hard-to-treat conditions such as major depressive disorder and PTSD.
The American Psychiatric Association said it "appreciates the FDA's public hearing and coordination with federal partners on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelics."
"The FDA's determination of safety and effectiveness... must remain the foundation for any future clinical use."
Jefferies analysts said the framework suggested the FDA was willing to consider flexible trial designs to address challenges including "functional unblinding," when a drug's noticeable psychoactive effects reveal to participants which treatment they received.
The administration's support has stirred fresh investor interest in the sector, with industry executives telling Reuters it could improve coordination between the FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration and help reduce regulatory delays, even as researchers noted that approved treatments were still likely years away.
Continued alignment among regulators, clinicians and developers on a safe, supervised rollout should benefit AtaiBeckley, Compass Pathways, Definium Therapeutics, Helus Pharma and GH Research, analysts said.
Helus CEO Michael Halstead said "the science continues to advance, and continued thoughtful engagement among regulators, researchers and clinicians is critical to advancing these promising new treatments."
