Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited New Delhi on 11 September 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit. During his visit, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and participated in several engagements on the sidelines of the summit. On 11 September 2026, Iran’s Ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, hosted an event in New Delhi where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, including Jain monk Acharya Lokesh Muni and Jagadguru Swami Satishacharya Maharaj.
In this context, a video of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bowing down is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him touching the feet of Jagadguru Ramanandacharya Swami Satishacharya to seek his blessings. Several news outlets, including Times Now Navbharat and ABP News, also reported that Pezeshkian touched the feet of Swami Satishacharya during the event. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet for blessings.
Fact: The video does not show Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet to seek his blessings. Pezeshkian bent down to pick up something that had fallen to the ground, while Satishacharya also bent down at the same time. The Iranian Embassy and people present at the event confirmed that the video does not show Pezeshkian seeking blessings from Satishacharya. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found reports published by News18 Hindi and Moneycontrol, citing sources from the Iranian Embassy, which reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a piece of paper. According to News18 Hindi, the Iranian Ambassador and diplomats organised a special reception and interaction programme at The Oberoi Hotel in New Delhi, attended by Jagadguru Satishacharya Maharaj, along with several prominent Indian interfaith leaders, intellectuals and businesspeople. During the event, Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a letter that had fallen to the floor, rather than touching anyone’s feet. Moneycontrol also reported, citing Iranian Embassy sources, that the letter had been handed to Pezeshkian by another leader and accidentally fell from his hand, prompting him to bend down and pick it up.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to social media posts by INN News (archived) and Ismat TV (archived). An INN News post featuring Sahil Naqvi, who was present at the event, addressed the viral video, claiming that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had bowed to touch the feet of a Hindu priest in India. According to the post, Pezeshkian had bent down to pick up a pen that had fallen to the floor, while the priest also bent down at the same time, creating the impression that the President was touching his feet. The post described the viral portrayal as misleading and said the footage was being presented out of context.
Ismat TV shared a video from another angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Swami Satishacharya bending down to pick up the pen. According to the account, Pezeshkian first attempted to pick it up, followed by Satishacharya. The post said that the incident was a gesture of respect and courtesy and did not show Pezeshkian bowing to anyone.
We then contacted Ismat TV and spoke to Hussain Mehdi, a photographer employed by the organisation. Speaking to Factly, he said that the channel’s staff were present at the event and that the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet is false. He also shared another video shot from a different angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Satishacharya bending down to pick up a paper.
We found a Facebook post by Acharya Lokesh Muni, who shared pictures of himself at the event standing next to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In the post, he said that he had invited Pezeshkian to host a first-of-its-kind peace summit in Iran, which the Iranian President accepted. He added that religious leaders and peace-loving groups from around the world would gather to promote peace through dialogue and discussion.
We contacted him, and speaking to Factly, he stated that the claim that the Iranian President touched the feet of a Hindu religious leader is false. He said that while he was showing Pezeshkian his magazine, Aahwaan, which is published by the World Peace Centre, an organisation he founded, the magazine fell from his hands. According to him, the video shows the Iranian President bending down to pick up the magazine for him as a courtesy, which was later circulated widely on the internet with a misleading claim.
We also contacted Maulana Taqi Haider Naqvi through the Iran Culture House, New Delhi, via WhatsApp. Naqvi, who was present at the event, also rebutted the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet. He also forwarded an Iranian Embassy statement regarding the matter, which reads, “The President bent down to pick up a letter that one of the leaders had given him and that had fallen to the ground.”
To sum up, this viral video shows Iranian President Pezeshkian bending down to pick up something, not to touch a Hindu religious leader’s feet.

How youth helped Nordqvist answer critics and deliver Solheim Cup win
- Published
Anna Nordqvist spoke in the build-up to the Solheim Cup about the European team being in a period of transition as she chose a line-up with four debutants.
Any fears about fielding rookies for the most pressure packed event in the women's game were proven unfounded in her team's thrilling 15-13 victory at Bernardus Golf last weekend.
Nastasia Nadaud (21), Julia Lopez Ramirez (23), Mimi Rhodes (24) and, eventually, Lottie Woad all delivered crucial points and gave an encouraging glimpse into Europe's future.
Three of the quartet were captain's picks, with the 22-year-old Woad the only debut automatic qualifier for the team that avenged defeat in Virginia two years ago.
"So many people said it was a bit of a risk having four rookies, but I was so impressed with them," Nordqvist said.
- 'Finally got our points' - Hull and Woad shine in European Solheim win 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Solheim Cup 2026 - scores and results 
  - Published3 days ago
- GB&I make history with first Walker Cup since 2015 
  - Published6 September
'I never felt like they were rookies'
Europe's skipper faced intense scrutiny throughout her captaincy, especially over her stubborn faith in Woad's partnership with fellow Englishwoman Charley Hull.
But she was ultimately vindicated, especially with her wildcard selections, which also included relative veteran Leona Maguire.
Between them they yielded eight and a half points, compared with five contributed by America's three captain's picks. Nordqvist's singles line-up also leant heavily on a willingness to trust in youth.
Of the youngsters tasting Solheim singles action for the first time only Rhodes failed to win and it took a brilliant performance from world number one Nelly Korda to beat her on the final day.
And the beaten Englishwoman had already contributed significantly alongside Nadaud with Friday fourball and Saturday foursomes wins that helped ensure 8-8 parity after the first two days.
In the singles Rhodes was sent out fourth, but it was positions six, seven and eight - Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Woad - that held so much significance to the final outcome.
All three delivered vital wins. "What people don't understand is they're so good when they come out on tour these days," Nordqvist said. "They just play fearless and they have so much personality.
"All of the four I had, I never felt like they were rookies. And the first day when I send out Nastasia and Mimi a lot of people questioned why would you send out two rookies, but I said why not. And they delivered.
"They delivered again on Saturday morning. And Sunday too. Mimi took Nelly down to 15. She's the number one player in the world, and she pushed her.
"Rookie Lottie making the winning putt. It's been really fun to have them and they bring out a fresh perspective.
"And I feel really old and I'm glad I'm retiring now because these girls are just so good."
'I said a few words' - Reid rallied Europeans
It fell to Woad to sink the putt that ensured Europe would win, with four matches still to be completed. Her 2&1 triumph over Auston Kim took Europe to 14 points with Carlotta Ciganda already unassailably three up on the 16th tee.
Europe were guaranteed to reach the magic number of 14½ points and there was nothing America could do about it. It should be noted, this was not a great US side with Korda, Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin being head and shoulders above the rest.
Nordqvist's persistent faith in Woad and Hull, playing her two highest ranked players together in the four opening sessions seemed a folly. She insisted stats justified the call, but the partnership never gelled, yielding only half a point.
It was all the more jarring because elsewhere Nordqvist had unmistakably fostered that famed European spirit which so often permeates through Solheim and Ryder Cup successes.
It was crucial in overcoming Jennifer Kupcho's hammer blow long range birdies late on the Saturday evening that allowed the United States to force an unlikely share of the foursomes and fourball spoils.
All the momentum was with the visitors on the Saturday night, but it was soon washed away as the rain drenched Sunday singles began.
"We were on the team bus, I said a few words," said assistant captain Mel Reid of the aftermath of Kupcho's heroics. "The team bus is a special place for Team Europe.
"I think it's where we really unite, we really get together. We put the music on and it's a special place. I'm just glad there are no cameras there.
"But we got to the hotel and we put on a song, and I felt like it changed the mood and united us. It was weird.
"We just forgot what happened, the disappointment, and we just got back on it."
Newcomers soak up Europe's unique bond
After a winless two days there was enormous pressure on Hull and Woad and the former barely missed a shot in an impressive 3&2 win over the tenacious Megan Khang.
The Englishwoman still could not buy a birdie putt on the slow greens but she never gave her opponent a sniff. Woad was equally strong and her decisive role at the end was in keeping with the spectacular start to her pro career.
There are no guarantees in golf, but in Woad, Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Rhodes Europe appear to have an exciting nucleus for the trophy defence at Valhalla in 2028.
America need to find something similar, maybe from their recent victorious Curtis Cup team. And, remarkably, that is the only one of the transatlantic trophies that now resides in US hands as the Solheim joins the Ryder and Walker Cups on this side of the pond.
In the Solheim, Europe's newcomers have soaked up the continent's unique bond. It has seeped into their bones and is best summed up by the irrepressible old stager Ciganda.
She might drive you mad with her glacial pace of play, but the veteran Spaniard knows as well as anyone what, for Europe, the Solheim Cup is all about.
"I just love it," Ciganda said. "I love beating the Americans. Yeah, winning for Team Europe, it's the best feeling."

Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to steal a UCP riding in Calgary
A surprise upset 5 weeks before referendum, and a whole year before next election
In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.
No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.
The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.
The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.
“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.
It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.
We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.
Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.
Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.
Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.
The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”
After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.
Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.
How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.
After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”
“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.
Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.
In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.
In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.
Ample time to interpret message
That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.
Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.
Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.
It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.
The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel, with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.
The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.

About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

In the quest for a seam-bowling all-rounder, particularly when Hardik Pandya’s battle with injuries has resembled a long-running television soap opera, India has backed Nitish Kumar Reddy for the best part of two years. The 23-year-old from Visakhapatnam has himself had his tryst with injuries of late, but evenings like the one at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Tuesday will go a long way towards boosting the youngster’s confidence.
Nitish, who has ramped up his speed in recent months, scalped three for 24 in his three overs as Shreyas Iyer & Co. restricted Afghanistan to 159 for eight and clinched a seven-wicket win in 14.5 overs. With it, India took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match T20I series.
After conceding 30 runs in two overs in Sunday’s opener, Nitish needed a productive outing with the ball, especially as he was returning from a quadriceps injury.
HIGHLIGHTS - INDIA vs AFGHANISTAN 2nd T20I
If Nitish stepped up, so did Sanju Samson. With 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi watching from the dugout, the pressure on the 31-year-old to hold his own as opener is unmistakable in every outing. In the circumstances, Samson responded ably with a belligerent 22-ball 57.
Once again, Jasprit Bumrah set the foundation with a first-over maiden. Arshdeep Singh reaped the rewards in the next over. Off the left-armer’s third delivery, Rahmanullah Gurbaz’s desperation to get Afghanistan off the mark manifested in a hasty pull. The miscue was pouched by Ravi Bishnoi at mid-on.
After the second-wicket stand between Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal accrued 51 runs, Nitish delivered the breakthrough as the Afghan skipper’s heave across the line found deep midwicket.
Bishnoi, who replaced the injured Varun Chakaravarthy, struck shortly after when Sediquulah holed out to Tilak Varma at long-off. More joy came India’s way as Gulbadin Naib skied Nitish to Samson.
A brisk 29-run stand between Azmatullah Omarzai and Darwish Rasooli was laced with lusty blows. Omarzai even had that tincture of luck that every batter needs, when Bishnoi spilled an easy chance off Axar Patel’s left-arm spin with the Afghan all-rounder on five. But when both batters departed in quick succession, the Afghans were back in a blind alley at 100 for six in 14.1 overs.
In getting to the total that Ibrahim & Co. ultimately did, Mohammad Nabi and Rashid Khan displayed their secondary skills. The spin duo, more than capable of chipping in with the willow, put together 48 runs for the seventh wicket.
Will such cameos suffice, however, against this Indian unit? Not on Tuesday’s evidence.

'I've turned the page' - Camara on Chelsea deal collapse

Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara says he has "turned the page" and is focusing on the Ligue 1 season after his £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Wednesday said that the government has designated the Pakistan-based Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) as a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). Shah said the move was in line with Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of maintaining zero tolerance towards terrorism. "The group is involved in smuggling of arms, explosives and narcotics across borders, apart from inciting youths and petty criminals into terrorism. Targeting India's democratic structure and the fabric of communal harmony, the syndicate also published hateful digital content," the minister said on X. The Union Home Ministry issued a gazette notification on Wednesday under Section 35(1)(a) of the UAPA, formally adding "Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)" to the Act's First Schedule, which contains the list of organisations designated as terrorist groups. The Centre said the designation followed its assessment that the SBN was involved in "terrorism and has participated in various acts of terrorism in India." According to the MHA, the Pakistan-based, ISI-backed SBN terror network has been linked to grenade, IED and petrol bomb attacks as well as targeted killings in different parts of India. The group has also allegedly paid local operatives to conduct reconnaissance of police, defence and religious sites and install CCTV cameras for espionage purposes. The notification says, "'Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)' is an organisation whose objective is to involve gullible youth and local criminals to smuggle arms, explosives, and narcotics from across the border, and through terrorist activities, pose a serious threat to the democratic system, communal harmony, and internal security of the country." The SBN seeks to "radicalising gullible youth" by providing inducements, encouraging them to engage in anti-national activities and gathering resources for such acts in coordination with other banned organisations and entities with similar designations, as per the notification. "And whereas, the 'Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN)' is promoting terrorism through violent activities that disrupt public order and by using various digital communication platforms to disseminate provocative messages, posing a serious challenge to the integrity of the nation," the notification read. The inclusion of SBN in the UAPA's First Schedule officially places the group among organisations designated as "terrorist" under Indian law. It is the 46th organisation to be added to the list. The notification also referred to criminal cases registered against individuals allegedly linked to SBN under several laws, including the UAPA, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Arms Act, Explosives Act, Information Technology Act and Prevention of Defacement of Property Act. Bhatti, 45, is a Lahore resident currently based in Dubai and is wanted in connection with several investigations in India. With greater clarity around the monetisation of UPI payments following’ the introduction of a new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework, Walmart-backed fintech PhonePe is set to revive its initial public offering (IPO) plans, which were put on hold earlier this year. Sources told Inc42 that the fintech startup is now targeting a public listing between February-March 2027. “They have an almost 45% share of merchant payments. With greater clarity on the MDR regime, PhonePe is now looking to revise its IPO plans and could target a listing between February and March 2027,” the sources said. PhonePe will look to file its updated IPO papers by the end of this year, seeking a valuation of $10 Bn, sources in the know told Inc42 on the condition of anonymity. Inc42 has sent questions to PhonePe to confirm the development. The story will be updated based on their response. Notably, the MDR framework was introduced by the Central government yesterday, bringing charges back on select UPI merchant transactions beginning October 15. The move marks a shift from the broad zero-MDR regime in place from 2020. The charges will apply only to select transactions, with merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000 attracting a 0.4% MDR. However, person-to-person (P2P) transactions up to ₹2,000 will continue to remain free. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR payments will also be exempt. A lower MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300, will apply to capital market payments, including transactions involving stockbrokers, securities dealers, mutual funds and investment platforms. The revised framework gives PhonePe, which has long been the UPI market leader, a greater clarity on monetising the service following years of no revenue. After filing for an confidential IPO in September 2025, PhonePe had filed its updated DRHP in March post receiving the SEBI’s approval for its OFS-only IPO. Existing investors including Walmart, Tiger Global and Microsoft were expected to sell shares. The IPO was earlier expected to value PhonePe at $9 Bn-$10.5 Bn, with the offering size estimated to be in the range of $900 Mn-$1.5 Bn. In its updated DRHP, PhonePe noted that UPI payments carried an MDR until 2020, allowing payment apps, aggregators and banks to earn revenue from transactions. The government later scrapped the MDR on UPI and RuPay payments to boost digital payment adoption. PhonePe’s DRHP also cited calls from the Payments Council of India to review the zero-MDR regime for large merchants and RuPay debit card transactions. The startup said a “carefully structured MDR regime” could support investments in infrastructure, innovation and merchant acquisition, while cautioning that changes to the MDR framework could affect its financial performance. PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam has now welcomed the new framework, saying that the revenue generated from high-value merchant transactions could be reinvested in the UPI ecosystem. Speaking to ANI earlier in the day, Nigam said around 70-80 Cr UPI transactions take place every day and that about 96% would remain free under the new framework. He said the 0.4% MDR would help the payments industry recover some operational costs and invest in merchant digitisation, marketing, innovation and new use cases. “Now that a limited MDR has been introduced, we hope it will contribute to the further growth of the UPI ecosystem,” Nigam said. On the financial front, PhonePe’s net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,727.4 Cr in the previous fiscal, as higher employee costs, marketing expenses, ESOP costs and one-time write-offs offset growth in revenue. Operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹467.4 Cr, total revenue grew 10% YoY to ₹8,387.9 Cr.

Women’s cardiovascular changes may begin nearly 20 years before menopause: Study
A new study found that pulse pressure begins rising in women in their late 30s, about a decade earlier than in men, regardless of when menopause occurs.
Changes linked to future heart disease in women may begin nearly two decades before menopause, a new study suggests, challenging the long-held belief that menopause is the main trigger for age-related cardiovascular changes.
The research, published in Hypertension on September 14, found that pulse pressure — the difference between the top and bottom numbers in a blood pressure reading — begins rising in women in their late 30s, about a decade earlier than in men. This has traditionally been attributed to menopause and the decline in estrogen levels. However, the new research suggests the process may begin years before menopause starts.
The study’s authors analysed data from more than 6,500 women and more than 3,000 men participating in the Framingham Heart Study, one of the world’s longest-running cardiovascular research projects. Participants underwent three health assessments over a 14-year period.
Also read: Rethinking heart risk in Indian women
Researchers found that pulse pressure reached its lowest point and then began rising about a decade earlier in women than in men. Among women, the shift occurred in the late 30s, while among men, it occurred in the late 40s. The pattern remained the same regardless of whether women experienced menopause early, late or at the typical age. By around age 60, women consistently had higher pulse pressure than men, the researchers found.
“To our huge surprise, our results suggest that factors other than the timing of the final menstrual period were likely involved in the accelerated increase in pulse pressure in women after midlife,” noted Gary F Mitchell, an investigator with the Framingham Heart Study.
Pulse pressure is closely linked to the stiffening of the aorta, the body’s largest blood vessel. The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body. As its walls become stiffer and less elastic with age, the heart has to work harder to pump blood through the circulatory system.
Also Read: Cardiac, respiratory ailments rise across age groups: Doctors
The study explains that widening pulse pressure is increasingly recognised as an important marker of cardiovascular health. Elevated pulse pressure is linked to a higher risk of heart disease, dementia and kidney disease. It may also make high blood pressure harder to control because some medications are less effective when arteries become stiff.
The findings of the new study suggest that changes affecting blood vessel health may begin much earlier in women than previously understood. Researchers said the results highlight the importance of paying closer attention to women’s cardiovascular health well before midlife and suggest that monitoring pulse pressure may help identify future heart risks earlier.

Chimpanzees are known to use rudimentary tools when foraging for food. According to a new paper in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, this learned behavior is passed down from adults to offspring through social learning. Specifically, adult chimps deliberately model the behavior, then turn their tools over to the youngsters so they can mimic the same motions.
“Receiving food and tools from experienced individuals, which we call food or tool transfer, may help chimpanzees learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” said co-author Andreu Sánchez-Megías, a graduate student at the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain in Senegal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.”
As we have previously reported, tool use was once thought to be one of the defining features of humans, although Charles Darwin observed chimpanzees using stones to crack nuts in 1871. In 1960, the late primatologist Jane Goodall observed a chimp named David Greybeard bend a twig, strip off the leaves, and use it to spoon termites out of a nest and into his mouth. When he learned of the behavior, Goodall’s mentor, Louis Leakey, famously observed, “Now we must redefine ‘tool,’ redefine ‘man,’ or accept chimpanzees as humans.” Since then, chimps have been observed making sponges out of leaves to soak up liquids, shaping sticks to collect algae, and sharpening rudimentary spears for hunting.
Other examples of tool use have been observed in various species, although the behavior seems to have evolved more frequently among monkeys and apes. Dolphins can toss objects as a form of play, which some scientists consider to be a type of tool use, particularly when it involves another member of the same species. Potential purposes include communication, social bonding, or aggression. (Octopuses have also been observed engaging in similar throwing behavior.)

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.

PM Modi's schoolmate gets land back days after meeting him as firm tied to BJP MLA backs down
Seven Eleven Constructions surrendered its building permission for a disputed Bhayander plot after owner Asgarbhai Vohra met Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Asgarbhai Vohra, an 81-year-old man who recently met his “schoolmate” Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has reportedly received a major relief in a land dispute in Maharashtra. A firm linked to BJP MLA Narendra Mehta surrendered its construction permission for the disputed plot, news agency PTI reported on Wednesday.
Vohra met PM Modi on September 8 and sought a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the dispute involving a 2,810-square-metre plot in Navghar, Bhayander East.
Vohra and the prime minister had studied at the BN School in Vadnagar, Gujarat.
What was the dispute?
Vohra had claimed that he purchased the plot in 1989 and that it was encroached upon by two firms, Swayam Builders and Seven Eleven Constructions, in 2011, both allegedly linked to Narendra Mehta, reported PTI.
“I bought the property around 37 years ago. But in 2011, it was grabbed by two builders, and I have been fighting this battle ever since. Now that I have met the prime minister, I hope to get justice,” Vohra earlier told HT.
Vohra maintained that though he had never sold or transferred the property to anyone, it was taken over in 2011, and subsequently divided into two parts - each controlled by the two firms allegedly owned by the BJP MLA.

Firm backs down amid land dispute
Seven Eleven Construction Private Limited has surrendered its commencement certificate for the disputed plot and asked the Mira Bhayander Municipal Corporation to cancel its construction permission, PTI reported.
The company cited the ongoing ownership dispute and sought a refund of the project fees. Separately, a 2015 police complaint against Vohra and his associate Ajay Dhokha, alleging criminal trespass and intimidation, is being withdrawn.

Letters confirming the withdrawal of the complaint and surrender of the construction permission were submitted to the concerned authorities ahead of the municipal hearing scheduled for September 16.
Inside meeting between schoolmates
As reported by HT, Vohra had studied at the same school in Vadnagar, Gujarat, as PM Modi and travelled from Gandhinagar to Mumbai on September 8 to meet him during the prime minister’s visit for the Global Fintech Fest.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

Sony unveils new PlayStation Pulse wireless headsets with 'planar magnetic' sound tech
The PlayStation Pulse and Pulse Edge headsets support both PS Link and Bluetooth connectivities.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Sony has introduced the new PlayStation Pulse and Pulse Edge wireless headsets, which both feature planar magnetic drivers and PlayStation Link connectivity. Planar magnetic headphones use thin flat diaphragms that sit between magnets and can deliver lower distortions and cleaner bass than those that use different types of drivers. The company launched its first planar magnetic headset, the Pulse Elite, in 2024, after it purchased the premium headphone brand Audeze, which was known for using the technology in its devices.
In its announcement, Sony says both the Pulse and the Pulse Edge make it easy to pinpoint directional cues, so that players can, say, easily tell where footsteps are coming from in first-person shooters. At the same time, PlayStation Link enables the headsets to deliver ultra-low latency audio and allows players to seamlessly switch between devices that support the connectivity, including the PS5, the PlayStation Portal, PC and Mac. That said, the headsets can also connect to other devices via Bluetooth.
Both models have integrated mics that feature AI-enhanced noise rejection to filter out background noises. However, the Pulse Edge has double the magnets of the Pulse, enabling it to deliver deeper bass. The Edge also comes with active noise cancellation and a detachable boom mic for clearer voice chat. Both models aren't available for purchase yet, but all signs point to the Pulse Edge being the more expensive of the two. To give you an idea of possible pricing, the PlayStation Pulse Elite currently sells for $149 on Amazon. Meanwhile, the PlayStation version of the newer Audeze Maxwell 2, which was unveiled at CES 2026, costs $329.

A Liberal factional figure has been left “high and dry” by fugitive property developer, Jean Nassif, but did not chase him for payments because “it’s how Jean does business”, New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has heard.
Jeremy Greenwood returned to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) commission on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”.
Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes.
Greenwood and Perrottet have said payments were for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood. Greenwood has previously described an agreement, which he said was written on a purple-pink piece of paper, under which they would be paid $1m for each Toplace development they could get fast-tracked.
On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood denied that invoices purportedly “in arrears” of almost $1m sent in a single day by Beckington to Toplace in September 2021, were “bogus accounts to cover up the scheme where Nassif is paying large amounts of money [in political donations]”.
“There’s no scheme,” he said. Greenwood, who told the commission he did not believe Beckington received all the money owed to it by Toplace before it began to pay JPG Advisory in 2022, was asked why he had not followed this up with Nassif.
“You’ve met him now,” said Greenwood. “It’s how Jean does business”.
Greenwood has told the inquiry he is a creditor of Toplace, which collapsed in 2023 after Nassif fled for Lebanon in late 2022 owing more than $1bn. On Wednesday, the commission heard that Christian Ellis was also a creditor and had publicly lodged that Beckington was owed $1.4m by Toplace for consultancy work between 2019 and 2021.
Greenwood, who has admitted to being in contact with Ellis during the inquiry, was asked if he had discussed with him “the proposition you were owed over $1m” by Nassif.
“I mean we’ve certainly discussed the fact that Jean, we believe, left us high and dry,” he said.
Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that it “is not something that you would want to openly disclose, the consultancy work you did with Jean Nassif”. Greenwood said he had “no issue disclosing that I worked for Toplace”.
Questions over Anita Perrottet work
On Wednesday morning, Greenwood was asked about his previous evidence on advice he said Anita Perrottet, sister-in-law of the former premier, gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.
Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two and a half years were her husband, Charles Perrottet’s, share of the money from Nassif.
Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work.
Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubble gum, as well as black market regulation.
On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”.
“I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes.
Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice.
After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant.
The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.”
Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?
“No,” Greenwood replied.
Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed.
Gleeson made a non-publication order over a racist message Greenwood had sent in 2020 about the chief of staff of then-treasurer Dominic Perrottet.
Ellis had shared a screenshot of messages with Greenwood in which he had written to ask to be connected with a treasury staff member on behalf of Toplace, to which the chief of staff responded: “We have no interest in doing favours for developers. All proposals will go through proper planning processes and be assessed on its merits.”
Gleeson paused proceedings, making a direction that it was in the public interest that a “racist remark” Greenwood sent to Ellis about the chief of staff be suppressed. Greenwood accepted Dwyer’s suggestion that the comment was “highly offensive”.
Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood was asked about folders shared by Anita Perrottet with him via email in March 2023 following parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe, titled “Greyhounds”, “British Tobacco” and “Catholic Cemeteries”.
Anita Perrottet previously told the commission she ceased to work for JPG Advisory before the parliamentary inquiry. After Dwyer alleged that the empty folders which were created as a “false documents trail” – which Anita Perrottet has denied – Greenwood said he could not speculate.
Dwyer later asked: “There is no reason that you can think of to send you empty folders at any time, is there?”
“No, unless you thought in future there might be a need to fill them,” said Greenwood.
Greenwood was not released from his summons at the end of his evidence on Wednesday but not is currently scheduled to appear again before the commission. As Dwyer’s questioning of Greenwood concluded on Wednesday, she put it to him that he had put Anita Perrottet “a very difficult position … because you and others, but let’s stick with you, were party to her lying to this [commission]”. Greenwood disagreed.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

Most people associate heart disease with men, and generally elderly men. This, however, is far from the real picture. Heart disease is a serious health problem in women as well, but still remains underdiagnosed and sub-optimally managed in our country. One of the main reasons for this is that in many cases, women may not have the ‘classic’ symptoms of a heart attack. This can result in symptoms being overlooked or misdiagnosed as acidity, stress, tiredness or other minor health issues.
Warning signs in women
Chest pain or pressure is common in women, but they can also get other, more subtle, symptoms. These may occur suddenly or slowly.
The following signs should be watched out for:
- Unusual shortness of breath, even without much exertion
- Abnormally excessive fatigue
- Nausea, vomiting, dizziness or sweating
- Back pain or discomfort in the back, jaw, neck, shoulders or arms
- A sense of pressure, weight or unease in the chest
Sometimes, both women and healthcare providers may ignore these symptoms or dismiss them as fatigue or digestive issues, particularly when there is no severe chest pain. But continued or atypical symptoms should never be left to self-diagnosis.
Understanding heart disease in women
The risks of heart disease can vary for women of different ages. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and high cholesterol contribute to the risk. Heart health can also be impacted by smoking, inactivity, poor diet and chronic stress. Some conditions that can occur during pregnancy are also likely to be factors in heart risk, and should be discussed with a doctor, including high blood pressure and diabetes during pregnancy. Hormonal changes may also play a role. Once women reach menopause, the risk of cardiovascular disease rises, as there is less protective oestrogen in the body.
Also, coronary artery disease is not always obstructive: a normal angiogram does not necessarily exclude heart disease. as women have a higher incidence of microvascular angina, and so, it is important to not stop evaluations.
What is also of great concern is that women might not seek medical treatment if symptoms are atypical. During a heart attack this delay can be fatal, as every minute counts.
Steps to make a difference
Protecting your heart health does not always mean making big changes in your lifestyle. Simple daily practices and regular health checkups can make a big difference.
These are some steps that women can take:
Know your numbers: Be aware of blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol—especially if there is a family history of heart disease.
Diet : Follow a balanced, nutritious diet, preferably a Mediterranean/DASH diet.
Be physically active: Walk, exercise or do something you enjoy regularly, to help maintain your heart health.
Stop smoking completely: This protects the heart and the rest of the body as well
Do not ignore unusual symptoms: Sudden difficulty in breathing, sudden weakness, chest discomfort or pain in the jaw, back or arms should be promptly evaluated.
Women don’t always experience noticeable symptoms when they have a heart disease. Sometimes, symptoms may not be obvious. For women to own their heart health, it is crucial to be aware of these symptoms, understand their risk factors, and seek timely medical attention. Women’s heart health should be also given increased importance in healthcare settings because their symptoms may be less apparent at times, and early detection and prompt medical intervention can make a huge difference.
(Dr. Saurabh Juneja is director & head, CTVS, cardiac sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. dr.juneja@gmail.com)

China criticises idea it is in 'malicious competition' over AI
- Published
China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition".
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race.
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US artificial intelligence labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity.
But US President Donald Trump has said that his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China.
On Monday, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters that "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest".
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added.
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting an agreement between the world's two leading AI powers.
An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely."
Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing.
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI.
But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday.
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation.
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently.
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and understand vulnerabilities.
In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI.
All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
Since then top industry bosses, such as Dario Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation.
"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities".
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks, saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins".
The competition is fierce.
The former Anthropic employee Coxon told the BBC that there needed to be "some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports.
It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development.
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the stakes are high for both countries.
"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments.
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."
