On the heels of the hottest summer on record and a United Nations report warning that global temperatures are likely to push climate risks to “increasingly dangerous heights,” the Trump administration overturned most of a Biden-era rule limiting climate pollution from power plants, the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions.
The Environmental Protection Agency announced a final plan Monday that guts the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which the agency said exceeds its authority under the Clean Air Act by requiring control technologies “that are not adequately demonstrated.” The agency also proposed revoking “all remaining GHG emissions requirements for power plants,” arguing their emissions “have no material impact on climate change.”
The plan to revoke the Carbon Pollution Standards was initially revealed last spring.
In 2007, the Supreme Court ruled that the Clean Air Act’s definition of air pollutants includes greenhouse gases, which cause climate change, and that if the EPA concludes that GHGs pose a danger to human health and the environment, it must act to reduce those emissions. The EPA made that “endangerment finding” in 2009.
“The Trump administration is now kicking the legs out from under the entire legal framework for regulating climate pollution by arguing that climate pollution does not harm human health or welfare,” said Zealan Hoover, a former senior advisor to the EPA during the Biden administration.
Hoover and other environmental and climate experts have not yet had a chance to review the specific arguments the agency is making to justify its actions.
Maggie Coulter, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, expects the Trump administration to make a “non-endangerment finding” so they don’t have to regulate greenhouse gas emissions at all. “That goes against really well-established science,” Coulter said. “Will this stand up in court? We would argue, definitely not.”

EXCLUSIVE: A group of House lawmakers is launching a new caucus focused on the economic and cultural impact of movies, music, entertainment and sports.
The Movies, Music, Entertainment & Sports (MoMEntS) Caucus is being launched by Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA), whose district includes Culver City, and she will co-chair it along with Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) and Troy Carter (D-LA).
Kamlager-Dove said in a statement, “America’s creative and entertainment sectors are economic powerhouses, generating more than $1 trillion each year and supporting over five million good-paying jobs. Yet for far too long, Congress has failed to give these industries and the workers and creators who power them the attention and support they deserve.”
The caucus comes amid an industry push for the establishment of a federal film and TV tax incentive as a way to address the flight of production to other countries.
Watch on Deadline
The caucus will have a broader focus than TV and film, and also include broadcasting; music; sports and live entertainment; fashion and beauty; gaming, esports, and interactive media; streaming and digital platforms; content creators and the influencer economy; literary and publishing; and visual and performing arts, organizers said.
Salazar said in a statement that the caucus “will bring lawmakers and creative industries together to better understand the challenges they face, protect creative rights, and keep American talent and innovation leading on the world stage.”
Carter said the caucus “provides a critical opportunity for us to prioritize America’s creative and entertainment industries, which contribute so much to our nation’s history, economy, and culture.”
The caucus also will focus on innovation, competition, and responsible platform practices, among other aims.
Other members of the caucus include Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC), Rep. André Carson (D-IN), Rep. Gilbert R. Cisneros, Jr. (D-CA), Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL), and Rep. Ted W. Lieu (D-CA).
Among those praising the formation of the caucus were Recording Academy President Harvey Mason Jr., TKO Group Chief Legal Officer Riché McKnight, TikTok USDS Joint Venture”s head of public policy Nicole Nason and Kathryn Busby, head of orginal programming at Starz.
Congress also has a Creative Rights Caucus, focused on copyrights, First Amendment rights and intellectual property rights. It is co-chaired in the House by Rep. Judy Chu (D-CA) and Rep. Laurel Lee (R-FL), and in the Senate by Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI).
Rep. Laura Friedman (D-CA) and Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) appeared on a press call on Tuesday to call for a federal film incentive, telling reporters that legislation is being drafted. President Donald Trump announced his support for a federal film incentive earlier this month.

F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco
- Published
Formula 1 has increased the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 World Championship.
Sprint events, which feature a shorter race on Saturday and an extra qualifying session on Friday, will be held for the first time in Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi.
The other sprints will be in Canada, Britain, Italy, Brazil, and Qatar, it was revealed as the calendar was formally announced.
The maximum number of sprints previously in a season has been six.
The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, followed by Saudi Arabia a week later, but both events will remain in doubt while the war in the Middle East continues.
Bahrain is the default season-opening race, but Australia has hosted the first grand prix for the past two years because of the timing of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan.
The 2026 season is due to end with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and while F1 is planning to complete the calendar as scheduled, it is working on contingency plans if those races cannot be held as a result of the continuing conflict between the US/Israel and Iran.
The same applies for the start of next season as F1 considers its options for an alternative opening schedule if racing in the Middle East looks impossible by the end of this year.
On Sunday, a summit involving some of the nations involved in or affected by the conflict released a statement urging "maximum restraint" in the war.
The British Grand Prix will be on 2-4 July, and the 2027 season re-introduces races in Portugal and Turkey, returning for the first time since being used as placeholder events during the pandemic.
Sprint events usually come at a higher price for race organisers but they are in demand because they increase the chance of selling more tickets, with competitive action on each of the three days of the meeting rather than only Saturday and Sunday.
Silverstone believe holding a sprint this year was a large part of the reason for the British Grand Prix’s highest ever attendance - 64,000 more fans attended over the course of the four days compared with the year before, which was not a sprint.
The inclusion of a sprint event in Monaco will inevitably raise eyebrows, given it is almost impossible to overtake around the historic street circuit.
However, F1 is selling it on the fact that it means there will be two qualifying sessions at Monaco - qualifying around the demanding track is renowned as one of the highlights of the season.
Two separate qualifying sessions could also provide two different grid orders, increasing variability.
The flip side of a sprint in Monaco is that, because of the lack of overtaking opportunities, the finishing order of the sprint will be pretty much locked in once the cars have completed the first lap, barring accidents.
F1 president and chief executive officer Stefano Domenicali said: "We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Turkey to the championship and to expand sprint racing to 10 events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special."
Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of F1's governing body the FIA, said: "The 2027 FIA F1 World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport.
"With 24 grands prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Turkey, and the opportunity for an expanded sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards."
Pre-season testing is also scheduled to be held in Bahrain on 24-27 February.

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

‘Unhinged’ Trump threw a ‘tantrum’ during Kennedy Center board meeting, congresswoman says
President was ‘screaming and hollering’ for nearly 10 minutes after a judge blocked attempts to rename the venue after himself, Beatty says
The congresswoman leading a legal battle against Donald Trump’s attempts to rename the Kennedy Center after himself said the president flew into a “tantrum" and repeatedly insulted her during a board meeting on the venue’s closure.
The Trump-controlled board voted to close the venue within hours after a federal judge blocked the institution from trying to add the president’s name to the building — again — after members proposed renaming it “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump.”
Trump, who appointed himself the board chair last year, then announced on Truth Social that the building will close “immediately,” and he won’t begin his much-touted, multi-million dollar renovation project unless courts agree to let him put his name on it.
“He went into a tantrum,” Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, the board member leading the legal fight, told MSNOW on Tuesday night. “I mean, let me just make it simple. It was the most unprofessional thing that I’ve ever witnessed.”
For nearly 10 minutes during the hourlong meeting, Trump was “unhinged” and “screaming and hollering” as he labeled her an “obstructionist” and “dumb,” according to Beatty.
“He said, ‘I think you’re incompetent.’ And I said, ‘I know you’re incompetent,’” Beatty said.
“He said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling and killed someone,” she said. “I said, ‘You’re already killing people. We’re at war. We also have people who are starving. You’re doing this.’”
Trump told her she had “never done anything” other than file a lawsuit against him, according to Beatty.
“So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room,” she told MSNOW.
“I mean, it really went there, because I was not going to let him,” she told the network. “He was there in his role as chairman of the board. I was not going to let him bully me, intimidate me, and the facts stand for themselves.”
The Independent reached out to the the White House for comment and spokeswoman Liz Huston said: “For decades, Democrats let the Kennedy Center rot as water damage spread, infrastructure crumbled, and a national treasure fell apart under their watch. President Trump did what Democrats wouldn’t by finally committing the resources and the leadership needed to restore the Kennedy Center and make it the finest performing arts facility in the world.”
The board voted to close the building for repairs after the Trump administration failed to convince a judge that the venue was in dire financial straits and could not continue to operate without his name on the building.
“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” District Judge Christopher R. Cooper wrote Tuesday.
“The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted,” he added.
In court filings, the Department of Justice has repeatedly argued that the performing arts venue is falling into “financial ruin” and rapidly deteriorating in a state of “terminal decline” — and that the president is the “sole hope” for its financial and structural survival.
At one point, the Justice Department even floated the idea of demolishing the building altogether.
But the government has offered “no proof that current or future donations hinge on President Trump’s name being on the building” and “no competent evidence that removing the Trump name would prevent the Center from fulfilling its artistic mission,” as it has done for the last 60 years, Judge Cooper wrote Tuesday,
In May, Cooper ruled that Congress made it “crystal clear” that the building is only to be named after the assassinated president, “and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial” based on a “unilateral say-so.”
The Trump administration has appealed the judge’s latest order.
The Kennedy Center had until June 12 to strip quickly-installed name plates that briefly rebranded the venue with Trump’s name, which was removed in the early morning hours of June 13.
Last month, the board proposed returning the president’s name to the building as a preemptive honor for what was promised to be a multi-million dollar renovation effort. “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” was set to appear directly below the sign.
The board was scheduled to review a new list of 10 ways to return Trump’s name to the building’s facade, but the item was abruptly removed from Tuesday’s agenda, which instead focused solely on the building’s closure.
“For years, the Kennedy Center has planned to undergo phased renovations, in which we both renovate and maintain some performances. This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate,” Beatty said in a statement shared with The Independent after the board vote.
“But donors, patrons, and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump,” she added. “Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity. That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution.”

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

H. The institute said patients from different financial backgrounds could access transplantation through government health insurance schemes.

MUMBAI: Shiv Sena (UBT) leader 
Aaditya Thackeray
 on Wednesday denied ever meeting actor 
Sushant Singh Rajput
’s former manager Disha Salian, terming repeated attempts to link his name to her death a “false campaign” and an effort at his character assassination.
In a post on X, Thackeray said he had “never met Disha Salian” and had no acquaintance with her.
He alleged that for the past six years, some people had been trying to link his name to the case for “political motives” and out of “personal enmity”, despite there being no evidence or connection.
The statement comes after the CBI registered an FIR in the 2020 death of Disha Salian following a September 2 Bombay high court order directing a probe into the case.
The FIR mentions Aaditya Thackeray, Dino Morea, Sooraj Pancholi, Rhea Chakraborty and several others among those whose roles require investigation.
Disha Salian, who worked as Sushant’s manager, died on June 8, 2020, after falling from the 14th floor of a residential building in Mumbai. Sushant was found dead at his Bandra residence nearly a week later.
The CBI FIR calls for examination of allegations relating to the alleged creation and propagation of what it describes as a false suicide narrative, as well as alleged suppression, destruction or fabrication of evidence.
It also seeks examination of the role of police and public officials in the handling of the case.
The probe followed allegations by Salian’s father, Satish Salian, who had approached the Bombay high court seeking a murder investigation and alleging lapses in the handling of the case.
The court had pointed to discrepancies in the investigation and ordered the CBI probe.
In his post, Thackeray called for the investigation to be conducted afresh without interference or political intervention and said the inquiry should be impartial.
“Allow the official machinery to conduct this inquiry afresh, without any interference, without political intervention, without character assassination, and impartially,” he said.
Thackeray also said that attempts to silence him through what he described as character assassination and false propaganda would not deter his “fight” for truth and against injustice.
Meanwhile, allegations made by Salian’s father’s lawyer that she had information about alleged illegal activities involving Thackeray and had shared it with Sushant have not been established by the investigation.
The CBI investigation is now expected to examine documents, record statements of police personnel involved in the initial inquiry, inspect the scene and question key witnesses, besides conducting forensic and technical analysis.

Australia A took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match T20 series against India A with a 30-run win over the host in the 2nd fixture at the PCA International Stadium in New Chandigarh on Tuesday.
Nicola Faltum won the toss and opted to bat and her openers got off to a fantastic start. Katie Mack and Rachel Trenaman stitched a 75-run stand in 55 balls to put the Indians under the pump. Niki Prasad struck twice, in the ninth and the 14th over, remocing Trenaman and then Charlie Knott, but Australia was largely unbothered as it raced away to 178/2 in 20 overs. Mack carried her bat, finishing with an unbeaten 83, a day after her 33rd birthday.
RECAP OF THE 1ST T20: Aussie pace too hot to handle for India in Mullanpur
A familiar script ensued for the Indian batting order. Shweta Sehrawat did not feature in this game and was replaced with allrounder Sujata Dey, but it made little difference to the Indian batting order’s returns, with the host losing its first five wickets with 54 runs on the board.
Minnu Mani and Niki Prasad, senior pros in this setup, stitched an important 53-run stand for the sixth wicket before Milly Illingworth sent back Minnu.
Niki continued, bringing up her half century too, but it proved to be a task too steep for her, India ultimately finishing 30 runs short.
This fixture also saw Tayla Vlaeminck feature for Australia A. The Victorian was condemned to a prolonged layoff after dislocating her bowling shoulder during the first game of the 2024 Women’s T20 World Cup in UAE. She made a return to competitive cricket in April in a three-day Green-v-Gold red-ball match, restricted to bowling six overs in each innings.
The express pacer registered 12 dot balls in her four-over spell but did bowl a particularly expensive 15-run over which featured a wide, a no ball and a leg bye, with Anushka Sharma and Tejal Hasabnis making the most of the pace on offer. She bounced back commendably, also removing Tanuja Kanwer off the first ball of the 20th over.

Agility Robotics has debuted its first humanoid robot engineered to work safely near humans without risking harm to flesh-and-blood coworkers. Such safety features could unlock many more opportunities to use such robots inside warehouses and automotive factories—all without requiring isolated robot work cells and physical separation barriers.
When Agility’s new Digit 5 robot detects a person at a distance, it can autonomously take precautions, like moving to avoid the person or standing still so the person can pass by without getting closer. If a person is getting into close proximity with Digit 5, the robot can even choose to squat and assume a seated position.
“The robot was designed with a complex safe motion system that can take a variety of different mitigations depending on exactly what sort of human presence is detected,” Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at Agility, told Ars.
Customers can expect to gain early access to the Digit 5 within the first half of 2027, with the robot becoming generally available by the end of that year, according to Agility’s announcement today. Agility has been retooling its RoboFab facility in Salem, Oregon, to produce its newest humanoid robot.
Agility’s leadership has consistently talked about safety as a crucial constraining factor in putting humanoid robots to work, despite being one of the humanoid robotics industry’s early movers. The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, became the first to deploy humanoid robots in full-time commercial operations at a GXO warehouse in Atlanta in 2024.
Since that time, earlier versions of the Digit robot have accumulated more than 65,000 hours working at warehouses and factories across North America. Clients that have piloted or deployed the Digit robots include GXO, Schaeffler, Amazon, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada.

An at-home wearable for the treatment of depression is now available by prescription in the US.
With roughly one in six American adults taking an antidepressant medication, Swedish firm Flow Neuroscience is positioning its device as an alternative to traditional drugs. But at the current four-figure price tag, it might take a while for the futuristic-looking headset to catch on with patients.
Worn on the forehead for 30 minutes a day and operated with an app, the device provides low-intensity electrical stimulation to the left frontal lobe of the brain, an area involved in regulating mood and emotions. People with depression tend to have lower activity and weaker neural connections in that part of the brain.
Flow received approval from the Food and Drug Administration last December, and its device is among a new breed of wearables that monitor, record from, or stimulate the brain. California-based Cognixion, for instance, has modified the Apple Vision Pro to build a communication system for paralyzed people that doesn’t depend on speech or motor control. A headband by Muse promises to improve meditation, and a device by Elemind is meant to help people fall asleep faster.
The Flow device targets the same part of the brain as transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, an approved treatment for depression that uses magnetic fields to activate neurons. With TMS, patients have to go to a clinic, and a full dosing series typically requires treatment sessions administered five days a week over several weeks. The whole course of treatment can cost up to $15,000 without insurance.
Flow CEO Daniel Månsson, a clinical psychologist before he cofounded the company, says he set out to make a more convenient option for patients. “In order to have a real impact on the problem, you need to create something that has the effect on the brain needed, but that can be used in a home environment in a safe and effective way,” he says.
In a trial of 174 people with major depressive disorder, 45 percent of participants who received Flow’s device experienced a remission in symptoms at 10 weeks compared to 22 percent of those in a control group who received a sham version. The trial included people who were taking antidepressants and those who weren’t—evidence that the device can, under medical supervision, be used in addition to medication, Månsson says.
Reported side effects were mild: Some people experienced skin irritation, headaches, and trouble concentrating. Antidepressants, meanwhile, can cause nausea, weight gain, drowsiness, dry mouth, and sexual problems, but these can go away a few weeks after beginning medication.
In Europe, where the device has been approved since 2019, more than 65,000 people have used the Flow device, says Månsson. The UK’s National Health Service is also piloting the headset.
In the US, patients will be able to get a prescription for the Flow device from a clinician in person or via telehealth. But at least for now, they’ll have to pay out of pocket to use it: $2,200 for 10 weeks and then $325 per month after. That’s a lot more than standard antidepressants, which are usually covered by insurance. Månsson says the company is working to get reimbursement from insurers.
Vinod Khosla, a billionaire venture capitalist and an early investor in Flow, thinks a nonchemical approach to treating depression is the way of the future. “My bet is, if you ask any person who's on depression drugs, they'd prefer not to be on them,” he says. “They'd like a nondrug, nonchemical treatment for it.”

'We will rule in CANADA': Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News
Documents detail year-long investigation into group behind extortion, shootings, arson and fraud
CBC News has obtained a copy of a letter the Lawrence Bishnoi gang sent Canada's "defence minister, army and police" last year claiming to have 5,000 gang members in Canada and "more guns" than the police.
The letter sent to the Abbotsford Police Department and signed "Lawrence gang from India" was released through an Access to Information Act request for exhibits from an Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) hearing for a Bishnoi associate who was ordered deported in July.
A police officer who testified at the hearing referred to the letter's existence, but the full text has never been made public.
"We are giving you a written warning and challenge. We are Indian gang Canada has no guts to stop us is that clear — we will rule in CANADA now no one can stop us we are very powerful," reads the letter, which is riddled with spelling errors and lacks punctuation.
"This is our time now Indian we have more than 5000 gang member in Canada they can do shooting for only $1000 can you stop us no way. You will see we will takeover CANADA soon."
'Tactical Guide' to the Bishnoi gang
The letter is part of a trove of documents and videos highlighting multi-jurisdictional, multi-agency efforts to disrupt the amorphous cells of young Indian nationals behind the extortion crisis gripping Canadian communities.
The documents include allegations against two men identified by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) this week for their links to Bishnoi-related extortion cases.
According to the files, Amitoz Bajwa and Sahibjot Singh were part of a web of Edmonton-based suspects in their early 20s implicated in shootings and threats against victims in Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia.
The documents include the CBSA's "Tactical Guide" to the Bishnoi organization, which traces the gang's growth in Canada from 2023 to late 2025.
Lawrence Bishnoi has been in jail in India since 2015, but has built an international organization from behind bars.
In Canada, Bishnoi has allegedly relied on his top lieutenant, Goldy Brar, who obtained a student permit in 2017 to attend Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops.
It's unknown if Brar actually attended classes, but he filed a refugee claim in 2019 which was deemed abandoned in 2022. His current whereabouts are unknown.
Goldy Brar and Goldy Dhillon
According to the documents, Brar and Lawrence Bishnoi split last year, becoming rivals.
"It is unclear if Goldy is leveraging his split from the Bishnoi Gang to take over operations in Canada, as recent intelligence indicates that Goldy's name is the one most often used in extortion cases in [Alberta]," the CBSA's guide reads.
This summer, the FBI posted a $50,000 reward for information leading to Brar's capture after announcing charges against Bishnoi and his associates for conspiracy and killings including the alleged murder of Sikh separatist leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey in 2023.
The CBSA's tactical guide names other gang leaders behind extortion cases in Canada, including Goldy Dhillon, a subcontractor believed responsible for "recruiting 'foot soldiers' to carry out criminal activities including targeted attacks and extortions in India and Canada."
Both Dhillon and Brar's names feature prominently in one of the most revealing documents contained in the information released to CBC News: a detailed ongoing investigative summary compiled by the Organized Crime Branch of the Edmonton Police Service.
'They all have to pay us'
At nearly 200 pages, the report on the probe known as Project Garter reads like a police procedural novel, with a through-line drawn from the daily reports of investigators overseeing more than a dozen files involving multiple extortion victims.
The investigation covers seven months starting in May 2025. The letter from the Bishnoi gang was delivered in mid-August 2025 and is copied verbatim into the report.
"Very soon every business owner have to pay protection money to us it is like TAX," the letter reads.
"No other way around for any business. so do not try to stop us and doesn't matter Indian or white or black community businessman they all have to pay us."
The report claims the letter fits a pattern of threats from the "Lawrence Group" and "the Lawrence Bishnoi Group" attached to shootings and extortion cases across the country.
In the Project Garter files, ballistics reports linked shootings in Edmonton, Calgary and Surrey. Police also doggedly followed social media accounts of suspects and obtained search warrants and tracking warrants for vehicles and phones to pinpoint movement.
When a Ford Mustang was reportedly stolen and used for drive-by shootings, investigators grilled one of the owners who reported the theft of the vehicle, combing through Instagram and the vehicle's "infotainment system" data to link the owner to other gang members.
'I am talking from Lawrence Bishnoi group'
The report also describes multiple victims, including the owner of a giant business targeted for millions of dollars by a suspect who verbally identified himself as Goldy Dhillon.
The victim told police another family member had also seen his Surrey-based business burned to the ground after similar demands.
In a separate incident, police warned another man about credible threats to his life.
The demands for money came from more than a dozen WhatsApp numbers — at least two of which were also linked to extortion files investigated by Peel Regional Police in Ontario. The report includes the translated text of one message left after a victim refused to respond.
"I am talking from Lawrence Bishnoi group. This time I shot at your house, next time it’s going to be you. I know exactly what your system is. Where you are what you do, I can find you," the message reads.
“Either talk to us and settle this and it will be good for you guys. Or shots will be fired at your entire family. Not answering the phone will not make this go away."
A gun with a pink slide
The documents obtained by CBC News were compiled by the CBSA for disclosure at an IRB hearing that resulted in a ruling of inadmissibility for Jashandeep Singh — a 25-year-old who came to Canada as a student in December 2022.
Singh was tied to the group through his friendship with Arshdeep Singh, a mid-level Bishnoi leader deported from Canada earlier this year after he was also found inadmissible for organized criminality.
Jashandeep Singh was accused of helping to conceal a distinctive weapon that linked Arshdeep Singh to shootings in Surrey and Edmonton.
The documents presented at the IRB included a video of Jashandeep Singh pointing the gun — which has a pink slide — to a friend's head.
CBC News has previously reported on the broad scope of allegations against Arshdeep Singh, but the police report includes detailed information about his alleged activities and an analysis of the contents of his phone.
Phone intercepts caught Arshdeep Singh talking about trafficking in heroin, opioids and cocaine and bragging about committing a murder that happened when he would have been 12 years old.
He was also allegedly caught speaking to an associate about shooting incidents in Surrey and instructing them to "go to your city and gather some weapons."
According to the documents, Arshdeep Singh has been linked to extortion cases in Ontario, including one in which he was caught on video allegedly directing others to throw Molotov cocktails at a building.
An analysis of his phone included messages containing information about dozens of vehicles which were later reported stolen — uncovering a ring in which thieves worked with owners to target cars and trucks, altering identifying information and defrauding insurance companies.
But it was the gun with the pink slide that would prove Arshdeep Singh's undoing.
According to testimony from Jashandeep Singh's IRB hearing, Arshdeep Singh came to Edmonton in August 2025 from Calgary to celebrate his birthday.
The evidence disclosed to the IRB includes videos of Arshdeep Singh and others fooling around with the gun at Jashandeep Singh's residence, before driving to a remote highway location with the weapon for further celebration.
Arshdeep Singh can then be seen in a video firing the weapon into the air at least five times. A birthday cake sits on the trunk of his car as his friends watch.
According to the police report, investigators saw the video on social media and attended the scene after Arshdeep Singh and the others left, finding bullet casings which ballistics reports would later match to one in a string of shootings at Kap's Cafe in Surrey.
That discovery set in motion a chain of police activity resulting in multiple arrests, the execution of numerous search warrants, the discovery of more weapons and, ultimately, the gathering of evidence that would result in deportation orders against numerous suspects.
Like many of those suspected in the extortion cases, Arshdeep Singh was never convicted of a crime in Canada. But the bar for immigration inadmissibility is lower than the level of evidence needed for a criminal conviction and a person can't be deported with charges unresolved.
Arshdeep Singh didn't challenge the deportation order against him, but told his hearing he was "not involved in any of the extortion, arson, any fraud anywhere."
The final pages of the package of documents released to CBC News include worrying claims about the evolution of the extortion crisis provided to the Edmonton Police Service by a confidential informant in May 2025.

The Kennedy Center Is Trump’s Hostage
The president berated a congresswoman during a board meeting, then posted that he would abandon the Kennedy Center if his name isn’t added to it.
Donald Trump has given the federal judiciary an ultimatum: Let him put his name on the Kennedy Center, or he won’t save it.
That threat came after a federal judge, Christopher Cooper, today blocked yet another effort to add the president’s name to the building. Moments later, Trump virtually joined a Kennedy Center board meeting, at which he slammed Cooper’s decision and lashed out at Representative Joyce Beatty—the ex officio board member challenging his overhaul of the institution in court—according to a person with knowledge of the meeting, who spoke with me on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal proceedings.
Later, Trump posted on Truth Social that the center’s “Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” adding, “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”
After months defined by empty theaters and canceled shows, the Kennedy Center has become a shadow of the premier performance venue it was just over a year ago. A Washington Post report this week revealed that the center’s finances are on the brink of collapse and that it could face bankruptcy. But while the institution has diminished, its leaders—and Trump’s allies on the board—have continued to push his plans forward, repackaging their oft-repeated claim that the only way to save it from financial ruin ahead of a two-year renovation is to emblazon it with Trump’s name. The crisis at the Kennedy Center is entangled in a larger effort by Trump to control what Washington looks like—a fight that has taken on higher stakes as his administration evades federal procedures designed to protect historic places from the whims of any one president.
The immediate outcome of today’s events adds more confusion. General trustees voted in favor of closing the center, and two staffers told me that leaders subsequently announced through the building’s broadcast system that the Kennedy Center was closed to the public. It was unclear if that announcement meant that employees would also be barred from the premises, according to one of the staffers, both of whom spoke with me on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Cooper issued a preliminary injunction in May to temporarily block the center from closing; if he does not lift or amend that ruling, the announced closure will put the board in violation of the court’s orders.
“The Board’s decision today reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else,” the center’s vice president for public relations, Roma Daravi, told me in a statement. “As the main building closes for urgent renovations—long overdue and desperately needed to protect the safety of patrons, artists and staff—the Center remains committed to pursuing a safe and efficient renovation through all legal means.” The White House referred me to Trump’s post when I asked for comment on this story.
Meanwhile, the latest evidence of trouble at the Kennedy Center is scattered on the velvet carpet in the Grand Foyer, after a portion of its ceiling collapsed during a storm on September 4. The incident, which did not result in any injuries, has become the primary example for leaders describing the building’s urgent needs—and, as Daravi put it, debate whether “decades of neglect and deferred maintenance” are to blame. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick doubled down last night, posting security footage of the moment the chunks of ceiling suddenly fell to the floor. “If a performance had been underway, patrons could have been killed,” he wrote. The rubble and the hole in the ceiling are still on full display, while signs, ropes, and a yellow cone caution people against entering the foyer.
The fallen ceiling has become a key image of the Kennedy Center’s crisis. Trump’s allies say it’s proof that the building’s troubles predate this administration, and can be resolved only by the appropriately recognized intervention of the president-as-master-builder. But to some who oppose his overhaul, the center’s loud publicization of the problem underscores the board’s eagerness—perhaps overeagerness—to shut down the building.
In a filing this week, Beatty’s team alleged that the center was citing the ceiling damage as justification for closure, but pointed out that a similar problem in 1977 was addressed without shutting down the center. (Beatty’s lawyers told the court that further discovery could show that mismanagement under Trump led to the institution’s insolvency.)
Either way, after the board’s latest vote to close, the next step is to wait and see if Cooper will allow it this time. It’s unclear if anything he heard today will persuade him—including a lengthy assessment of the building’s conditions that a real-estate firm prepared for the board—given his previous statement that the initial closure plans were “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” But a crumbling ceiling might just do the trick: During the hearing today, Cooper indicated that he would consider amending his preliminary injunction to authorize closure for urgent circumstances.
The other emergency—the money—is even messier. The Washington Post reported on Sunday that Kennedy Center leaders are warning trustees of financial collapse within weeks, saying that the institution could soon be unable to make payroll or cover routine bills. The alarm follows an earlier Post report on internal financial records showing that the center could face a deficit of $23 million—even amid its drastic spending cuts this year.
To keep Trump’s plans for the center alive, the board has already appealed today’s ruling against adding his name to the facade, and Beatty revealed in a court filing to Cooper that leaders had been weighing 10 different ways in which Trump’s name could be added back to the center’s edifice. “The Board seeks to provide multiple options so that President Trump can be legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the facade of the Kennedy Center so that he agrees to carry the burden of managing the renovation and provides the Center with a much required financial rescue,” a resolution that the board had prepared for this week read, though it was later dropped from the board’s agenda so trustees could focus exclusively on closure.
In his ruling today, Cooper reiterated the conclusion he had already reached four months ago. “Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” he wrote, adding that the latest renaming plan “bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”
Trump’s reaction today to Cooper’s decision—both online and before the board—underscores the bargain that has defined his stewardship of the Kennedy Center. Its leaders say that it is nearing financial and structural collapse, and that Trump is uniquely capable of raising the money and overseeing the work to turn the institution around. Today’s hearing brought up new questions about those claims, including what bankruptcy would even mean for a charitable trust organization created by Congress. If its finances are truly as bad as leaders and reports say, the court might eventually need to consider placing the center under the control of an independent receiver. For now, the venue is trapped between self-inflicted crises and the conditions that have been attached to solving them. But saving the Kennedy Center may ultimately require something its leadership has gone out of its way to resist: separating the future of the institution from the wishes of the president.

THE HAGUE – Former Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in the courtroom on Wednesday for the first time since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges regarding his war on drugs.
Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for setting up, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.
Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Duterte did not speak in court, but sat quietly sipping water during the proceedings. He stood and waved to family members in the public gallery.
“We’re happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight,” said Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, watching a television broadcast of the hearings from Manila.
In court, presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked prosecutors to find ways to shorten the trial, set to begin in November, due to the defendant’s age and health.
“It’s important this trial goes ahead as quickly as possible,” she said, pressing parties to limit the number of witnesses and focus on key evidence.
Duterte’s attorney, Peter Haynes, called disclosure by the prosecution “enormous and impossible” and said his team could never examine tens of thousands of pieces of evidence in time.
“If I had a younger and healthier client, I would request pushing back the trial by six months,” he said.
Details of Duterte’s condition were not discussed in open court Wednesday, but his lawyers have said he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning, and is not well enough.
In January, ICC judges said Duterte’s health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.
The warrant for Duterte says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including his time as the mayor of the southern city of Davao.
ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown.
Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defence and told supporters he was ready to “rot in jail” if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.

Harleen Deol is raring to go for the newest opportunity in her career: Women’s Caribbean Premier League (WCPL).
The India international became the fifth Indian to join the ongoing edition after a last-minute move saw her sign for defending champion Barbados Tridents.
She’ll share the dressing room with pace-bowling all-rounder Pooja Vastrakar and big-hitter Kiran Navgire. Meanwhile, wicketkeeper-batter Yastika Bhatia and pace ace Shikha Pandey have been drafted by the Trinbago Knight Riders.
“It’s been amazing. I’ve just attended one practice session, and then we went on a cruise for a team bonding activity. That was a really nice experience,” Harleen, for whom this is a maiden international franchise stint, told reporters on Friday.
The 28-year-old has been part of the Women’s Premier League since its inaugural edition in 2023, representing Gujarat Giants for three seasons. Most recently, she played for the UP Warriorz. She has amassed 653 runs in 28 innings overall, striking at 116.19.
“Shashank Shekhar Tapikar (Cricket Operations, Barbados Tridents) sir had approached me and asked whether I wanted to play in WCPL. I said ‘why not’. It’d be a different experience, different wickets, and different people. Franchise cricket is a bit different but it’s good for learning,” the 28-year-old batter revealed.
Harleen was part of India’s 2025 ODI World Cup-winning squad and travelled to England for the historic first-ever women’s Test at Lord’s, although she didn’t feature in the four-day fixture.
However, the Punjab player did not make the T20 World Cup 2026, Asia Cup, and the Asian Games squads. The last time she played a T20I for India was last December. Moreover, she was also left out of the India A squads for the ongoing multi-format home series against the visiting Australians after captaining One-Day A squad during the England tour in May. India won the 50-over leg 2-1, with Harleen registering a half century in the opening fixture too.
Missing out on action with the Indian setup, at A or senior level, doesn’t bother her.
“I don’t think a lot about these things. Wherever I am, it’s the same cricket that is to be played. I just want to play and enjoy, and give my best wherever I’m playing,” she explained.
“I don’t think as a player you change a lot in your technique. Yes, you can watch someone and learn something from them. But I don’t think you can change your technique through this method. I have not changed too much,” she said when asked whether she would use this WCPL stint to better her T20 game.
“If we talk about internationals, it’s not that I haven’t done well in T20Is. It’s about the combinations that fit in.”
For now, Harleen wants to bank on a tried and tested mantra during her stay in the Caribbean: going with the flow.
“ Ye sab plan karte karte banda fass jata hai (You get stuck as soon as you start planning what you want to achieve). I’m someone who takes it one day at a time. If you think too much ahead, it can disappoint you. In T20 cricket, I’m focussing on my process and not the result.”

Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled.
As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere.
Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.
According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely.
Though total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to their lowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply.
“Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year.
In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and their Russian auxiliaries with ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties.
Mali’s defence minister died in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed.
Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta in Mali three years ago.
Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries.
Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries.
In Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recent United Nations report based on intelligence supplied by member states.
Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies.
“In the Sahel, Islamic State and al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin.
The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years.
“In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.”
Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Chad and Nigeria, where they were targeted by US airstrikes last year.
The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing.
Though sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks.
At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes. Al-Qaida was also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds.
However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”.
Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022.
Instead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-old Saif al-Adel, who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe.
The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US.
In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”.
But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa, the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%, from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled.
Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.

Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
The Pro camera’s major upgrade offers minor image quality improvements — whether or not you know what an f-stop is.

That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro.
The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera.
It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro
The Good
- Manual exposure controls in the native camera app, finally
- Marginal improvements to image quality
- Photographing sunstars with a smartphone camera rules
The Bad
- $100 more expensive than last year
- Manual exposure controls are tiny
- Higher storage tiers are quite pricey
