Inside, the iPhone 18 Pro has a revamped thermal management design that allows its new A20 Pro chip to sustain full performance for longer, but the biggest truly new idea is inside the main camera, where Apple has added a moving aperture to control how much light hits the sensor. This is a big deal, and also a small deal, which I promise makes sense.
With a few exceptions, phone cameras have fixed apertures. Their sensors and lenses are so small that most of your scene is in focus even when you’re shooting wide open, and it’s usually best to get as much light as you can on that tiny sensor anyway. But there are some edge cases where a narrower aperture is helpful, even on a phone camera. It could also be helpful in other situations, particularly in low light, to open up the aperture even further than the iPhone’s traditional f/1.8. So Apple seems to have said, “Screw it. Let’s have it both ways,” and put in a variable aperture.
So there are really two separate things happening here. The maximum aperture is now bigger, at f/1.48 vs. f/1.8, and has the ability to get smaller, with stops available at f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. And while both the larger and smaller apertures do offer marginal improvements to photo quality in some cases, the differences are generally marginal.
One of the reasons photographers like a wider aperture is for its ability to throw more of the background of a photo out of focus. But the small lens and sensor on a smartphone camera don’t allow for the same kind of soft background blur you get from a bigger camera system. At the iPhone’s old maximum aperture of f/1.8, most things are in focus most of the time, and going to the slightly wider f/1.48 doesn’t make a huge difference.
A bigger aperture does offer an advantage for low light photography. On a traditional camera, letting in more light allows the system to keep noise down by using a faster shutter speed, a lower ISO, or both. It’s not quite the same on a smartphone camera that’s combining multiple frames at different exposures to create the final image, but broadly the concept of “more light = better photo” holds.
Maybe because phones are already so good at coping with low light through these computational methods, the low light gains in the 18 Pro look pretty minor. If I look closely at the detail in a shot at f/1.48 versus f/1.8, I can see a difference, but it’s subtle.
The biggest advantage might be for Night Mode. At f/1.48, the system can use a slightly shorter Night Mode capture time compared to f/1.8. That’s less time you have to try and keep your hand still and less noise that the system needs to try and process out.
On the other side of the dial, a smaller aperture is useful for extending depth of field and keeping more stuff in focus, particularly if your subject is close to the camera. If you’re taking a close-up photo of a statue, at f/1.48 or f/1.8 the back part of it might look a bit soft. Stopping down to f/4 sharpens up the part in the background.
That’s helpful! But once again, you’ll find these benefits on the margins. That’s because the iPhone’s new f/1.48 maximum aperture actually equates to about f/5 on full frame in terms of depth of field, which already puts a lot of the stuff in front of and behind your subject in focus. Unless you’re really close to your subject, most things are in focus or close enough when you photograph them with a smartphone camera.
If you don’t know or care about f-stops, you’ll still get along just fine with this updated camera. By default the aperture is set to automatically adjust based on lighting conditions, and it seems to stay at f/1.8 most of the time in good lighting. The aperture does open up to f/1.48 in dim light automatically, and will close down to f/4 when taking a group photo with someone who’s standing further back. And I saw it consistently dropping down to f/4 when I was taking a photo of some close-up text. That’s a situation where f/4 will help you get more in focus and make for a potentially more usable photo. But that’s an awfully narrow set of use cases, whether you’re the kind of person who wants to take manual control over the aperture or not.
That’s the big update, and the effect is a relatively small one. But it’s not the only camera update. Friends, in the year of our Lord 2026, you can finally change the exposure controls by yourself in the iPhone camera app. Apple has added pro controls for the aforementioned aperture as well as shutter speed, white balance, and focus. There’s also the exposure compensation control that existed before, though no direct ISO adjustment, which someone coming from a traditional camera system would probably look for. But there’s enough control here for anyone who is so inclined to get a little more creative and hands-on with the stock app than ever before.
I noticed that when I was using a manual shutter speed, the results appeared to have been less processed. Apple spokesperson Stephanie Ng confirmed that the camera is indeed capturing a single frame rather than using the typical multi-frame processing. That means you lose a bit of dynamic range, though the final image will still include a gain map if there are highlights bright enough to warrant it. That’s not ideal if you’re trying to capture detail in both highlights and shadows, but on the other hand, this is one way to get the less-processed iPhone photo that some folks have been clamoring for. It’s a bit hidden, but it’s finally here.
On top of that, there’s a new set of texture controls for Photographic Styles, with the ability to add a film-inspired glow to highlight areas of your photo, overlay film grain, or soften skin. It’s another first for Apple: the ability to make your photos a little bit worse. But you know, tastefully, Film simulation modes for digital cameras are as popular as ever, and Apple is trying to catch that wave. The recently released Pixel 11 series includes so many ways to customize the look of your photos that their camera team had an escalation meeting about it. Likewise, Samsung has added any number of ways you can restyle your photo into what you envisioned it would be. After basically a decade of pushing the technological envelope year after year, the major phone manufacturers seem to be opening up to other definitions of image quality.
If you put all these updates together alongside the less-important but completely underrated addition of a first-party wrist strap (!) accessory for Apple’s own 18 Pro cases, maybe there’s something more camera than phone here. When I got my hands on the 18 Pro last week, I wondered if I could convince myself that the iPhone is a camera camera now.
I will go so far as to say that I had a better time shooting with the 18 Pro than I’ve ever had using an iPhone camera in the past. I shot sunstars peeking out behind some leaves in Battery Park. I took it to the US Open and documented the excitement of a night match at Arthur Ashe Stadium. I took a video of a sizzling fajita plate and converted it to a cinematic masterpiece* after capture. But I never forgot I was using a phone. The pro control icons are pretty small on the 18 Pro’s screen, and I had to focus just to hit them properly. I had to dismiss a spam call in the middle of a shoot. And after a morning of battery-draining photo and video shooting, it became really important to top the battery off so as not to lose my lifeline to the rest of the world. It’s a step closer, and the moving aperture is a bit closer to that dream of a phone that’s also a camera. But it’s still a phone.
*I use the term masterpiece loosely.
Apple, Google, and Samsung have each achieved their own kind of excellence in shaping what a smartphone camera can be. So it’s interesting watching them pivot to flexibility and embracing some of the flaws that are turning people on to old digital cameras. But taking photos with one of their flagship phones still feels like using a phone, whether there are moving aperture blades inside or not. One of the reasons I found the wrist strap so appealing was that it made the process of handling the phone as a camera feel more like, well, a camera. I’m hoping for the day when one of the few phone makers who sell devices in the US at scale tries something like the Xiaomi photography kits or Vivo’s telephoto lenses. That would feel like a whole new camera experience.
Apple is also using the 18 Pro to introduce something it calls Reference Image, which is a method the company has developed for verifying the authenticity of a photo taken on the iPhone. Apple will start using Google’s SynthID standard to tag photos with AI edits, but Reference Image comes at the problem from the other direction: helping people to identify which photos are real. Apple designed a new main camera sensor for the 18 Pro and Pro Max that adds encrypted data to the images it produces, so it’s limited to photos taken with the main camera on those two models. It’s complicated and clunky right now, but it also seems to be a pretty robust system with a lot of room to grow.
You need to enable it as a camera mode in the settings app in order to use it, and then actively switch the camera app to Reference mode to capture a Reference Image. The resulting image file contains the encrypted data from the main sensor, which means it’s bigger than a normal photo — a standard 4MB image I shot of a city street is an 8MB file when I shoot it in reference mode. If you send a Reference Image to someone who wants to verify that a Reference Image hasn’t been tampered with, they can push a button to send it to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, where that encrypted data will be “developed” showing the image basically as it came off the sensor. (Apple’s metaphor here is having the original negative of a traditional film photograph.)
It’s hard to use at the moment, but the idea is that it’s almost impossible to tamper with. Apple is releasing an API for third-party developers to add an option to view reference photos when they’re attached to an image, and the company seems eager to push this into the wider ecosystem now that all of this has been announced.
There are some meaningful updates on the video side of the aisle, too. There’s updated focus tracking that uses AI to stick to a subject. It’ll even pick them up if they leave the frame briefly and come back, but in my brief testing it seems to forget about someone if they’re gone for more than a few seconds. You can also convert video footage from the main camera to Cinematic after the fact, in the same way that you can convert regular photos to portrait mode after you take them. I often wish I’d taken video in cinematic mode but I never remember to in the moment, so this is a nice update. Video files don’t appear to be vastly bigger compared to similar clips from the 17 Pro, so this doesn’t come at a big cost to your storage space, either.
And that’s no small thing. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are each $100 more this year, with the 18 Pro starting at $1,199 with 256GB of storage. But each jump in storage tier will cost you dearly — all the way up to a $2,399 version for 2TB. Likewise, the Pro Max starts at $1,299.99 with 256GB of storage and goes all the way up to $2,499 for the 2TB version.
You’re not getting nothing for that price hike. There’s a new chipset, the A20 Pro, plus an updated vapor chamber that’s supposed to move heat away from the chipset more effectively to help with sustained performance compared to the 17 Pro. I noted the phone getting pretty warm on my first few days of using it, which are usually pretty taxing as you’re going through setup, app downloads, and data indexing, but haven’t noticed it as a consistent problem.
Battery life is the eternally impossible question to answer about a phone after a week of using it. I haven’t experienced anything like a “normal day” for the past week, but I haven’t seen any surprising battery drain from the 18 Pro in my downtime, either. It survived a day of intense use during a video shoot without a recharge at any point, which is no small feat. Apple quotes a modest gain in battery life for the smaller Pro model — 36 hours of video playback, up from 33 hours on the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro Max offers a bigger increase: 45 hours of video playback compared to 39 on the 17 Pro Max. Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has been testing the Pro Max, and he says it’s been lasting more than a day, although he also noted the same early setup vibes. He also points out his 17 Pro Max battery was a champ when it was new and now can’t make it through a day after a year of heavy use, so the real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle.
The real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle
The 18 Pro I’m testing uses Apple’s new in-house C2 modem, marking the first time that a Pro iPhone has shipped with an Apple-made cellular chip. It seems that the homegrown stuff has finally cleared Apple’s quality bar for inclusion at the very high end, and I can’t say I’ve found any reason to fault it over the past week. The C2 is paired with the N1 wireless networking chip, and the system overall seems quick to jump off a Wi-Fi signal when I’m in an elevator and just as eager to pick up a cell signal when I step out. Here’s hoping it’s just as quick to ditch my home Wi-Fi when I’m in the carport outside of my house trying to start GPS navigation — truly, the dream.
One other notable update here is that the Dynamic Island is smaller. On the 17 Pro, the black bar encompassed the Face ID sensor in addition to the front-facing camera. On the 18 Pro, the Face ID sensor is hidden under the regular part of the screen until that real estate is needed by the Dynamic Island. Apple went to great lengths to disguise the sensor under a unique pixel pattern that uses black pixels to allow the IR signals necessary for Face ID to pass through. Pretty cool, though I can’t say I noticed the Dynamic Island’s smaller size even a single time as I was using the phone, and jumping back to the 17 Pro’s larger Dynamic Island hasn’t bothered me. And I have yet to need three items in the Dynamic Island at one time, rather than two, but this is a new capability that exists on the 18 Pro.
Possibly an even bigger deal than the launch of a new $1,200 phone is the release of iOS 27, and with it the new-new AI Siri. We previewed it in detail earlier this summer, and it continues to impress me. Particularly, its ability to search across email and messages all at once — this keeps feeling more and more like a superpower the longer I use it. We also noted when it debuted that Siri as an AI chatbot is much less chatty and eager to keep you engaged than the likes of Gemini or ChatGPT, which is something I also appreciate the more I use it. iOS 27 has just gone fully public this week, and it will be interesting to see how people take to the new Siri. It has a lot of work to do to earn the trust of the public that it can do anything more complex than setting a timer reliably, but Siri seems to be on the right track at least. Finally.
Unlike Siri, the 18 Pro’s big hardware update is much less visible. The aperture is hard to see without the right light and the help of a macro lens. It’s as small as my thumbnail, and it’s under layers of optical glass. Most people who buy this phone probably won’t go looking for it, and that’s fine. It’s the kind of feature that can live in the background and just jump in to help here and there, unseen, when you need it. You don’t need to know what it is or how it works. Which is kind of the point of personal technology, anyway.
So why make a big deal out of such a small thing? Is the defining feature of Apple’s new phones really an iris as thin as a human hair that most people will never see? I think two things are true at once: Adding a major new hardware feature to the world’s most popular camera is notable to those of us who pay attention to such things. But it’s also beside the point.
The iPhone camera’s most important job is to always take a usable photo, by default, no matter what. This new aperture mechanism provides some benefits to that end, and on top of that, allows a more hands-on photographer access to camera controls that weren’t there before. But the first part of that mission is the most important, and the 18 Pro upholds that mandate. Most people who use this phone will never touch the aperture control, and that’s fine. They might get a picture of a menu that’s fully in focus thanks to the camera dropping down to f/4, or a night shot that’s a little more detailed thanks to a brighter maximum aperture. Otherwise, it will feel like the same camera they’ve come to expect from a Pro iPhone.
As long as you don’t expect a revolutionary new camera experience, then the 18 Pro is what it should be: a little better than the version that came before it.

The US Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a comprehensive cryptocurrency bill backed by President Donald Trump, Reuters reported. The procedural vote failed 49-50 on Tuesday, falling short of the 60 votes required to advance the bill. Four Republican senators, Jerry Moran, Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Thom Tillis, joined Democrats in voting against it. The bill's failure effectively puts it on ice as Congress is set to leave Washington this month ahead of the November midterm elections, when Republicans will seek to retain control of both chambers. Quick answers to key questions The Clarity Act is a proposed bill aiming to create a federal regulatory framework for digital assets. Its significance lies in providing legal certainty for crypto companies, which have lobbied extensively for clearer regulations to foster institutional participation and stability in the market. The Senate's rejection of the Clarity Act led to an immediate decline in Bitcoin's price, reflecting market sentiments that were hoping for regulatory clarity. This uncertainty contributed to increased volatility in the crypto market, as investors reacted to the setback. The failure of the Clarity Act may prompt the SEC and CFTC to set their own rules for crypto, but these could be less stable than legislative frameworks. This situation keeps regulatory ambiguity alive in the industry and affects long-term institutional investments. Some Democratic senators opposed the Clarity Act due to concerns about its ethics provisions, which sought to address potential conflicts of interest for public officials involved in the crypto industry, particularly regarding President Trump's financial interests. For Indian cryptocurrency investors, the failure of the Clarity Act has no direct impact on their operations, as they fall under Indian regulations. However, it signifies a missed opportunity for a potential regulatory model that could have influenced India's crypto framework. Tillis switched his vote from yes to no in a procedural move that preserves the possibility of bringing the bill back for reconsideration. The Clarity Act sought to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, which crypto companies have argued would provide greater legal certainty for the industry. With the legislation stalled, the focus is now expected to shift to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which could set rules for the crypto market using their existing authority. According to Shiv Ram Pande, Chief Business Officer, BitSave, there will be little day-to-day change for crypto companies and investors in the near term. Spot Bitcoin and other crypto ETFs will continue to trade, while banks and asset managers can continue offering custody and crypto-backed lending. "What stays open is the question Clarity was meant to settle. Which digital assets fall under the SEC, and which fall under the CFTC, and most importantly what protections do investors get?" Pande said while talking to Mint. He said the regulatory questions remain particularly relevant following the Terra-Luna and FTX collapses in 2022. Pande added that the failure of Congress to pass the legislation could push the SEC and CFTC to establish rules themselves. While that could help in the near term, such rules could be more easily rewritten under a change in administration than legislation, potentially making a material difference for institutions with a long-term investment horizon. The US regulatory setback has no direct impact on Indian crypto investors or platforms, Pande said, as they continue to operate under Indian regulations. India's existing tax treatment, including a 30% tax on gains and 1% TDS on transfers, remains unchanged. The indirect impact, however, could be significant because India loses a potential reference point for crypto regulation. "A US market-structure law would have been a tested template for classifying digital assets and splitting oversight between regulators," Pandey said. Bitcoin is also priced globally, meaning volatility in the US market can reach Indian investors on the same day, he added. Bitcoin fell from around $78,000 before the vote to about $76,000, according to the latest update. It had fallen more than 5% as the Senate vote appeared headed for failure, its biggest one-day percentage decline since June, according to Reuters. Shares of crypto exchange Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle also fell as much as 10%. The crypto industry spent hundreds of millions of dollars campaigning for the legislation, which would have created a regulatory framework for digital assets. Trump had urged Congress to pass the bill after courting support from the crypto industry during his 2024 presidential campaign and describing himself as a "crypto president". Trump has also earned more than $1.4 billion from his family's crypto ventures. Markets are also awaiting the US Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision, due at 11.30 pm IST on Wednesday. The latest update says markets have largely priced in a rate hike aimed at curbing inflation. Higher rates could weigh on risk assets, including cryptocurrencies, in the short term. The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

The Information and Broadcasting Ministry on Wednesday announced the reconstitution of the 
Central Board of Film Certification
 (CBFC), with an 18-member board featuring several well-known names from the film and entertainment industry. The new panel includes actors 
Preity Zinta
, Suniel Shetty, Roopali Ganguly, 
Pallavi Joshi
, Pankaj Tripathi and Prosenjit Chatterjee, among others.
The board has been reconstituted under the powers conferred by the Cinematograph Act for a period of three years or until further orders. The move comes after a considerable gap, with the CBFC’s previous board having been formally reconstituted in August 2017. The board had also held its first meeting in six years earlier this month, where members discussed issues related to film certification and the functioning of Revising Committees.
Other members of the newly constituted CBFC include Vinod Anupam, Manoj Joshi, Abhishek Jain, Ricky Kej, Priyadarshan, Hansraj Hans, Supriya Yarlagadda, Yatindra Mishra, Nila Madhab Panda, Nishigandha Wad, Waman Kendre and Ramesh Patange.
The reconstituted board will function under chairperson Shashi Shekhar Vempati, who heads the statutory film-certification body under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. 
The CBFC is responsible for certifying films for public exhibition in India under the Cinematograph Act.
Meanwhile, the CBFC also addressed concerns surrounding the song ‘Shoorveer’ from ‘Mirzapur - The Movie’. In a separate post, the board said, "Over the last few days several concerns were received over the song ‘Shoorveer’ in film “Mirzapur - The Movie”. Excel Entertainment Private Limited have since informed CBFC that they will voluntarily replace the song ‘Shoorveer’ from the relevant sequence pending formalities."

During a June 2026 congressional hearing, Steiner said a proposed rule would mean the Postal Service would not mail out ballots in states that failed to hand their absentee voter lists to the federal government. The service created the rule to comply with an executive order President Donald Trump signed in March, supposedly to ensure "citizenship verification and integrity in federal elections." Stipulations in the order included the use of secure envelopes with barcodes and a demand that states send their voter rolls to the service for eligibility verification purposes. However …
… The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility in the mailing out of blank ballots, not returning completed ballots. Also, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block the delivery of mail-in ballots, as users alleged.
Snopes readers emailed us to ask about this rumor, with some of them attaching a screenshot of a Threads post. The screenshot, showing a partial profile image, read:
Postmaster General has already said there are ways he WILL block mail-in ballots, so… The minute you get your ballot, fill it our and take it to the nearest drop box, usually near libraries. Do NOT mail your ballot through USPS!
Find a BALLOT DROP BOX only !!!!
Please copy this and share on your feed.
(Received via Snopes reader email)
A reverse image search for the same screenshot located users sharing the same image on Facebook, Threads and X.
A Threads search found the original post (archived) matching the partial profile image from the above screenshot. That user presented the claim and the advice to avoid mailing completed ballots on Sept. 2:
(@kirkanthonyb2020 via Threads)
A search on X for similar text located a popular post (archived) from June 25 that contained a version of the claim about the postmaster general, without the advice to use designated drop boxes. That post read, "JUST IN: U.S. Postmaster General CONFIRMS he'll BLOCK mail-in ballots to states refusing to share citizenship and voter data with the Trump administration":
(@jackunheard via X)
On June 24, one day before that X post, Steiner was a witness in a televised hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. During the hearing, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., asked Steiner, "Yes or no: If a state refuses to turn their absentee voter list over to the federal government, will the Postal Service still mail their ballots under this proposed rule?"
Steiner answered, in part, "Under our proposed regulation, no." (The full hearing is available on YouTube, with pertinent remarks beginning at the 30:37 mark.)
In sum, this rumor about the postmaster general's alleged statements and guidance on voters delivering their completed ballots mixed truth and falsehood.
It's true that, during the June hearing, Steiner confirmed one way the Postal Service might block, or decline, the delivery of mail-in ballots. At the time, Steiner was referencing a proposed rule. The rule
That rule, which may restrict mail-in voting, stemmed from an executive order President Donald Trump — who has repeatedly promoted false claims of massive voter fraud — signed in March. Part of that order mentions of the use of secure envelopes with barcodes. It also stipulates that states that intend to use the Postal Service to deliver mail-in or absentee ballots should send their voter rolls to the service so that it can verify voters' citizenship and eligibility to vote in federal elections.
However, the claim that voters should avoid mailing their completed ballots through the Postal Service and instead directly deposit them into designated ballot drop boxes doesn't accurately reflect what the new rule means in practice. The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility before mailing out blank ballots — not when completed ballots are mailed back in — meaning that while there's nothing wrong with using drop boxes to ensure delivery of completed ballots, the reason some users recommended them was not reflected in the rule.
Additionally, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block delivery of ballots, as users alleged.
On Sept. 14,
Snopes contacted the Postal Service to request comment about the rumor, and spokesperson Nikolaj Hagen shared the following statement in an email:
The Postal Service is committed to fulfilling our role in the electoral process when public policy makers choose to utilize us as a part of their election system. We rely on longstanding, robust and tested policies and procedures, which have proven successful in the secure and timely delivery of Election Mail. Through August 28, the Postal Service has delivered 233.3 million pieces of Election Mail nationwide during Fiscal Year 2026, with an on-time score of 97.94%.
White House spokesperson 
'Misinformation and speculation'
In a Sept. 4 news release, Steiner addressed what he called "misinformation and speculation" about the issuance of the Postal Service rule and defended the service's duty to comply with Trump's executive order.
The release also featured a recent whistleblower complaint that warned of "potentially catastrophic problems in the development of the United States Postal Service's new system for handling federal election ballot mail." The complaint specifically referenced the service's new rule establishing a voter verification system that officials would use to determine which voters receive blank ballots via mail.
One part of the complaint alleged that if one barcode on a single ballot in a bulk mailing of 10,000 blank ballots failed to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch would be rejected and sent back to the state, meaning none of those voters would receive their ballots.
Steiner said the Postal Service "takes these concerns seriously," as well as that, "Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery."
For further reading, we previously reported about the many details of the new Postal Service rule, Trump's executive order and the beginning of the many legal challenges associated with the matter.

When a woman has difficulty conceiving or experiences repeated pregnancy loss, the focus often turns to the uterus, the quality of the embryos or ovarian reserve. However, hormones, too, can play an important role, and one hormone that deserves attention is prolactin.
Prolactin is produced by the pituitary gland and is best known for its role in breast milk production. Its levels naturally rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Outside these periods, however, persistently elevated prolactin, a condition known as hyperprolactinaemia, can interfere with normal reproductive function.
The symptoms are not always obvious. Some women may have irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving or an unexpected milky discharge from the breasts. Others may have no noticeable symptoms at all.
Prolactin and fertility
Reproductive hormones work as a closely connected system. Prolactin is part of this system, and when its levels remain elevated, it can interfere with the hormonal signals required for ovulation.
High prolactin can suppress the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the brain. This can subsequently affect Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), which are involved in follicle development and ovulation. As a result, some women may ovulate irregularly or stop ovulating altogether. Their periods may become longer, unpredictable or absent, making conception more difficult.
Prolactin also interacts with reproductive hormones after ovulation. This is one reason why its possible role in the early stages of pregnancy has attracted clinical attention, although the relationship is more complex than simply linking one abnormal hormone level to pregnancy loss.
The link to repeated pregnancy loss
The relationship between elevated prolactin and recurrent pregnancy loss is documented in clinical literature but described with appropriate caution. A 2025 guideline published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada found that elevated prolactin is associated with pregnancy loss and may contribute to luteal phase deficiency. The guideline recommends prolactin testing in women with recurrent pregnancy loss who also present with irregular periods or unexplained breast discharge.
The clinical nuance here is important. Hyperprolactinaemia is one contributing factor among several more established causes of recurrent pregnancy loss, such as chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, uterine structural issues, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction. This does not reduce the clinical relevance of elevated prolactin, but it does mean that a single elevated test result should not be treated as the explanation before other causes have been assessed. The 2025 guideline is explicit on this: elevated prolactin should be confirmed through repeat testing before any treatment is initiated, and thyroid function should be checked first, as hypothyroidism can independently raise prolactin levels.
The connection with PMOS
Among women with PMOS, earlier known as PCOS, mildly elevated prolactin levels are occasionally found alongside the more typical hormonal pattern of the condition. Some research has found a mean hyperprolactinaemia prevalence of 11.9% in women with PMOS, though the range across studies is wide, reflecting how variable the relationship is across different populations and diagnostic thresholds. Hyperprolactinaemia is not considered a clinical manifestation of PMOS, and the two conditions are assessed and managed independently.
Why the elevation
The causes of elevated prolactin are varied. A benign, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour called a prolactinoma is among the more significant causes and is identified through an MRI when prolactin levels are substantially elevated. Hypothyroidism, certain medications including antipsychotics and some antihypertensives, and occasionally stress or intensive exercise can also raise prolactin levels transiently. This is why repeat testing under standardised conditions such as fasting and avoiding physical stress before the blood draw, is important before a diagnosis of hyperprolactinaemia is established.
When true hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed, dopamine agonist medications such as cabergoline or bromocriptine are effective at normalising prolactin levels in most cases. Research has demonstrated successful restoration of ovulation and term pregnancy outcomes in women with hyperprolactinaemia following dopamine agonist therapy, including in cases involving pituitary tumours. The condition, when properly identified and treated, is one of the more manageable contributors to fertility challenges.
What women should know
For women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss or difficulty conceiving, prolactin testing is a reasonable part of a comprehensive hormonal evaluation. The results need to be interpreted alongside thyroid function, ovarian reserve, and a full assessment of both partners, because the factors that influence reproductive outcomes are rarely operating in isolation.
(Dr. Prachi Benara is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon. prachi.benara@birlafertility.com)

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.
She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.
At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign
As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.
“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom
Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.
“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.
While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers
Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.
“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?
According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.
Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

India is in the middle of its biggest food-regulation crackdown in years, and the Supreme Court has now weighed in. During a hearing on September 10, the apex court intervened on what a mandatory front-of-pack warning label should look like. It told the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) that its proposed red hexagon symbol for packaged foods high in sugar, salt or saturated fat was broadly acceptable in principle, but that several important details were still unclear. The bench said it was "concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children". It directed FSSAI to file a response affidavit within 10 days, addressing everything from the scientific basis for its thresholds to the size of the hexagon relative to the pack and whether a red symbol risks being confused with the marker quick commerce apps already use for non-vegetarian food. The case is set to be heard on September 28 again, which could likely be a consequential call for packaged food companies, D2C brands especially. At the heart of the matter is FSSAI, which has been issuing a wave of notices to food companies over labelling and advertising claims it says are misleading, unsubstantiated or, in some cases, simply not true. The marquee names caught up in this include FMCG giants: Dabur was told in August to strip "100% Natural" and "100% Pure" off its honey, ghee and cooking oil; Marico had to explain the "Heart Pro" claims on its Saffola cooking oil. But it's a different, younger set of companies that this crackdown seems to be squeezing hardest: the new-age D2C food brands that spent the last five-odd years building an entire identity, and raising a large amount of the VC capital, on the promise of "clean" eating: no added sugar, 100% natural, zero maida, organic, vegan and many other claims. By Inc42's estimates, at least 20 such brands from The Whole Truth and MasterChow to Pluckk, Raw Pressery, Two Brothers Organic Farms, Troovy, Healthy Master and Neuherbs have received FSSAI notices since May 2026 alone, almost all of them for the same underlying reason: a claim printed on the front of the pack that the regulator says doesn't hold up. For an industry that has spent years selling itself as the antidote to Big Food, the ensuing regulatory crackdown fundamentally questions this market positioning as a healthy alternative to the legacy packaged food products across millions of retail shelves in India. For these brands, the notices have come on top of a demand problem that's eating into growth. Indian D2C nutrition brands have struggled to boost repeat purchases, with ingredient costs and the difficulty of demonstrating an actual nutritional benefit weighing on them well before FSSAI started reading their front labels. But a lot has changed since the FSSAI crackdown began. Till now, convention dictated that a disputed claim would be settled between a brand, its competitor in arbitration or outside the courts. The Supreme Court's intervention on September 10 moves it into a proceeding that now has a date attached, and this could direct the course of the entire industry, not just one brand. Manisha Kapoor, CEO and secretary general of Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) told Inc42 that there is an expansion in the number of products and claims entering the health and wellness space, particularly in nutraceuticals, functional foods and products positioned around metabolic health, gut health and immunity. “Our Annual Complaints Report 2025-26 found that food and beverages accounted for 376 cases; the previous year it was 332 cases. These figures indicate that F&B advertising has continued to be a significant violative category of the ASCI Code,” she added. Inc42 has reached out to the several of the flagged brands — The Whole Truth, MasterChow, Pluckk, Two Brothers Organic Farms and Healthy Master among them — for comments. We will update the story as and when they respond. Where It Actually Started If there's a single moment that preceded this entire crackdown, it's The Whole Truth's dark chocolate bars. In fact the claims and counter claims of "No Added Sugar" on The Whole Truth dark chocolate bars began three years before FSSAI's enforcement wave began. The Whole Truth is exactly the kind of brand that triggered a wave of "clean-label" packaged food startups in India. The company raised nearly $83 Mn from investors including Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia India), Matrix Partners, Sofina and Sauce.vc. Its pitch has always been ingredient transparency — whey, protein bars, granola and chocolate with nothing hidden on the label. So when rival chocolate brand Paul & Mike filed a complaint with ASCI in August 2023 and later with FSSAI arguing that The Whole Truth's "No Added Sugar" claim on its dark chocolate bars didn't hold up because the bars were sweetened with date powder, it struck at the company's core promise. The Whole Truth's founder, Shashank Mehta, initially defended the claim, arguing publicly that dates have a glycaemic profile closer to boiled carrots or apples than to refined sugar, and that globally this distinction is "clear and settled." But as the FSSAI notice moved through 2024 and 2025,the company eventually agreed to change its labelling replacing "No Added Sugar" with "Sweetened with Dates," and spelling out the exact composition on pack, for instance "55% Cocoa, 45% Dates." Mehta later took to social media himself to explain the change, and, by most accounts, apologised specifically for how long it took the company to actually roll out the new labels, citing procurement lead times and existing inventory as the challenges behind it. MasterChow, the ready-to-cook brand that has raised roughly $9 Mn across four rounds, was served a notice by the FSSAI on June 19, one of 14 companies flagged that week, over "100% Natural" and "Freshly Made" claims on its ramen noodles. By August 19, MasterChow was named again, this time among a group of companies that had gone further and voluntarily removed the word "100%" off their packaging entirely, following a broader FSSAI directive that the term 100% has no defined legal meaning under Indian food law and risks implying an absolute purity that can't really be verified. The same June 19 batch of notices hit Pluckk, the farm-to-fork and functional-nutrition brand that has raised about $15 Mn including a ₹100 Cr round this year. The FSSAI notice to Pluckk was over a "No Added Sugar" claim on its mango fruit juice, a product that turned out to be roughly half sugarcane juice by volume. Pluckk cofounder and CEO Pratik Gupta while responding to our questions stated that while its product and label was already compliant with the law, the company has responded to the questions by FSSAI and they have advised the brand to add “contains naturally occurring sugar”in front of the pack, along with the no added sugar claim. “We will comply with this change. In fact, to go a step further in consumer transparency, we are moving our ingredient disclosures directly to the front of the pack,” he added. Raw Pressery, the cold-pressed juice brand that had raised close to $34.5 Mn over its lifetime before being acquired by Wingreens Farms in 2021, was flagged the same week for claiming its Alphonso mango drink contained only "naturally occurring sugars," despite added fructose. According to Inc42's analysis and media reports, through the months of June and July, a second wave had hit a longer list of health-positioned brands like Neuherbs, for calling itself "True Vitamin"; Troovy and Healthy Master, for using the word "healthy" in their branding; Two Brothers Organic Farms and Storia, for "organic" and "healthy" claims that FSSAI wants tied to actual certification rather than marketing language. Storia's case did not stop at FSSAI. The CCPA fined the brand in June over the same class of "100%" claim. By this time Juza Foods, a Kerala-based baby food brand again hit by the FSSAI crackdown, discontinued its "100% Ragi" and "100% Vegan" claims in mid-August and briefly suspended its own ecommerce site to fix its labelling. With FSSAI ordering an entire industry crackdown especially those promoting healthy clean alternatives through marketing, labelling, their major distribution channels like quick commerce platforms are also under the scanner. The Quick Commerce Trap There's a reason this crackdown is landing on D2C food brands with particular force, and it has less to do with the brands themselves than with where most of them are actually sold: on quick commerce apps, where a consumer might have relatively less time to decide purchases. In fact, quick commerce and ecommerce together gave rise to a wave of clean-label food brands and beverages marketed as healthy alternatives. Rahul Hariprasad, founder of the D2C healthy food brand Sureats, said, "In a physical store, packaging gives the consumer an opportunity to look at the front, back, ingredients and nutrition information. Online, the consumer may see only a product image, a few claims and the price before clicking 'buy.'" This purchasing behaviour has made it all the more pertinent for the brands and marketplaces to be explicit and careful in their front-label marketing claims. According to a survey conducted by LocalCircles in August, 89% of its poll respondents want any front-of-pack warning label to also show up prominently on ecommerce and quick commerce listings, before a product is even added to a cart. Sachin Taparia, founder of LocalCircles, told Inc42 that he doesn't think the logistics of adding that warning to a listing page will be much of a hurdle for quick commerce apps which already display a small red marker to indicate non-vegetarian products. Now the material change as a result of the FSSAI crackdown and the Supreme Court hearing will be a red hexagon symbol for high-sugar or high-salt items, but that shouldn't be a meaningfully bigger lift. Parul Sharma, cofounder and CEO of the D2C food brand Gladful, said that quick commerce has made the product page an extension of the pack. "That makes consistency critical including the product title, images, claims, nutritional information and ingredient list should all tell the same story," she added. So while the quick commerce platforms may have to make listing adjustments when new rules come into effect, Taparia said there could be a likely change in consumption behaviour and hence spending on these platforms. "A consumer who is buying a packet of chips ten times a month may replace two of those purchases with roasted makhanas or peanuts because of the awareness which was exactly the idea behind the rule — to move society towards healthier consumption through awareness," he said. Notably, the ongoing crackdown isn't limited to the brands selling through quick commerce either — the platforms themselves aren't exempt. In July, Swiggy Instamart was hit with nine separate FSSAI notices over products sold through the platform, alleging that some had reached customers rotten, spoiled or past their expiry date. One of the brands named was Swiggy's own private label, NOICE, whose eggs, the regulator said, were being sold under a name not covered by Instamart's existing FSSAI licence. Instamart is not the only platform under scrutiny. In August, Zepto had a Bengaluru dark store sealed over food safety violations, an enforcement action aimed at the platform's own facility rather than at any brand listed on it. But right now the brands caught in FSSAI's crosshairs, which almost owe their existence to the quick commerce platforms, have been forced into a course correction. "That means D2C brands will need to think about the entire digital shelf — product images, titles, descriptions, nutritional information, claims and warnings — with the same seriousness as physical packaging," the Sureats CEO said. "When consumers can compare products instantly, brands will increasingly need to win on what the product actually contains rather than simply how well it is marketed," he added. Karthik Srinivasan, a communications strategy consultant known for his social media commentary on brand messaging, argued that consumer awareness over the last few years has substantially grown and impulse-driven quick commerce shopping should not lead the brands to mis-sell or mislead consumers under the guise of healthy alternatives. "Quick commerce is about faster delivery, but that doesn't mean customers make impulsive purchases of new products without doing any research. Otherwise, we wouldn't have people seeking specific details on sugar content, fat content, protein. Customers have always been discerning, and they also look at larger trends in health whether it is high-fibre or high-protein. That is hardly justification for brands to skimp on truth and mis-sell their products," he said. ASCI’s Kapoor noted that as food advertising increasingly moves across digital formats, brands need to ensure that their claims remain substantiated and that important qualifications are not lost. “Even if consumers scroll past information quickly, it is the brand’s responsibility to make sure that adequate information required to be provided to the consumer under food laws is present clearly,” she added. A Reckoning For Clean Label The larger question that looms over these clean-label new-age brands is that some of these marketing claims have also unearthed formulations which consumers likely were not aware of — natural sugars addition, no verifiable means to claim 100% purity or vegan/organic sourcing among others. So far the response to this crackdown has been an instantaneous change in the labelling and marketing of products. For instance, The Whole Truth swapped "No Added Sugar" for "Sweetened with Dates." MasterChow dropped "100%" from its ramen packaging. But for an entire industry carved out of a genuine need of "healthy, clean-label" products in India, would this be enough especially when the brands claimed themselves as manufacturing products for the above consumer cohort? The Sureats CEO said that the industry will have to rethink beyond the packaging claims and shift the focus to transparency in terms of formulations too. "This could actually create an opportunity for brands that genuinely have better nutritional profiles. Instead of competing only through claims such as 'healthy' or 'natural,' brands can differentiate through transparent ingredient lists, meaningful nutritional advantages and, where commercially viable, probably reformulation too," he added. "Clean label cannot simply be a marketing claim. It has to show up in the ingredients, formulation and nutritional profile. The answer is not finding safer words for the same promise. It is building products that can stand on their ingredients and nutrition, and letting the marketing follow," the Gladful founder said. She added that brands need to have stronger internal checks around how claims are developed, reviewed and substantiated paired with a return to basics with consumers "Show the ingredients, show the nutrition, explain the choices, and give consumers a reason to trust you again," Gladful’s Sharma added. "Beyond that: does the verbiage on the pack and marketing collaterals mislead or overclaim? These are basic checks that didn't get enough pushback earlier, but now they do," Srinivasan added. ASCI’s Kapoor argues that most D2C brands tend to have lower than required evidence for the claims they make. “They tend to present study results in exaggerated ways that mislead consumers about the product delivery. D2C brand marketing teams may not always be well trained and familiar with the nuances of food regulation, but ignorance of the law is not a legitimate excuse. This is a training gap they need to bridge proactively given the nature of claims they make and the seriousness of the category in which they operate,” she told Inc42. The Accountability Question Amidst the heated debate on front-of-pack labelling and revisiting formulations, Vishal Sharma, founder and principal consultant at Legal Defence Advisors (LDA), said that if a company doesn't comply, or the claim is serious enough, it can escalate into licensing action or a penalty proceeding for misbranding or misleading advertising. "We've already seen the regulator go further than a notice this year. In August, it invoked its power to actually stop a company from selling a product, in Dabur's case, though that particular order has since been stayed by the Delhi High Court for want of a proper hearing," LDA’s Sharma said. The escalation is not confined to the FMCG names. Storia, among the brands FSSAI pulled up in June, drew a CCPA penalty the same month — a D2C brand moving from a notice to a fine rather than to a relabelling, which is the outcome most of the brands in this story are still betting they can avoid. Correcting the label, he added, doesn't retrospectively clean the slate for the brand. "When an adjudicating officer decides on a penalty, the law requires them to weigh things like whether the company gained financially from the claim, how widespread the harm was, and whether it was a one-off or a repeated pattern. A quick correction can work in a brand's favour at that stage, but it doesn't erase the fact that a violation occurred in the first place," he added. Srinivasan places the responsibility across the entire chain that produces a claim, not on any one function. "It’s also on the founders who passionately market their own products on their personal handles as much as the over-eager marketing and creative teams who are desperately looking for the next attractive word or phrase to convince buyers in a very crowded market," he said. His test for founders wanting to get ahead of a notice is less about legal review than personal accountability. "Would they feed that product daily to their own five-year-old child, or their 77-year-old grandmother? What would an 11-year-old understand when she reads the label — would she be able to comprehend what the product is good for and not good for? Would a grandmother be able to comprehend it?" he said. Those questions are not specific to food. The vocabulary which the FSSAI has targeted is the same one that built India's D2C beauty and personal care brands. Clean beauty has been THE pitch for a decade's worth of brands. Instead of the FSSAI, these brands are being governed by state-level food and drug administrations such as the one in Maharashtra. Brands will be tested on their compliance with consumer protection law and health regulations when it comes to their product claims, rather than food safety and hygiene laws. Whether this is a just an issue about untested and fake claims made by manufacturers or a real change in how retail food manufacturing, it is not just about one retail company, brand or category, this could change the course of the new-age retail industry as a whole and raise the entry barrier for new D2C brands. The European Union has announced it will restrict children’s access to social media across member states in a bid to free them from what President of the Commission Ursula von der Leyen described as the “capture [of] their attention, their focus, their minds” by the platforms.
The total ban on social media for children under 13 was announced in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech, where von der Leyen set out the Union’s priorities for the year ahead.
It’s part of an EU Kids Act, which the Commission will unveil fully on Thursday. Children aged 13 to 15 will also not be allowed personal social media accounts but will be able to access social media through mini accounts set up and supervised by parents and guardians, with limited features, for one hour per day. Platforms will also have safe design obligations for users up to 18, with the Union planning to tackle addictive design further in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act in Autumn.
“I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree,” von der Leyen told the European Parliament. “We do not have to accept addictive features, we do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content, we do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for-AI generated sexualised images,” she added. “Europe has the power to act; it is us who decide the rules, not Big Tech.”
The EU was largely expected to follow other countries in restricting children’s access to social media, which von der Leyen said has been responsible for sleep loss, anxiety, self harm, and even the deaths of European children. 17 of the bloc’s 27 member states are already negotiating or preparing draft legislation to protect minors online, including by setting out a minimum age to access certain services. Among those is France, whose top court last month struck down a ban on social media for under-15s because it infringed upon freedom of expression.
“Cleaning up that mess, getting everyone on the same page, then running through the EU legislative process,” will probably take until 2029, expects Ashurst Perkins Coie technology lawyer Arnav Joshi. Still, he believes companies will welcome the clarity and simplicity provided by a single set of EU-wide rules. The tiered approach is designed to placate any judicial challenges by being proportionate—a rare example of where “the EU law, by not introducing a blanket ban, is perhaps even a little bit more permissive than others,” he told WIRED, referencing the sweeping social media bans in the UK and Australia.
But the measures still force oversight on both guardians and the social media platforms themselves, which could risk privacy infringements. Parental monitoring could be “problematic” says Joshi, who advises global technology companies on children’s online safety, warning: “anything that has deep dive, God-mode style parental access can have a bit of a chilling effect on how children actually use that service and could have issues in terms of their own right to privacy.”
The European bloc will also face similar challenges to other countries in effectively enforcing the age limits. Children in Australia have widely been able to circumvent the country’s under-16s ban on social media access. "A key issue is how to carry out the age checks and it’s not straightforward,” Joanna Conway, digital regulation partner at law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, told WIRED. Making age checks accurate, without infringing on privacy rights or harming user experience, is a challenge, she added. The EU introduced an app earlier in the year so members can prove they are over 18 and access adult-restricted sites, which it says can be applied to other age groups.
Von der Leyen also acknowledged that Europeans are more widely worried by the “dizzying” speed of technology and its impact on their livelihoods and society. Artificial intelligence “has not yet delivered” value in the real economy—like factories, hospitals, and energy grids—she added, teasing initiatives that will be announced in November to address these concerns across health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, and defence and space. She also referenced the upcoming Quality Jobs Act, designed to ensure AI helps develop skills, improve the quality of jobs, and “give workers a fair chance,” and said she would invite the main artificial intelligence frontier labs for a discussion on how the EU can support industry efforts to pace the frontier.

Japan’s average retail price of pork loin this month came to ¥293 per 100 grams, hitting the highest level since the survey began in August 2003, the agriculture ministry has said.
Prices for a pack of 10 eggs averaged ¥309 in the latest reporting month, matching a record high marked in March, May and June, according to the ministry data released Tuesday.
Demand for domestic pork is increasing amid higher prices of imported produce, reflecting the yen’s weakening and increasing pork demand worldwide.
The rise in egg prices was attributable to the lingering impact from the spread of avian influenza last year and the start of sales of seasonal products using eggs at fast food chains.
The monthly price survey covers a total of 470 stores — 10 each in the country’s 47 prefectures. The latest survey was conducted from Sept. 7 to 9.
